answers.question: What does Scrapr (The Kabadiwala) charge partner kabadiwalas (subscription or commission), and how many of its kabadiwalas are active in Bengaluru? Is ScrapUncle actually operating in Bengaluru or only Delhi NCR?
answers.answer: "Scrapr" is The Kabadiwala's partner platform (operator ASAR Green Kabadi Pvt. Ltd.; terms dated 20 May 2024): in metros including Bengaluru the company does not run its own pickups but routes household bookings to local kabadiwalas through the "TKW Partner - Buy Kabad" app (Play id app.scrapr.partner, 10K+ installs, updated 18 Aug 2026), as co-founder Anurag Asati described on 23 Sep 2025. Partners pay a lead-based subscription, not a commission: the pricing page (read 29 Sep 2026) gives 15 free leads on joining, then Starter Rs 49/month for 5 leads (struck from Rs 99), Pro Rs 199/month for 35 leads (from Rs 399) and Unlimited Rs 499/month (from Rs 999) for unlimited leads, the last requiring 50 leads or Rs 20,000 of business value and being online 6 hours a day (7am-8pm) or a refund applies; leads count only once accepted, and an optional Rs 299 onboarding kit (t-shirt, cap, board and poster designs) adds 10 free leads. No percentage cut of the scrap value is published; Scrapr's terms instead let the partner add "collection charges" and "surge" fees to the household and reserve the right to add membership or per-order fees later. The Bengaluru headcount is not public: Scrapr claims "5000+ Kabadiwalas" across 11 cities and its Bangalore page lists 24 localities (Koramangala, Indiranagar, Jayanagar, Domlur, KR Puram, Kalyan Nagar, Jakkur, Begur, Haralur and others) with no partner names or counts, and the partner app's 10K+ national installs imply an active base per city in the dozens to low hundreds, not thousands. Best default until tested: 30-100 active partner kabadiwalas in Bengaluru, concentrated in those 24 areas. ScrapUncle (Swapeco Solutions Pvt. Ltd., Okhla, New Delhi) is still officially a Delhi NCR service: its Play listing updated 19 Sep 2026 says the service is "currently available in most parts of Delhi NCR", and its Rs 22 Cr pre-Series A (Inc42, 28 Jan 2026; 300K+ pickups, 20 Mn kg) was for Delhi NCR plus "the foundation" for other metros. But it has since soft-launched in Bengaluru: scrapuncle.com/rates now carries separate Delhi NCR and Bengaluru rate cards, and Deccan Herald's Bengaluru guide (5 Aug 2026) lists ScrapUncle among live doorstep services with free pickup above a 10 kg minimum and rates shown in the app. Treat ScrapUncle as an early-stage Bengaluru competitor for households (own gig pickers, instant payment, 10 kg minimum), not a Delhi-only one; its Bengaluru coverage and volume are unknown.
answers.decision: Keep kabadiwala tools free for the pilot (Scrapr has set the market at Rs 49-499/month for leads, so a later fee under Rs 49 or a per-accepted-lead charge is defensible), and position against ScrapUncle on Kannada, no 10 kg minimum, and letting the household choose the buyer.
answers.whoToAsk: Book 5 test pickups through The Kabadiwala app in different Bengaluru areas and count distinct partner names; book one ScrapUncle pickup in a pilot ward to confirm Bengaluru service and coverage; email contact@scrapr.app for partner counts.

answers.question: What do Recykal.Market and Attero's MetalMandi charge small aggregators, and what minimum lot sizes and payment terms do they set? Do the Android apps of The Kabadiwala, ScrapUncle, MetalMandi and Recykal offer Indian languages?
answers.answer: Recykal.Market (Rapidue Technologies) publishes no fee schedule: its Terms of Use say "Recykal shall raise invoices towards the platform fees to the users" without an amount, and Forbes India (2 Sep 2021) only says it "makes a marketplace fee", so the fee percentage is an open item. Its terms make lot size and credit negotiable per trade ("pricing, minimum order quantities (MOQs), credit period ... may be mutually negotiated"), with payment "within the credit period agreed at the time of order (7, 15, 30 days, or as otherwise mutually agreed)", the buyer required to fund escrow before the seller dispatches, buyer QC at delivery with deductions by debit note, and full rejection sending the truck back at the seller's cost; marketing pages promise "payment before the truck returns" and "Payment Insurance". Sellers must complete KYC with GST certificate, PAN and bank details (GSTIN is a mandatory field on the electronics sign-up), which shuts out unregistered kabadiwalas; scale claims are 10,000+ verified businesses, 3 Mn+ tonnes and Rs 2,500 Cr+ traded (recykal.market) and 5,000+ aggregators and 675+ recyclers (Analytics India Mag, 20 Mar 2026). Attero's MetalMandi charges sellers nothing: its FAQ (published 26 Mar 2026) says "MetalMandi charges zero commission" and the app promises "zero transaction fees", because Attero has so far been the sole buyer and earns on the spread (Financial Express, 13 Apr 2026). Attero told CNBC-TV18 (13 Apr 2026) it will open the platform to third-party buyers and then monetise "a certain percentage of the traded value"; no percentage is set yet. MetalMandi publishes no minimum lot ("small or bulk quantities"), pays by NEFT/RTGS "after pickup and inspection" with no stated timeline, and requires one-time KYC (Aadhaar/PAN) plus GST for dealers and businesses; it reports 2 lakh+ downloads, 1.1 lakh registered users, about 50,000 monthly actives and about 15,000 t/month across 100+ cities (Tribune 7 Apr 2026; FE 13 Apr 2026), having launched in Jan 2025 (Economic Times, 15 Jan 2025). On languages, none of the four Android apps advertises an Indian language: the Play descriptions of The Kabadiwala (updated 18 Sep 2026), ScrapUncle (19 Sep 2026), MetalMandi (11 Sep 2026) and Recykal.Market for Sellers (15 Sep 2026) are English-only, none has a Hindi-localised store listing, and the same apps' iOS builds declare English as their only language in App Store metadata. MetalMandi's listing does use Hindi trade words in Latin script (laal maal, rassa, purja, botal), which is the closest any of them gets; Google Play does not publish in-app language lists, so a hidden in-app language toggle cannot be fully excluded without installing each app.
answers.decision: For pilot business trades default to zero platform fee (matching MetalMandi and undercutting Recykal's invoiced fee), no hard minimum lot below yard level (a soft 100 kg floor), simulated escrow funded before dispatch with 0/7/15-day settlement options mirroring Recykal's 7/15/30, and a debit-note QC deduction flow; ship Kannada, Hindi and English UI at launch, since no competitor does.
answers.whoToAsk: Recykal sales (+91 77999 96255) for the actual platform-fee percentage and typical credit days; 3 Bengaluru aggregators already selling on Recykal or MetalMandi for real settlement times; a 15-minute install of the four apps on a Kannada- and Hindi-locale phone to confirm there is no in-app language switch.

answers.question: Will BEE add a material-recovery or recycling methodology to the Indian Carbon Market offset mechanism (waste is a listed sector), and what floor and forbearance prices has CERC approved for carbon credit certificates? How many offset methodologies are approved today?
answers.answer: BEE's official list (last updated 7 July 2026) shows 12 approved offset methodologies; the only waste-sector ones are BM WA03.001 Landfill methane recovery, BM WA03.002 Flaring or use of landfill gas and BM WA03.003 Production of compressed biogas, plus a composting tool (BM-T-013). There is no material-recovery, MRF or recycling methodology, none has been published for comment, and BEE's carbon-market page lists no route for a private party to propose one (it only shows public-comment notices on draft procedures and PDDs). 'Waste handling and disposal' is a Phase I sector, so a recycling methodology is legally possible, and BEE has so far adapted CDM methodologies (the CDM already has AMS-III.AJ for recycling, which Verra's VMR0007 builds on), but a 13 Feb 2026 LiveLaw analysis points out the obstacle: the SWM Rules 2026 (in force 1 April 2026) make segregation and recycling mandatory, which collides with the CCTS regulatory-surplus rule, so BEE would have to resolve that before crediting municipal recycling. On prices: CERC notified the CERC (Terms and Conditions for Purchase and Sale of Carbon Credit Certificates) Regulations, 2026 on 27 February 2026 (gazetted 3 March 2026); CCCs trade monthly on power exchanges within a floor price and forbearance price that CERC approves on a proposal from BEE, and the band is written for the compliance mechanism. As of the latest dated commentary we could open (Reclimatize 7 April 2026, Mondaq 12 May 2026, rsustain 27 May 2026) BEE had not proposed and CERC had not approved any rupee values; analyst guesses range Rs 400–1,200/tCO2e (rsustain) and Rs 600–1,200/tCO2e (Reclimatize), and these are not official. Offset projects must have started on or after 1 January 2025, so an October 2026 pilot would qualify on timing if a methodology ever appears. Open item: no public figure for a CCC floor or forbearance price exists today.
answers.decision: Do not put CCTS carbon revenue in the pilot model. Record tonnes by material, source ward and destination from day one so the data is methodology-ready, check BEE's methodologies page monthly, and file a public comment asking BEE to adapt AMS-III.AJ once the SWM 2026 conflict is clarified.
answers.whoToAsk: BEE Carbon Market (offset mechanism cell) on whether a recycling methodology is planned and how to propose one; CERC / BEE on when the floor and forbearance prices will be notified.

answers.question: Can a tonne of plastic that generated a CPCB EPR certificate also earn a Verra plastic credit (WRC/WCC), given PWRM0001's additionality test? Is paper or cardboard creditable under any active methodology (VMR0007, GS 448)?
answers.answer: No for the same tonne: Verra's 12 August 2024 clarification to PWRM0001 v1.1 says 'under no circumstances may a project generate Waste Collection Credits for amounts of collected plastic that have already been directly financed through a relevant EPR scheme', and the regulatory-surplus step (Step 1) requires every mandatory EPR scheme in the region to be listed even when the collector is not the obligated party. In India the EPR certificate is generated by the registered recycler for each tonne recycled (against GST invoices of recycled product sales) and sold to PIBOs, so a tonne that produced a certificate has been EPR-financed and is out; PWRM0002 (recycling credits) applies the same test, so a recycler cannot stack a WRC on a certificate either. Beyond that, collection of any material type covered by a mandatory EPR scheme is treated as non-additional unless the scheme is shown to be 'not fully effective' (compliance or collection rate below 50% in the region, from official or third-party data) or the project exceeds a specific mandated threshold; CPCB-reported figures (17 million tonnes of certificates since 2022 against about 3.8 million tonnes of plastic waste generated a year, Down To Earth 1 Sept 2026) make a below-50% showing hard for packaging categories I–III, whose 2026-27 recycling targets are 70%/50%/50%. Plastics outside the packaging EPR (household durables, PVC pipe, toys) and any tonne the recycler does not certify remain candidates, but the VVB decides. Paper and cardboard are not eligible under the Plastic Program at all (only PWRM0001 and PWRM0002 are active, both plastic-only). They are creditable as carbon (not plastic) credits under Verra's VMR0007 v1.0 (4 Sept 2023), a revision of CDM AMS-III.AJ that covers paper/cardboard, plastics, glass and metals, credits avoided landfill methane where the baseline is decay in a dumpsite and applies a 30% discount to virgin-material displacement; AMS-III.AJ is a small-scale methodology (60,000 tCO2e/yr cap). Gold Standard 448 v1.0 (2 May 2025) covers only metals, alloys and minerals, so paper is not creditable there, and it too excludes recycling mandated by law unless non-enforcement above 50% is documented. Open item: the tCO2e per tonne of paper under AMS-III.AJ default factors was not extracted, so revenue per tonne cannot be stated.
answers.decision: Treat EPR certificates and Verra plastic credits as mutually exclusive per tonne; route packaging plastics to EPR-certified recyclers and keep the certificate value, and only consider plastic credits for non-packaging or uncertified streams after a VVB opinion. Paper and cardboard: track tonnes and destinations for a possible VMR0007 carbon project later, not for plastic credits.
answers.whoToAsk: A Verra-approved plastic VVB (SCS Global Services or Control Union) for a written view on whether Bengaluru's EPR scheme is 'fully effective' for each material type; CPCB EPR portal data for regional compliance rates.

answers.question: Should Luma.Green be the project proponent of a Verra grouped plastic project or partner with a developer such as Hasiru Dala Innovations or Plastics For Change? What does verification cost in India and how many tonnes a year does a plastic-credit project need to pay for itself? What revenue share do collector programmes (Plastic Bank, others) pay collectors, and will a verifier accept ward-level household location as evidence of source?
answers.answer: Partner, do not be proponent in the pilot. Verra's Plastic Standard v1.0 (10 Feb 2021) does allow a grouped project: geographic areas drawn as geodetic polygons, new kabadiwala or Saathi 'instances' added at each verification if they meet pre-set eligibility criteria and the proponent holds ownership evidence from each instance's start date, a 7-year crediting period renewable twice (or 10 years fixed), verification at least every three years, and validation can be done together with first verification. But being proponent means carrying the additionality file (see Q2: EPR-covered packaging is probably non-additional in Bengaluru) and the audit bill, and Verra has only 36 registered plastic projects in 20 countries after five years (11 Mar 2026), with India listings limited to JB Ecotex/EnKing in Surat (WRC, Sept 2022), Green Worms/rePurpose 'Hara Kal' in Kerala and Recykal 'Clean Kedarnath' (Nov 2022); we found no Verra project for Hasiru Dala Innovations or Plastics For Change, whose model is WFTO fair-trade and OBP-certified supply (HDI–PFC–The Body Shop, 64 t PET), while rePurpose Global already runs 'Project Sada Shakti' in Bengaluru with Saahas Zero Waste (Oct 2024). Verra's own fees are small: USD 500 account opening plus 500/yr, registration at USD 5 per estimated annual tonne capped at 7,500 (credited against levies), and an issuance levy of USD 1 for the first 100 credits, 3 for 101–500, 5 for 501–1,000, 7 for 1,001–2,500, 10 for 2,501–5,000; that works out to about USD 900/yr at 200 t, 4,300/yr at 1,000 t and 19,800/yr at 3,000 t, i.e. under USD 7 a tonne against 2022–24 price indications of USD 200–800 per credit. The real gate is the VVB audit (validation plus each verification) and MRV staff, which Verra does not track and no VVB publishes for India, so the break-even tonnage cannot be stated honestly; the rule is tonnes × (net credit price − collector premium) must cover VVB fees + MRV cost + Verra fees, and the missing number is a written VVB quote. Collector economics are thin in public: Plastic Bank pays local junk-shop rate plus a bonus, reported as USD 0.16/kg on top of about USD 0.34/kg for PET in the Philippines (The Walrus, Apr 2025, updated Dec 2025) with incomes up 20–35%, while Plastic Bank's own help centre cites a USD 0.01/kg bonus; rePurpose sells credits at about USD 0.50/kg (EIB, Feb 2022) but does not publish the worker share; Plastics For Change offers a guaranteed minimum price plus a fair-trade premium to a community fund with no published percentage. On evidence of source: PWRM0001 requires sources to be 'clearly identifiable' and dry weight measured and cross-checked with invoices and goods-receipt notes at each transfer; the Aug 2024 clarification lets the project 'region' be an administrative unit such as a municipality; and the Plastic Standard accepts, for many collection sites, at least one geodetic coordinate plus enough geographic information for the VVB to sample, so ward-level household location plus kabadiwala shop GPS, weigh slips and invoices is the expected evidence, with the VVB's sampling visit deciding acceptance.
answers.decision: Default: keep plastic credits out of the pilot P&L; approach rePurpose/Saahas (already operating in Bengaluru) or Plastics For Change/HDI to supply verified tonnage and ward-level data as a partner, and revisit becoming proponent only when Luma.Green has 12 months of audited weigh-slip data, a VVB quote, and at least ~1,000 t/yr of demonstrably non-EPR-financed plastic.
answers.whoToAsk: SCS Global Services and Control Union (Verra-approved plastic VVBs) for validation and verification quotes for a Bengaluru grouped collection project; rePurpose Global/Saahas and Plastics For Change/HDI for partner terms and the collector premium they actually pay per kg.

answers.question: After MeitY's January 2026 consultations, were the DPDP Rules 2025 deadlines (about 13 May 2027 for core duties) shortened for any class of company, and what applies to a small startup handling phone numbers and photos?
answers.answer: No. The DPDP Rules 2025 (G.S.R. 846(E), gazetted 13 November 2025) still run on the original three-step clock written into Rule 1: Rules 1, 2 and 17-21 (Board machinery) since 13 Nov 2025; Rule 4 (Consent Manager registration) from 13 Nov 2026; and every duty that touches Luma - Rules 3, 5-16, 22 and 23 (notice, consent, security safeguards, breach reporting, retention, children, rights) - 18 months after publication, i.e. 13 May 2027 (PIB counts from the 14 Nov publication and says 14 May 2027; plan for 13 May). At a closed-door meeting on 22-23 January 2026 MeitY floated pulling Rule 13 (Significant Data Fiduciary audits and DPIAs) forward to 12 months (13 Nov 2026), forcing the Rule 8(3) one-year log-retention duty on all fiduciaries within about 3 months, and switching on a few state-facing provisions (Rules 15, 23; Section 17(2)) immediately, with comments due 4 Feb 2026; the MeitY Secretary said on 11 March 2026 that no decision would be taken until industry inputs were in, and as of the latest checks we opened (Mondaq 14 Aug 2026; the dpdprules.org and dcomply trackers verified 8-28 Sep 2026) no amending gazette exists, so no class of company has an earlier deadline - and the 12-month cut was aimed at Significant Data Fiduciaries, a class the government has not yet even designated, not at a Bengaluru pilot. There is no small-company carve-out either: the Act has no size or turnover threshold, and the Section 17(3) power to exempt 'startups' from notice (s.5), retention/erasure (s.8(3), 8(7)), children's data (s.10) and rights (s.11) has never been exercised. The Third Schedule's automatic-erasure timers bite only e-commerce entities with at least 2 crore registered users (50 lakh for gaming, 2 crore for social media), so they do not apply to Luma, but Rule 8(3)'s one-year retention of processing logs and Rule 6's minimum safeguards (encryption or masking, access control, access logs, backups, processor contracts) will. Phone numbers, names, listing photos and KYC photos are all personal data, so from 13 May 2027 Luma must give a standalone plain-language notice with itemised purposes and a withdrawal route (Rule 3), publish a contact for data questions (Rule 9), answer grievances within a published period of at most 90 days (Rule 14), tell every affected person 'without delay' and the Board within 72 hours after a breach (Rule 7), and obtain verifiable parental consent for anyone under 18 (Rule 10). Penalties run to Rs 250 crore (safeguards), Rs 200 crore (breach notice, children) and Rs 50 crore (anything else), although the Data Protection Board still has no Chairperson or Members (MeitY invited applications on 6 May 2026; none appointed as of 1 Aug 2026). Until May 2027 the IT Act s.43A / SPDI Rules 2011 remain the live law: a published privacy policy and reasonable security practices are already mandatory, and bank or payment-instrument details (which UPI IDs arguably are) count as sensitive personal data under those rules.
answers.decision: Build the pilot to the DPDP standard from 13 October 2026 rather than waiting for May 2027, because it is cheap at pilot scale and the pilot will still be running when the duties bite: consent notice at signup, purpose-limited fields (no Aadhaar numbers, no photos beyond the listing and KYC need), 18+ accounts only, encryption at rest, one-year access logs, a 72-hour breach runbook, a published privacy contact and deletion-on-request; have a privacy lawyer spend half a day on the notice wording. Do not plan around a startup exemption (none exists); re-check egazette.gov.in monthly for any G.S.R. amending Rule 1 of the DPDP Rules, since the only floated acceleration that could touch Luma is Rule 8(3) log retention, which you would already satisfy.

answers.question: Have amendments to the IT (Intermediary) Rules in 2025-26 changed the 36-hour takedown or the 24-hour/15-day grievance timelines? Which Indian accessibility rules (RPwD Act 2016, IS 17802, GIGW 3.0) apply to a private platform?
answers.answer: Yes, twice, and the 36-hour window is gone. G.S.R. 775(E) of 22 October 2025 (in force 15 November 2025) rewrote Rule 3(1)(d) so that government takedown intimations must come from an officer of Joint Secretary rank (Director where none exists) or a DIG-rank police officer, be reasoned, cite the legal basis and exact URL, and be reviewed monthly, but it kept 36 hours. G.S.R. 120(E) of 10 February 2026 (in force 20 February 2026) then cut the clocks for every intermediary: court or government takedown orders 36 hours to 3 hours; grievance disposal 15 days to 7 days (the 24-hour acknowledgement is unchanged); complaints seeking removal of Rule 3(1)(b) prohibited content 72 hours to 36 hours; and non-consensual nudity, sexual content or impersonation/morphed images 24 hours to 2 hours, plus new labelling duties for AI-generated content (MeitY confirmed the 3-hour rule to the Lok Sabha on 25 March 2026). The August 2026 '2-hour takedown' headlines were re-reporting these February rules (SpicyIP, 9 Aug 2026), and the 30 March 2026 draft Second Amendment (comments closed 14 April 2026; safe harbour tied to MeitY advisories, MIB oversight, longer retention) proposes no new clocks and had not been notified in any coverage we opened through September 2026; a March 2026 idea of cutting 3 hours to 1 hour was never notified. Luma hosts listings, photos and household-kabadiwala messages, so it is very likely an 'intermediary' for that third-party content and Rule 3 applies in full - which also means a Grievance Officer's name and contact on the home screen, a user agreement listing the prohibited-content categories with periodic reminders, keeping removed content for 180 days and registration data for 180 days after account closure. On accessibility, the RPwD Act 2016 binds private companies: s.40 lets the Centre set standards, s.46 says service providers 'whether Government or private' must comply within two years of the rules, and s.89 fines Rs 10,000 for a first breach and Rs 50,000 to Rs 5 lakh after; Rule 15(1)(c) of the RPwD Rules 2017, amended 11 May 2023, names IS 17802 Part 1 (2021) and Part 2 (2022) as the ICT standard for websites, applications and ICT-based services, and that is the standard the Chief Commissioner for PwD has enforced against private apps (Practo 2022; audit order 30 Jul 2024; Rs 10,000 fines on 155 establishments in Feb 2025 and Rs 50,000 on 96 in June 2025). GIGW 3.0 (2023) is the manual for Government websites and apps certified by STQC and does not apply to a private platform except as a checklist; IS 17802 is freely downloadable and, per the law-firm notes we read, aligned with WCAG 2.1 Level AA. The Supreme Court (Rajive Raturi, 8 Nov 2024) struck Rule 15(1) for being merely persuasive, and the result is the draft RPwD (Amendment) Rules 2026 (S.O. 3962(E), 16 Jul 2026; comments closed about 19 Aug 2026) which would make IS 17802 mandatory for every establishment offering websites or apps to people in India, with 12 months for companies above Rs 500 crore turnover, 18 months for everyone else, full conformance in 2 years, and a published Accessibility Conformance Report signed at Director level; DEPwD told Medianama (23 Sep 2026) it aims to notify around January 2027, when the Supreme Court next hears the case. Two items are not settled on public pages: whether counsel agrees Luma is an intermediary for its listing and chat features, and the final shape of the 2026 accessibility rules.
answers.decision: Treat Luma as an intermediary from day one: name a Grievance Officer (a founder) on the app home screen and website, wire an in-app report flow with 24-hour acknowledgement and 7-day closure, a 36-hour path for prohibited-content removal requests and a 2-hour path for intimate or impersonation images, keep one phone on call for a 3-hour court or government order, and log removals for 180 days. For accessibility, build to WCAG 2.1 AA now (labels, contrast, screen-reader names, large tap targets, Kannada and Hindi alt text), run an automated plus manual audit before 13 Oct 2026, and keep the results in an ACR-style document so the 2026 rules' 18-month runway costs nothing extra; skip GIGW/STQC certification, which is for government sites.
answers.whoToAsk: A technology lawyer (30 minutes) to confirm Luma is an 'intermediary' for user-posted listings and chat and that the simulated escrow does not change that; an IAAP-certified accessibility auditor if you want a paid pre-launch audit; the Chief Commissioner for Persons with Disabilities (ccdisabilities.nic.in) or the Karnataka State Commissioner for PwD for the current enforcement posture toward small private apps.

design-facts.cluster: Languages, digits, pictures and offline behaviour

answers.question: Which languages do Bengaluru's likely pilot wards (Yeshwanthpur, Peenya, Malleshwaram, Rajajinagar, Mathikere) speak and read (census and local data), and how large is the share who can read numbers but not words? Do Bengali, Marathi and Urdu readers in India prefer international digits or native-script digits in apps and prices?
answers.answer: There is no official ward-level language data: Census 2011 (still the last count) publishes mother tongue only down to district/city, so the five wards must be read from city figures plus local signals. For Bengaluru city in 2011 the shares were Kannada 42.05%, Tamil 16.34%, Telugu 13.73%, Urdu 13.00%, Hindi 4.64%, Malayalam about 3.2% and Marathi about 2.1%, and 50.6% of residents were migrants; Malleshwaram (laid out 1889) and Rajajinagar (1949, half industrial plots and half housing) are old Kannada-majority layouts with Tamil and Telugu minorities, while Peenya and Yeshwanthpur (industrial estates plus the APMC yard) and adjoining Mathikere draw Hindi-belt and Bengali workers: a 2022 Indian Journal of Labour Economics study interviewed 49 Bengali-speaking migrants in Bengaluru found at road junctions, construction sites, scrap collection centres and manufacturing units. Reading: Bengaluru Urban's Census 2011 literacy rate was 87.67% (men 91.01%, women 84.01%), so roughly 1 in 8 people aged 7+ could not read or write any language, and NFHS-5 (2019-21) puts Karnataka's tested literacy at 73% of women and 85% of men aged 15-49, so among women and migrant labour expect 20-30% who cannot read words. No Indian survey measures 'reads digits but not words'; the closest evidence is Microsoft Research's Bangalore slum work (2006 ICTD paper, 80+ domestic workers; 2011 ToCHI paper across India, Kenya, the Philippines and South Africa) which describes its users as 'functionally illiterate or semiliterate but partially numerate' and keeps numbers in a text-free UI because 'many nonliterate people can read numerical digits'. ASER 2023 (released 16 Jan 2024, rural 14-18-year-olds) adds that 25% cannot read a Std II text fluently and only 43.3% can do 3-by-1-digit division, so assume digit recognition is near-universal but arithmetic (totals, per-kg maths) is not; the app must do the multiplication and show the result. Digits: the Unicode CLDR data inside every browser and Node defaults Bengali to Bengali digits (০-৯), Marathi to Devanagari digits (०-९) and Urdu-India (ur-IN) to Extended Arabic-Indic digits (۰-۹), while Hindi, Kannada, Tamil, Telugu and plain 'ur' default to Latin; I verified on Node 24 that the app's bare locale codes already print '১,২৩৪.৫০' for bn and '₹१,२३४.५०' for mr, and '₹1,234.50' for ur. Readers of those languages do meet native digits daily: on 30 Sep 2026 Anandabazar's home page used 66 Bengali versus 4 Latin digits, Loksatta 151 Devanagari versus 68 Latin, Inquilab (Urdu) 43 Arabic-Indic versus 10 Latin, whereas Kannada's Udayavani used Latin only; Bengali and Marathi Wikipedias standardised on native numerals while urban Hindi readers prefer Latin (CIS-A2K, 24 Sep 2022). But no published study shows a preference for native digits in app prices, and every part of the money trail a seller compares against (rupee notes, UPI apps, bank SMS, the shop's scale display, GST invoices) uses Latin digits, and in Bengaluru these readers are small minorities who also read Hindi or Kannada.
answers.decision: Ship kn, en, hi, ta, te and ur for the pilot (94% of the city's mother tongues) with bn switched on for Peenya scrap shops; format every price, weight, phone number and OTP with Latin digits in all 12 locales (set numberingSystem 'latn' in the next-intl formats and add a test that bn/mr/ur money strings contain only ASCII digits), keeping native digits off until a seller asks; treat about 1 in 8 adults (up to 1 in 4 among women and migrant workers) as unable to read words but able to read digits, so every material and action gets an icon plus a spoken label and the app does all arithmetic.
answers.whoToAsk: Ward-level language mix and the digits-not-words share cannot be settled from public pages: have Saathis run a 5-minute doorstep card test with 10 scrap shops and 30 households per ward in the first pilot week (show a price card in Latin and native digits plus a word label; record which they read aloud correctly). BBMP ward offices hold no language data.

answers.question: Is there evidence on whether low-literacy users recognise materials faster from photos or drawn pictures? Do the SWM Rules 2026 bin colours (wet, dry, sanitary, special care) clash with a green/amber/sky palette for materials? Does the Convex React client keep unsent mutations across an offline reload, or must a weigh-and-pay queue be stored on the phone? What are the licence terms of IconScout, Blush and Icons8 illustrations for commercial apps?
answers.answer: Photos versus drawings: the best evidence is from Bangalore itself; Medhi, Prasad and Toyama (WWW 2007) showed 13 health symptoms to 200 illiterate adults in 10 formats and found static hand-drawn pictures were better understood than photographs or icons, voice annotation sped comprehension, and 'richer information is not necessarily better understood', and the 2006 Bangalore-slum study likewise found people could identify both photos and cartoons but preferred semi-abstract cartoons, with photorealism useful only when drilling into detail. For sorting specifically, UBC's three experiments (Journal of Environmental Psychology 58, 2018, literate students, four bins) measured 75.9% accuracy with pictures and 75.2% with icons against 70.2% with words, and found that adding 'not allowed' items to icon signs hurt, so use simple drawn pictures of the exact local item (milk sachet, newspaper bundle, cooking pot) with a spoken name, keep photos for the drill-down, and never rely on text-only labels or 'not this' lists. Bin colours: the SWM Rules 2026 (S.O. 388(E), gazetted 28 Jan 2026, in force 1 Apr 2026) make four-stream segregation mandatory and direct local bodies that public bins 'for storage of wet waste shall be painted green, those for storage of dry waste shall be printed blue and if required in public toilets bins painted in red may be placed for sanitary waste'; special-care waste gets no colour (the annual-return forms still count 'green, blue and black bins', black being the old domestic-hazardous colour), and BBMP has used green-wet and red-sanitary bins since at least Aug 2019. Luma's current chips (src/components/sell/family.tsx) put paper on amber, plastic and glass on sky, e-waste on brand green and metal on neutral: the one real clash is green, which every Bengaluru household has been trained to read as 'wet waste', so green on a material chip (e-waste today) or as a 'good to sell' signal muddles the message; sky/blue is actually consistent because everything Luma buys is dry waste, amber has no household-bin meaning (yellow is a hospital biomedical colour only), and red must stay reserved for reject/hazard. Convex: the React client 'automatically retries mutations until they are confirmed to have been written to the database', guarantees each runs once, and 'will warn users if they try to close their browser tab while there are outstanding mutations' (the unsavedChangesWarning option), but that queue lives only in memory; in convex 1.46.0 as installed in this repo the RequestManager keeps in-flight requests in a JavaScript Map and the client code never touches localStorage or IndexedDB, and Convex's own FAQ says it 'doesn't currently provide a full offline sync mechanism'. So a reload, a killed tab or a phone restart while offline silently drops unsent weigh-and-pay records, and the queue must be stored on the phone. Licences (checked 30 Sep 2026): IconScout licenses every asset 'to a single end product', its Digital License allows unlimited use in websites and mobile apps but no redistribution, logo use or print merchandise, free assets carry per-asset attribution requirements shown at download, and the Individual plan is $14.99 per user per month billed annually ($19.99 monthly). Icons8's Universal Multimedia License (effective 27 Nov 2025) requires free accounts to embed a visible, clickable link to icons8.com wherever the assets appear ('Icons by Icons8'), a paid subscription drops attribution and lets you keep using downloaded assets after cancelling, and nobody may ship assets so that third parties can extract them as standalone files. Blush states 'All Illustrations published on Blush can be used for free' in commercial products with unlimited copies and no attribution, forbids reselling, merchandising or compiling a competing library, and Pro adds SVG, print-resolution PNG and the full catalogue; its price is drawn only inside the sign-up widget, so that number is an open item.
answers.decision: Use drawn, semi-abstract pictures of the actual local item with a spoken label for every material, photos only in the drill-down. Re-colour the chips: a blue 'dry/recyclable' header, amber, neutral and a third non-bin colour (for example violet) for families, green only for brand, verified and CO2 accents, red only for reject/hazard. Keep a weigh-and-pay outbox in IndexedDB keyed by a client-generated UUID, make the mutation idempotent on that key, replay on reconnect, and show 'saved on phone, not yet sent' until the server confirms. For artwork, start with Blush free (no attribution, PNG only) or one IconScout Individual seat ($14.99/month) licensed to the Luma app as the single end product; if any Icons8 free asset ships, put the link credit on the About screen.
answers.whoToAsk: Blush Pro price: open blush.design/plans while signed in (not in the public page). Chip colours: confirm with a 10-household card sort in the first pilot week. Convex outbox: ask the Convex team on their Discord whether a persisted mutation queue is on the roadmap before building anything larger than the pilot needs.

dwcc-partners.cluster: Dry-waste centres, NAMASTE and NGO partners

answers.question: How many dry waste collection centres (DWCCs) operate in Bengaluru today (figures range from 119 in Sep 2025 to 164/166), who runs them and under what contracts with the city?
answers.answer: The only dated, city-wide operating count on a public page is Citizen Matters' 15 Sep 2025 report: of the 198 centres sanctioned (one per old BBMP ward, after the 2010 Lok Adalat order upheld by the High Court in 2012), 'only 141 remain, and just 119 are operational', serving 127 wards; Hasiru Dala's Nalini Shekar put the total at 140 on 18 Oct 2024, and Deccan Herald (11 Jan 2025) said 'more than 160' exist but a source estimated only 30-35 run efficiently. The 166 figure is the May 2019 functional count (166 of 198 sanctioned); '164' could not be traced to any dated page, and the OpenCity copy of BBMP's DWCC map (re-uploaded 25 Nov 2025) has 336 pins including old sites, so it is not an operating count. The denominator also changed in 2025: the 198 wards became 369 across five city corporations under the Greater Bengaluru Authority, so roughly 120 centres now cover about a third of today's wards. The city does not run them: DWCCs are BBMP-owned sheds operated by NGOs, waste-picker self-help groups and individual waste-picker entrepreneurs; Hasiru Dala supports 35 (33 in 2019), Swachha and Gilgal Charitable Trust are named as other resource organisations, ITC ran the Shivajinagar 'Kartavya' centre (2015), and the garbage contractors' association says dry waste is 'entirely the responsibility of non-governmental organisations and self-help groups' (Jan 2025). Contract terms: BBMP's DWCC operating procedure (annex to the ward services agreement) makes the centre BBMP property, obliges the operator to accept all dry-waste streams, sort into at least five categories, log daily weights on BBMP's portal and report monthly, with the collection contractor dropping low-value waste free; operators keep the sale proceeds and, per the original design, get 'zero subsidies in operations'. The 2020-vintage MoUs paid Rs 56,316 for six months of operation plus Rs 23,316 a month for maintenance where BBMP supplied no vehicle, but BBMP owed Rs 9.41 crore across 46 wards (980 centre-months) by May 2023, and by Sep 2025 the MoUs had lapsed so that 'there are no transactions between the waste pickers and the BBMP'; operators live off recyclables sales. BSWML's May 2025 collection tender routes household dry waste to 'dry waste collection centres operated by not-for-profit organisations', and on 16 Aug 2025 the state ordered a DWCC or MRF in every ward 'by partnering with ragpickers' while moving collection from BSWML to BBMP zonal commissioners and then to the five corporations, with BSWML keeping processing and disposal. Bengaluru generates about 1,925 tonnes of dry waste a day, of which about 1,200 tonnes is processed (Aug 2025).
answers.decision: Model Bengaluru as roughly 120 operating DWCCs (not 166) run by NGOs and waste-picker SHGs with no city payments flowing; treat each centre as a candidate 'yard' node whose operator (not the city) is the counterparty, and confirm the live list for the pilot wards with the city corporation's SWM wing before 13 Oct 2026.
answers.whoToAsk: The SWM chief engineer of the city corporation covering the pilot wards (under GBA) and BSWML for the current DWCC list and MoU status; Hasiru Dala for its 35 centres and their operators.

answers.question: Does the NAMASTE waste-picker component continue beyond FY2025-26, which resource organisation is empanelled for Karnataka, and has waste-picker registration started in Bengaluru?
answers.answer: The waste-picker component was approved by the Standing Finance Committee on 20 Jun 2024 for FY2024-25 and 2025-26 only; the Revised Scheme Guidelines (MoSJE, PDF dated 15 Dec 2025) say it 'may be continued thereafter in the light of an evaluation done by the MoSJE and MoHUA', and the parent NAMASTE scheme was itself sanctioned for three years to 2025-26 with Rs 349.70 crore (PIB, 25 Aug 2023). No gazette, Cabinet note or budget line approving continuation into FY2026-27 was found on an official page, but the scheme is visibly still running: a Lok Sabha reply of 17 Mar 2026 put 2.34 lakh waste pickers under its ambit, MoS Ramdas Athawale distributed NAMASTE and Ayushman cards to 300+ waste pickers in Delhi on 4 Sep 2026, a 22 Sep 2026 ministry update reports 2,51,756 waste pickers profiled in 34 states/UTs (up from 37,980 validated in Aug 2025 and 1.52 lakh validated by 23 Jan 2026), and on 21 Aug 2026 the Centre was reported (citing The Hindu and PIB) to be proposing a rural expansion costing about Rs 498.73 crore through 2030-31 — treat that as a proposal, not an approval. The guidelines pay CSOs, CSCs, ROs or ULBs Rs 250 per e-KYC-validated waste picker (raised from Rs 150), an RO management fee of Rs 10,000 per DWCC per month for 12 months, and up to Rs 5 lakh capital subsidy per DWCC for up to two collection vehicles, against targets of 2.5 lakh profiles and 750 DWCCs; occupation can be verified by 'recent receipts from sale of scrap' or endorsement by scrap-shop owners, which Luma.Green's receipts could supply. Resource organisations are empanelled centrally by NSKFDC through an Expression of Interest (states not covered may empanel locally); the NAMASTE portal's dashboard showed 11 ROs, 9 training providers and 10,894 profiles across 3 states as of 28 Feb 2025, but no public page names the RO for Karnataka, and the state-wise annex to the 22 Jul 2025 Lok Sabha answer is a scan we could not read. On Bengaluru, Citizen Matters (15 Sep 2025) reports the 2013 BBMP ID cards have expired after 10 years, new waste pickers 'are not able to obtain ID cards', and no NAMASTE profiling camp is mentioned; Nalini Shekar (18 Oct 2024) said Karnataka has about 4.23 lakh waste pickers and only about 25,000 ID cards. Pune was the first city to formally implement the component (26 Mar 2025); NSKFDC's Aug 2025 slides show 700+ ULBs in 30 states/UTs had started profiling (about 91,000 surveyed, 42,000 validated), so Bengaluru may be among them, but that is unconfirmed.
answers.decision: Do not gate Saathi onboarding on a NAMASTE ID; capture it as an optional KYC field, and design Luma.Green's sale receipts so they qualify as the 'recent receipts from sale of scrap' evidence the guidelines accept, so a partner RO can profile Saathis at Rs 250 each if and when Bengaluru profiling runs.
answers.whoToAsk: NSKFDC (nskfdc-msje@nic.in, +91-11-26382476) for the Karnataka RO and the FY2026-27 continuation order; Karnataka Directorate of Municipal Administration and the pilot city corporation's SWM wing for whether profiling has started in Bengaluru; Hasiru Dala for ground truth on camps and ID cards.

answers.question: Would Hasiru Dala, Saahas, ITC WOW's centre operators or the Karnataka waste-pickers' union co-run kabadiwala and Saathi onboarding, or run a DWCC as a pilot yard, and on what terms do such NGOs usually work (fee per onboarding, grants, CSR)? What is Hasiru Dala Innovations' own traceable-plastic business with brands, and how should Luma.Green avoid competing with it?
answers.answer: No public page says any of them will co-run Luma.Green onboarding — that takes a meeting — but their models show who fits which role. Hasiru Dala is a member-based waste-picker organisation (annual membership fee Rs 50 in its early years; registered 2013) that is the resource organisation behind 35 Bengaluru DWCCs (Sep 2025), has secured 11,300+ occupational ID cards across Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh, checks waste pickers' documents and enrols them in schemes, and is grant- and CSR-funded (FCRA, 80G, 12A, CSR-1 certified); its 2013 DWCC plan already assumed three partners — BBMP building the shed, a sponsor paying user fees, and the collective operating — so it is the natural Saathi-onboarding and DWCC-as-pilot-yard partner. The Karnataka waste-picker union (registered with the state, 2,300+ members, formed around 2023) and the Thyajya Shramika Sanghatane collective that petitioned BBMP in 2022 and 2023 over unpaid DWCC dues are the bodies to consult on Saathi pay and pickup terms. Saahas is an NGO (2001; 226 livelihoods, 5,227 MT dry waste managed; CSR partners Juniper Networks, Tata Realty, Rainmatter) with a sister company Saahas Zero Waste (Pvt Ltd, 2013; 420+ staff, 100+ tonnes a day, 112 informal workers formalised, a 10-TPD MRF at Jigani and a 25-tonne-a-month textile facility) whose 'Let's Transform' programme, funded by IKEA Social Entrepreneurship since 2022, onboards informal scrap-dealer micro-entrepreneurs (three so far, each employing about 20 workers) with equipment, compliance and a business model in return for plastic supply and supply-chain analytics — the closest existing template for kabadiwala onboarding. ITC's WOW is a corporate CSR programme (17,900+ waste collectors, 150+ social entrepreneurs, 67,100 MT of dry waste in 2024-25) that works through 'super franchisee' aggregators and its own dry-resource collection centres, ran BBMP's Shivajinagar DWCC in 2015, and routes paper to ITC's mills. Public fee benchmarks: NAMASTE pays Rs 250 per validated profile and Rs 10,000 per DWCC per month to resource organisations; the lapsed BBMP MoUs paid Rs 56,316 per six months plus Rs 23,316 a month; The Body Shop works on 'long-term fixed-price contracts'; no NGO publishes a per-onboarding fee, so that number is an open item. Hasiru Dala Innovations (HDI) is a separate for-profit (Nov 2015; Rs 5 crore revenue in FY2017-18, investors including Social Alpha) running total waste management for 370+ clients, 800+ events, EPR compliance services, and a 'plastics circularity' line: WFTO Fair Trade Guaranteed, blockchain-traceable post-consumer plastic aggregated from waste-picker entrepreneurs, DWCCs and scrap dealers (327 'supplier clients') at its own aggregation centre and sold to recyclers (e.g. Vishuddh Recycle) and brands — since 9 May 2019 supplying The Body Shop through Plastics for Change (250 tonnes in year one, 900 tonnes over three years, up to 2,500 Bengaluru waste pickers), and Plastics for Change's brand list now includes L'Oréal, Estée Lauder, Unilever and IKEA. HDI is therefore a buyer competing for the same kabadiwala and DWCC material, so Luma.Green should stay a neutral ledger that records cash and UPI sales, never buys, sells or brokers material or EPR credits, does not pitch brands, and invites HDI's aggregation centre in as a 'yard' node whose traceability export can feed its WFTO and EPR audits.
answers.decision: Open with Hasiru Dala for Saathi onboarding and one of its 35 DWCCs as the pilot yard, and with Saahas Zero Waste for kabadiwala onboarding, each under a written MoU paying a per-onboarding fee benchmarked to NAMASTE's Rs 250 and a monthly support fee benchmarked to Rs 10,000 per centre (funded by Luma.Green or a CSR grant); treat HDI as a downstream yard/recycler partner by never trading material or EPR credits, and bring ITC WOW in only after the pilot.
answers.whoToAsk: Hasiru Dala's leadership and its DWCC operators, Saahas Zero Waste's founder, HDI's management and the Karnataka waste-picker union's office-bearers for actual willingness and fees (one meeting each, since none is published); a CA or counsel on routing CSR money to the fees under Section 135 and the partner's CSR-1 status.

answers.question: Is Luma.Green an 'e-commerce operator' under CGST s.52 (0.5% TCS) and under the Income-tax Act 2025 (the successor to s.194-O, 0.1% TDS) for bookings and trades where money never passes through it? What changes once escrow through a payment aggregator starts?
answers.answer: GST: not during the pilot. CGST s.52(1) only makes an operator collect TCS on supplies "where the consideration with respect to such supplies is to be collected by the operator"; CBIC Circular 194/06/2023-GST (17 July 2023) confirms the collector is the operator that actually releases payment to the supplier, and "net value" counts only supplies by registered persons, so a platform that merely records cash/UPI paid hand-to-hand has no TCS, no s.24(x) registration and no GSTR-8 duty (the rate, if it ever applied, is 0.5% total, 0.25% CGST + 0.25% SGST, since Notification 15/2024-Central Tax of 10 July 2024). Income-tax: very likely yes from day one. The Income-tax Act 2025 (assent 21 Aug 2025, in force 1 April 2026) re-enacts s.194-O as s.393(1) Table Sl. No. 8(v): "any e-commerce operator" deducts 0.1% of the gross amount of sales of goods or services by an "e-commerce participant" that it facilitates, nil threshold, and Note 3(ii) deems any payment made by the purchaser directly to the participant to be paid by the operator, so cash or UPI moving outside the app does not take you out; the s.402(13)-(14) definitions are wide ("owns, operates or manages digital or electronic facility or platform for electronic commerce"; a participant is any resident selling goods through it), and the only published safe harbour, CBDT Circular 20/2021 (25 Nov 2021), covers e-auction portals that do price discovery only with contract, delivery and payment all outside the portal and no knowledge of payment quantum or schedule, conditions Luma.Green's bookings, Saathi pickups, verified counterparties and recorded prices fail. Relief for households: s.393(4) Table Sl. No. 11 exempts an individual/HUF seller whose gross sales through the operator are at most Rs 5 lakh in the tax year and who has furnished PAN or Aadhaar, which covers practically every household, but only if the app captures PAN or Aadhaar, because s.397(2)(b) sets the no-PAN rate for this entry at 5% instead of 0.1%. For the business legs (kabadiwala to yard to recycler to manufacturer) Luma.Green must deduct 0.1% of the gross trade value (GST excluded if shown separately, per CBDT Circular 20/2023 of 28 Dec 2023) at credit or payment, whichever is earlier, deposit it and file TDS returns under its TAN; because it holds no money it must recover that 0.1% from the seller by contract (a monthly debit or offset) or fund it itself, and once it deducts, no other TDS (such as the buyer's 0.1% on purchases over Rs 50 lakh) applies to the same trade. When escrow through a payment aggregator starts, GST flips: Luma.Green then collects the consideration (the PA is only a conduit; under the 2023 circular the operator that releases payment is the collector), so it must register as a TCS collector under s.24(x) in Karnataka and any state where its sellers sit, collect 0.5% on the net value of taxable supplies by registered sellers each month, deposit by the 10th and file GSTR-8 (s.52(3)-(4)); unregistered kabadiwalas selling through a TCS-collecting operator must then register or use the Notification 34/2023-Central Tax route (31 July 2023, in force 1 Oct 2023: PAN, intra-state only, one state, and an enrolment number on the GST portal before any supply, which the platform must gate), the goods threshold being Rs 40 lakh (Karnataka is not a special-category state). Income-tax does not change with escrow except that deduction becomes mechanical: CBDT Circular 17/2020 (29 Sept 2020) says the payment gateway/PA need not deduct where the operator already has. RBI: Luma.Green must not itself pool buyer money and settle sellers; under the RBI (Regulation of Payment Aggregators) Directions 2025 (15 Sept 2025) that is PA business needing authorisation (Rs 15 crore net worth at application, Rs 25 crore by year 3), so use a licensed PA's escrow and expect the PA to KYC every kabadiwala and yard as a merchant, because a PA must ensure a marketplace does not accept payments for sellers not onboarded on its platform. Separately from operator status, since 10 Oct 2024 registered buyers pay GST under reverse charge on metal scrap (tariff chapters 72-81) bought from unregistered sellers and deduct 2% GST TDS on B2B metal-scrap contracts of Rs 2.5 lakh or more; those duties sit on yards and recyclers, not on Luma.Green, but its trade records should carry them.
answers.decision: Treat Luma.Green as an e-commerce operator for income-tax s.393 from 13 Oct 2026 (obtain a TAN now, capture PAN or Aadhaar from every household at sign-up so the Rs 5 lakh exemption applies, deduct 0.1% on all business-to-business trades and recover it from the seller under the platform terms), and treat it as NOT a GST s.52 collector until escrow goes live; the month escrow starts, register under s.24(x), collect 0.5% and file GSTR-8, gate unregistered sellers behind a Notification 34/2023 enrolment number, and route all money through a licensed payment aggregator rather than Luma.Green's own account.
answers.whoToAsk: A chartered accountant who handles TDS/GST for marketplaces, to confirm (a) that recording a booked trade with an offline cash/UPI payment counts as 'facilitating' a sale under s.393 (no CBDT ruling covers a record-only platform), (b) when 'credit' occurs for a trade Luma.Green never pays, and (c) the Karnataka TCS registration set-up before escrow; consider a CBDT advance ruling only if trade volumes justify the cost.

answers.question: Are households 'consumers' under the Consumer Protection Act when they sell scrap and get a free pickup, and do the Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules 2020 as amended in 2026 apply to Luma.Green (grievance officer, 48-hour acknowledgement, seller disclosures)? Or should it adopt those norms voluntarily?
answers.answer: For the scrap sale itself, no: s.2(7) of the Consumer Protection Act 2019 makes someone a "consumer" only when they buy goods or hire/avail a service "for a consideration", so a household selling scrap is the seller, and the kabadiwala who buys is expressly excluded as "a person who obtains such goods for resale or for any commercial purpose" (though Explanation (a) keeps a buyer who purchases solely to earn a livelihood by self-employment inside the definition, which many small kabadiwalas would fit). For the free pickup, s.2(42) says "service" "does not include the rendering of any service free of charge", which on its face keeps households out; but in Indian Medical Association v V.P. Shantha (AIR 1996 SC 550) the Supreme Court held that a nominally free service remains a "service" where its cost is borne by paying users or a third party, and here the pickup is paid for out of the kabadiwala's margin and the scrap changing hands, so a Bengaluru district commission could plausibly treat a household as a consumer of the pickup, and the moment Luma.Green charges households anything (priority slot, bins, subscription) they are consumers outright. That point is genuinely unsettled and cannot be closed from public pages. The Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules 2020 (notified 23 July 2020) apply to "all goods and services bought or sold over digital or electronic network" and all e-commerce models, and define an "e-commerce entity" as anyone who "owns, operates or manages digital or electronic facility or platform for electronic commerce", so Luma.Green fits on its face; Rule 2's only carve-out is for "any activity of a natural person carried out in a personal capacity", which frees the household seller from seller duties but not the platform. Practitioner analysis (Trilegal, 5 Aug 2020) reads the Rules as governing consumer purchases, so the pure B2B legs (kabadiwala to yard to recycler to manufacturer) fall outside them except where a buyer buys for self-employment livelihood, but the Rules also impose duties toward "users" (anyone who accesses the platform), which is why the same analysis flags ambiguity for B2B platforms. The Amendment Rules 2026 (G.S.R. 789(E), 9 Sept 2026, in force 1 Jan 2027) do not narrow scope or add a small-platform threshold; they keep the 48-hour acknowledgement and one-month resolution (already in the 2020 Rules, as the Ministry's Lok Sabha answer of 25 Mar 2026 records) and add giving the complainant a copy of the complaint, mandatory National Consumer Helpline convergence, display of legal name/HQ address/website/grievance contact, plain-language ranking disclosure, labelled sponsored listings, a 30-day prior-price rule for discounts, an annual dark-pattern self-audit with a displayed certificate, seller GSTIN/MSME identifiers, and express consent before consumer data is used for the platform's own products. One structural trap: Rule 4(1) expects an e-commerce entity to be a company incorporated in India (or a foreign company or office owned by a resident) with a resident nodal person, and the 2020 analysis notes it is unclear whether an LLP qualifies, so check the pilot entity's form. Recommendation: adopt the norms voluntarily from 13 Oct 2026 rather than argue about scope; the cost is one named grievance officer, a published address and contact, a 48-hour/30-day complaint clock, seller (kabadiwala/yard) disclosures you already gather during verification, a plain sentence on how kabadiwalas are ranked, no dark patterns, explicit consent for data, and joining NCH convergence (1,398 companies had by March 2026), which also pre-empts CCPA attention (Rs 3.00 crore of penalties across 477 class-action notices by 9 Mar 2026). Doing this does not concede that households are consumers; word the terms as "user" grievance rights and keep household-facing statements accurate about weights and rates, which is where any unfair-trade-practice complaint would come from.
answers.decision: Adopt the 2020 Rules and the 2026 amendments voluntarily from the pilot start (named grievance officer, 48-hour acknowledgement with a copy of the complaint, 30-day resolution, published legal name/address/contact, verified-business disclosures, a plain explanation of kabadiwala ranking, no dark patterns, express consent for data, NCH convergence enrolment) without conceding that households are 'consumers', and get a one-page counsel opinion on the free-pickup point and on whether the pilot entity's legal form satisfies Rule 4(1) before 1 Jan 2027.
answers.whoToAsk: A Bengaluru consumer-law counsel for (a) whether the free pickup makes households consumers under s.2(42) read with IMA v Shantha, and (b) whether an LLP or partnership satisfies Rule 4(1)'s company requirement; the Department of Consumer Affairs' National Consumer Helpline convergence desk (contact given in the Lok Sabha answer of 25 Mar 2026) to enrol the platform.

answers.question: Has MSTC's EPR Electronic Trading & Settlement Platform been approved and launched since June 2026, and have direct buyer-to-seller certificate transfers on the CPCB portals stopped?
answers.answer: No on both counts, as far as public records show up to 29 September 2026. MSTC's platform (EPRETP) is built but not trading: on its Q1 FY27 earnings call (transcript filed with BSE on 14 August 2026) MSTC said development "is now complete along with all the integrations necessary for immediate operationalization" and that it is "awaiting the go ahead" from government/CPCB, opening first for five streams (plastic, e-waste, batteries, tyres, used oil). CPCB put the exchange site (etp.cpcb.gov.in) and the Common EPR single-sign-on portal (epr.cpcb.gov.in) up in early February 2026 for viewing and KYC only, and switched off the standalone plastic portal on 28 June 2026 with data migrated to the common portal, but no CPCB go-live notice or MoEFCC order authorising trading has appeared, and the non-ferrous section of the same common portal was still not live on 20 September 2026. Direct recycler-to-producer transfers on the CPCB portals have therefore not stopped: a June 2026 industry explainer describes both routes as available with EPRETP "not mandatory", and on MSTC's own call an analyst noted that large recyclers are still transferring certificates directly to brand owners. What changes on go-live is fixed by CPCB's EPRETP guidelines (uploaded 31 December 2024, reported 15 January 2025): certificates keep being generated and held on the CPCB portal, but price discovery, trading and payment for the listed transfer types "shall be permitted only through the EPRETP", with bilateral trading allowed for six months only for entities registered as both obligated entity and processor, and no brokers. Users will pay a registration fee equal to 50% of the EPR-portal application fee plus an annual fee of 25% of that, and MSTC pointed to a 4% CPCB charge on transaction value in the tender documents.
answers.decision: Model certificate movement in the pilot as a direct portal transfer from a registered recycler to a PIBO (Luma records the transfer reference and price; it does not move certificates), keep an EPRETP adapter as a stub, and re-check etp.cpcb.gov.in and MSTC's Q2 FY27 call (mid-November 2026) before promising any exchange-based pricing.

answers.question: What evidence do CPCB's verification guidelines under the 31 March 2026 plastic amendment (and Registered Environment Auditors) require from processors, and does the plastic EPR portal accept receipts without GST for purchases from informal collectors, as the e-waste portal does? Do the CPCB EPR and SWM portals accept bulk uploads or API connections?
answers.answer: The Plastic Waste Management (Amendment) Rules, 2026 (G.S.R. 237(E), 31 March 2026) list no new evidence themselves: they insert "or Registered Environment Auditor" after "designated agency" in Rule 17(5) and Schedule II paragraphs 12.4 and 13.1, define an REA by reference to the Environment Audit Rules, 2025 (S.O. 3973(E), 29 August 2025), and order CPCB to prescribe a "guideline for audit and verification for use of recycled content" within six months, i.e. by 30 September 2026; as of 29 September 2026 no such guideline appears on CPCB's plastic-waste guidelines page, so this is an open item. An REA is a certified auditor (or a firm of two or more) registered with the Environment Audit Designated Agency and assigned by random allocation, and the 2025 rules expressly cover audits "under the Extended Producer Responsibility framework" including the plastic, e-waste and battery rules (PIB, 3 September 2025). The evidence a processor must hold today is what the CPCB portal already demands: for each plastic-waste purchase the recycler enters supplier name and address, category, quantity, date and the supplier's GST number, and CPCB's Guidance Manual (February 2023, section 3.2.1) says "if GST is not available then PAN/Aadhar of supplier has to be provided" (GST is mandatory only for waste-to-energy, waste-to-oil and co-processors), with a "copy of invoice/GST e-invoice (as applicable as per GST Act)" uploaded; CPCB's third-party audit checklist then samples procurement records from both registered and unregistered suppliers, checks GST, e-way bills and e-invoices, and requires a site visit with "transaction receipts, source of procurement, transportation details" plus photos or videos. So the plastic portal does accept non-GST purchase receipts from informal collectors identified by PAN or Aadhaar, the same posture as the e-waste portal, whose CPCB FAQ of 23 January 2024 says informal-sector purchases need "any sales receipt having name and address of the seller"; the difference is that plastic certificate generation is locked to the recycler's output sale, for which since April 2025 PWPs must upload a GSTN-validated GST e-invoice (IRN and QR code) before the portal issues certificates. On uploads: the plastic portal has a bulk-upload option for procurement or sales from a single counterparty (Excel format with two-year totals plus one PDF), CPCB added a bulk transaction-upload provision with an SOP for PIBOs in 2023, and a CEPP mobile app (April 2025) lets users scan e-invoice QR codes, while PWP purchase entries are single-entry in the manual. No public API exists for any CPCB EPR portal (the only APIs documented are "secured APIs" between the CPCB portal and the EPRETP exchange), and the SWM portal (swm.cpcb.gov.in, live for bulk-waste-generator registration since 31 May 2026 under the SWM Rules 2026 in force from 1 April 2026) documents neither bulk upload nor API.
answers.decision: Build receipts to the strictest existing checklist rather than wait for the guideline: every purchase from an informal collector records seller name, address, mobile, PAN or masked Aadhaar, date, category, weight, price and a photo of the paper receipt; every recycler-side sale carries a GST e-invoice number/IRN; transactions export as CSV/Excel in the CPCB bulk-upload column layout; API integration is out of scope for the pilot.
answers.whoToAsk: CPCB WM-III / EPR portal helpdesk for whether the recycled-content verification guideline has issued and whether any API exists; a CA for GST treatment (reverse charge, e-way bill thresholds) of purchases from unregistered kabadiwalas.

answers.question: Are EPR regimes for non-ferrous metal scrap and for construction and demolition waste in force in 2026, and do they cover kabadiwala metal trades (copper, aluminium, brass)? What did the Delhi High Court decide on the e-waste EPR floor price (₹22/kg)? What are the current recycled-content requirements for plastic packaging after the 2024–2026 amendments?
answers.answer: Non-ferrous EPR is in force in law but not in practice. The Hazardous and Other Wastes (Management and Transboundary Movement) Amendment Rules, 2025 (G.S.R. 438(E), 1 July 2025) added Chapter VIII on EPR for scrap of aluminium, copper, zinc "and their alloys" (so brass is covered; ferrous scrap is not) from 1 April 2026, requiring manufacturers, producers, collection agents, refurbishers and recyclers to register on a CPCB portal, letting bulk consumers (1,000 tonnes or more a year) hand scrap only to registered entities, and setting producer recycling targets of 10% (2026-27) rising to 30% (2028-29), 50% (2030-31) and 75% (2032-33 onwards), with recycled-content minimums of 5% in 2028-29 rising to 10% aluminium, 20% copper and 25% zinc by 2031-32. A kabadiwala buying copper, aluminium or brass scrap and selling it on is, on the text, a "collection agent" (an entity that collects non-ferrous scrap and supplies it to registered recyclers, uploading transactions) and no small-trader threshold has been published, but Business Standard reported on 20 September 2026 that the CPCB non-ferrous portal is still not operational despite the 1 October 2026 deadline in Rule 50(3), the "average product life" parameter needed to compute targets is unpublished, first half-yearly returns fall due 31 October 2026, and Rule 50(4) lets the Centre relax filing by up to nine months, so nobody, kabadiwalas included, can currently register or be penalised for not registering. C&D EPR is also in force: the Environment (Construction and Demolition) Waste Management Rules, 2025 (G.S.R. 219(E), April 2025) apply from 1 April 2026 only to projects of 20,000 sq m or more (25% of prior-year waste recycled in 2025-26 rising to 100% from 2028-29; 5% recycled materials in construction in 2026-27 rising to 25% in 2030-31), with producer and recycler registration on cdwm.cpcb.gov.in (dashboard still showing zeros) and metals expressly outside the EPR base (resalable iron, wood, plastic and glass are excluded and managed under other rules), so C&D EPR does not reach kabadiwala metal trades. On the ₹22/kg e-waste floor (the E-Waste (Management) Amendment Rules, 2024 of 8 March 2024 tied certificate prices to 30–100% of environmental compensation, which CPCB set so consumer electronics floor at ₹22/kg), the Delhi High Court has decided nothing final: petitions filed from April 2025 by Daikin, Voltas, Samsung, LG, Havells, Blue Star and later Carrier (Hitachi withdrew) were opposed by the Centre on 8 July 2025; on 24 December 2025 the court stayed, for Blue Star, CPCB's 12 December 2025 requirement that buyers and sellers self-attest compliance with the floor and listed the matter for 27 January 2026; as of the latest report found (13 June 2026) there is no judgment and the floor remains operative, with recyclers pricing at ₹22/kg while some producers ran reverse auctions as low as ₹5.9/kg. Recycled content after the 31 March 2026 amendment: producers, importers and brand owners must use recycled plastic in packaging at Category I (rigid) 30% in 2025-26, 40% in 2026-27, 50% in 2027-28 and 60% from 2028-29; Category II (flexible) 10%, 10%, 20%, 20%; Category III (multi-layer) 5%, 5%, 10%, 10% counted on the plastic layers only; exemptions apply where FSSAI, CDSCO, the Central Insecticide Board or a mandatory Indian Standard forbids recycled content (proof filed in the annual return); the 2025-26 shortfall for food-contact packaging can be carried forward over three years from 2026-27 with at least one-third cleared each year; importers cannot count recycled content in imported material and must buy certificates from PIBOs that exceed targets on an exchange CPCB is to build; and Rule 11(2) now mandates IS 14534:2023 labelling of recycled content. The 14 March 2024 amendment (G.S.R. 201(E)) changed only definitions and compostable/biodegradable labelling, not these targets.
answers.decision: For the pilot, record copper, aluminium, brass and zinc lots as ordinary scrap trades tagged "non-ferrous EPR-relevant" (weight, price, buyer, seller) so they can be reported if CPCB opens collection-agent registration; promise no metal EPR certificates; leave C&D out of scope; and keep any e-waste certificate revenue assumption at the ₹22/kg floor until the Delhi High Court rules.
answers.whoToAsk: Counsel (or a Delhi High Court case-status check on the Havells/Voltas/Blue Star petitions) for the e-waste ruling; CPCB's hazardous-waste division or KSPCB on whether small scrap dealers will be treated as collection agents and whether any threshold or SOP will apply once the non-ferrous portal opens.

answers.question: Will Razorpay Route or Cashfree Easy Split let a platform split settlements to sellers before it has ₹40 lakh of its own turnover under RBI's September 2025 payment-aggregator directions? If not, what are the alternatives: onboarding each yard as its own merchant, or a bank escrow with a trustee (RazorpayX Escrow+, Castler), with their pricing and KYC requirements for kabadiwalas without GST registration?
answers.answer: No. The RBI (Regulation of Payment Aggregators) Directions, 2025 (15 Sept 2025, RBI/DPSS/2025-26/141), Table 1 'permitted debits' (iv), let a payment aggregator pay a third party on a merchant's instruction only when that merchant has annual domestic turnover above ₹40 lakh (or export turnover above ₹5 lakh) and the third party is the payee who actually deals with the payer; clauses 10(a) and 13(g) otherwise restrict settlement to the contracted merchant's own bank account. Razorpay applies this literally: Route needs GST-3B returns (FY25 or FY26) showing outward taxable supplies above ₹40 lakh or an FIRC above ₹5 lakh, a self-declaration is accepted only for GST-exempt or first-year businesses and must still declare more than ₹40 lakh, proofs were due 31 Dec 2025, and 'if your business does not currently meet the turnover criteria, Route access cannot be continued' (its suggested fallback is to take full settlement yourself and pay vendors from your own account; pricing is 2% gateway fee + 0.1% Route transfer fee + 18% GST). Cashfree's public Easy Split pages (0.20–0.25% split fee on top of a 1.95% gateway rate, or 0% up to ₹20 lakh cumulative GMV until 31 Mar 2027) print no turnover gate and say the product is enabled by your account manager, but the RBI rule binds Cashfree too, so assume the same test until Cashfree confirms otherwise in writing. Alternative A (recommended): onboard each yard and kabadiwala as its own merchant — Razorpay's Partner sub-merchant onboarding APIs let them complete KYC inside your app and accept 'individual', 'proprietorship' and 'not_yet_registered' types; an individual needs only owner PAN, a bank account and Aadhaar/passport/voter ID, GST is 'optional' for a proprietorship (an MSME/Udyam or Shops & Establishment certificate serves as business proof); Cashfree Easy Split vendors likewise need PAN plus one address proof, 'individual vendors do not need a GSTIN', and business vendors need one only after ₹20 lakh of settlements in 12 months. RBI clause 13(b) allows a merchant with turnover up to ₹40 lakh to be onboarded with PAN or Form 60, a physical contact-point verification and one officially valid document (mandatory for merchants onboarded from 1 Jan 2026), so kabadiwalas without GST are onboardable — the buyer then pays the seller directly and Luma.Green collects its own fee separately, so no third-party split ever occurs. Alternative B: a bank escrow with a trustee — RazorpayX Escrow+ (RBL, ICICI, Yes Bank; trustees Axis Trustee and Mitcon Credentia; steps: escrow checklist, bank approval, escrow agreement, account opening, API integration; marketplaces listed as a use case) or Castler (15+ banks including HDFC, SBI, Canara, Union; 'hold buyer funds until delivery is confirmed, then release to the seller'; KYC links, AML screening and penny-drop for every counterparty) — but neither publishes pricing, and Castler's own guide lists PAN/Aadhaar/incorporation documents for all parties, a signed escrow agreement and a board resolution, so it is a slower fixed-cost route suited to yard-to-recycler volumes rather than ₹500 kabadiwala payouts. Whatever you choose, Luma.Green itself must never pool buyers' money in its own account: that is payment-aggregator business needing RBI authorisation with ₹15 crore net worth at application and ₹25 crore by the end of the third financial year — the pilot's simulated escrow is fine precisely because no money moves.
answers.decision: Keep the pilot cash/UPI-recording only. At go-live use the direct-to-seller model (each yard and kabadiwala onboarded as its own Razorpay or Cashfree sub-merchant with PAN + bank + ID, GST optional), bill Luma.Green's fee separately, and apply for Route/Easy Split only once a GST-3B shows more than ₹40 lakh of outward supplies; get Escrow+ and Castler quotes now but treat escrow as a later yard-to-recycler feature.
answers.whoToAsk: Razorpay Route team (whether a >₹40 lakh self-declaration from a first-year company is accepted); Cashfree account manager (Easy Split eligibility below ₹40 lakh, in writing); escrow-rzpx@razorpay.com and Castler sales for pricing and set-up time; a payments lawyer to confirm the sub-merchant plus separate-fee design never makes Luma.Green a payment aggregator.

answers.question: Is the 0.4% UPI merchant fee on payments above ₹2,000 from 15 October 2026 confirmed by NPCI or RBI, what small-merchant limit avoids it, and what are today's UPI per-transaction limits?
answers.answer: Yes, it is confirmed by the Government and NPCI, though the rate itself is not in any gazette: notification S.O. 5067(E) of 14 Sept 2026 (Department of Financial Services, under s.10A of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act) now protects only RuPay debit cards and 'UPI transactions upto Rs. 2,000' from charges, and the Ministry of Finance press release and FAQ of 15 Sept 2026 (PIB PRID 2310586; NPCI hosts the same FAQ) set the framework effective 15 Oct 2026, with NPCI's UPI Steering Committee deciding operating parameters. The numbers: 0.4% MDR on person-to-merchant (P2M) UPI payments above ₹2,000, charged on the whole amount (₹3,000 → ₹12; ₹50,000 → ₹200), capped at ₹300 for payments of ₹75,000 and above; a flat ₹5 for railways, telecom, insurance, fuel, agricultural inputs and utilities; 0.02% (cap ₹300) for capital-market payments; P2P transfers, payments up to ₹2,000 and UPI AutoPay mandates carry no MDR; merchants may not pass it on and apps may not add platform fees; 5% of collections go to a small-merchant fund; NPCI clarified on 22 Sept 2026 that 18% GST applies on the MDR fee itself (a ₹5,000 receipt costs ₹20 + ₹3.60), recoverable as input credit by GST-registered merchants. RBI endorsed the framework on 16 Sept 2026 ('an important step towards strengthening the long-term sustainability of India's digital payments ecosystem') but has issued no circular, and on 28 Sept 2026 the Supreme Court asked the Centre to explain the levy's legal basis on affidavit within four weeks while refusing an interim stay — so plan for 15 Oct and watch late October. The small-merchant escape is the P2PM category: merchants 'receiving up to Rs 1 lac per month through UPI QR directly into their accounts' pay zero MDR on every payment, even above ₹2,000, with no GST registration needed; acquiring banks and PSPs run velocity checks, and a P2PM merchant whose inward UPI credits exceed ₹1 lakh a month for three consecutive months is moved to P2M. For Luma.Green that means most kabadiwalas stay MDR-free if their UPI QR receipts stay under ₹1 lakh/month, while yards (P2M) will pay 0.4% + GST on receipts above ₹2,000 from 15 Oct; a household paying a kabadiwala's personal VPA is P2P and free. Today's UPI limits: NPCI's default is ₹1 lakh per transaction and per day for P2P and ordinary merchant payments (about 20 transactions a day, banks may set lower caps); after RBI let NPCI set P2M limits on 9 Apr 2025, NPCI's circular effective 15 Sept 2025 raised verified merchants in capital markets, insurance, travel and loan EMIs to ₹5 lakh per transaction and ₹10 lakh per day, credit-card bills to ₹5 lakh/₹6 lakh, jewellery ₹2 lakh/₹6 lakh, digital term deposits and GeM ₹5 lakh, and tax, hospital and education payments to ₹5 lakh — scrap trade is not a special category, so yard-to-recycler payments above ₹1 lakh need IMPS/NEFT/RTGS. I could not open NPCI's own circular page (script-rendered), so the category table rests on the government's NewsOnAir summary and dated industry write-ups.
answers.decision: Model 0.4% (cap ₹300) plus 18% GST on every yard-side UPI receipt above ₹2,000 from 15 Oct 2026; store each seller's UPI mode (P2P VPA / P2PM QR / P2M) in the ledger and warn kabadiwalas approaching ₹1 lakh a month; cap UPI entries at ₹1 lakh per transaction and route larger payments to bank transfer.
answers.whoToAsk: Each kabadiwala's UPI app/acquiring bank to confirm P2PM classification; watch NPCI's operating circular and the Centre's Supreme Court affidavit (due around 26 Oct 2026) for any change to the 15 Oct start.
