answers.question: Which banks or NBFCs lend to small scrap dealers and yards in Bengaluru (Mudra loans through partner banks, NBFC purchase finance such as Oxyzo), and would they accept a platform's verified trade history as part of underwriting? Are there examples of recycling-sector lending programmes in India?
answers.answer: The default lender for a kabadiwala or small yard is any bank, RRB, small finance bank, NBFC or MFI lending under Pradhan Mantri MUDRA Yojana: collateral-free loans for 'manufacturing, trading and services' — Shishu up to ₹50,000, Kishore ₹50,000–5 lakh, Tarun ₹5–10 lakh and, since 24 Oct 2024, Tarun Plus ₹10–20 lakh for borrowers who repaid a Tarun loan — guaranteed under CGFMU; MUDRA itself never lends, so the yard applies at a bank branch, and the first step is a free Aadhaar-based Udyam registration, which needs PAN and GSTIN only 'as per applicability of the CGST Act'. For yards and recyclers with scale, Oxyzo (OfBusiness's NBFC) offers purchase finance that pays the supplier directly with 60–120-day repayment, unsecured limits up to ₹5 crore, interest 'from 12% per annum' and fees from 1% — but it requires ₹3 crore+ annual turnover, 3+ years' vintage, GSTIN and audited financials, so it fits recyclers and large yards, not kabadiwalas; Kinara Capital, a Bengaluru-headquartered NBFC, advertises collateral-free ₹1–30 lakh loans for trading businesses registered 2+ years (its pages blocked my fetch, so verify on its site). On platform trade history: banks will not underwrite on it alone (they need bank statements, bureau data and KYC), but anchor-led NBFC programmes do — Progcap (22 June 2025) runs 'transaction-led underwriting' with 128 anchor brands, 30,000+ borrowers, a ₹10 lakh average ticket and 1.1% gross NPAs, and Rupifi embeds 15–90-day B2B credit inside marketplaces funded by Muthoot Finance, UGRO Capital and LiquiLoans; the RBI Digital Lending Directions of 8 May 2025 let a platform act as a Lending Service Provider for 'customer acquisition, services incidental to underwriting and pricing … recovery', with any default-loss guarantee capped at 5% of the disbursed portfolio, so Luma.Green can become the anchor once it has 6–12 months of reconciled per-party trade data — whether a given lender bites is a pilot outcome, not settled from public pages. Recycling-sector precedents exist: in Bengaluru, S3IDF, Hasiru Dala and Rang De (2017) channelled crowdfunded low-interest micro-loans to informal waste entrepreneurs, with S3IDF guaranteeing part and repayments routed through Hasiru Dala, replacing moneylenders charging 24–40%; the EU/GIZ marine-litter project's Risk Sharing Facility at SIDBI (EUR 3.8 million corpus, Bengaluru a project city) guarantees 50% of bank/NBFC working-capital or capex loans to waste firms under ₹25 crore turnover (25% above) and by its mid-term review had backed NEPRA's working-capital loan and GPS Renewables' biogas plant, with MoHUA/HUDCO planning a scaled-up version. Government schemes: MSE-SPICE (launched 20 Dec 2023, ₹472.5 crore outlay to 2026-27, SIDBI-implemented) gives Udyam-registered micro/small units a 25% capital subsidy on plant and machinery, max ₹12.5 lakh on projects up to ₹50 lakh, brownfield only, for plastic, rubber, e-waste and other circular sectors — Bank of Baroda joined on 9 Sept 2025 with CGTMSE collateral-free loans; NAMASTE's waste-picker component (guidelines 2024) pays a capital subsidy of ₹2.5 lakh plus 25% of the remaining cost (max ₹5 lakh per dry-waste collection centre, 750 DWCCs) for waste-collection vehicles bought by waste-picker SHGs; and SIDBI–Shell Foundation's EN-Trans RSF (22 Apr 2026, US$3.1 million second-loss cover for roughly ₹250 crore of loans via banks, RRBs, SFBs and NBFC-MFIs) is the newest template, though aimed at solar assets. ANDE's Sept 2024 sector guide confirms the gap: early-stage waste businesses usually get working capital only from NBFCs at 16–18% against about 12% from banks, and guarantees or FLDG structures are what unlock bank money.
answers.decision: No lending in the pilot. Get every yard and kabadiwala Udyam-registered during KYC; build the ledger so each party has an exportable six-month statement (volumes, counterparties, settlement times, disputes); after the pilot pitch an anchor programme to Kinara Capital (kabadiwalas and small yards) and Oxyzo (recyclers), point yards buying balers or vehicles to MSE-SPICE and waste-picker SHGs to NAMASTE, and ask SIDBI Bengaluru about the risk-sharing facility.
answers.whoToAsk: Kinara Capital and Oxyzo partnership teams (appetite for an anchor programme on Luma.Green's ledger); SIDBI Bengaluru regional office (RSF and SPICE); a public-sector bank branch manager on PMMY appetite for scrap traders; a fintech lawyer on LSP obligations before Luma.Green refers any loan.

answers.question: Is Karnataka's e-way bill limit for intra-state movement ₹50,000 for all goods (confirm from the e-way bill portal or a Karnataka notification), and is the SMS e-way bill facility enough for small yards? Do small yards need a GST filing partner (GSP) to generate e-way bills and e-invoices, and what do such services cost?
answers.answer: Yes. Karnataka requires an e-way bill for any intra-state movement of taxable goods worth more than ₹50,000 per consignment, with no higher state limit and no goods-specific carve-out: it was the first state to switch on intra-state e-way bills on 1 April 2018 under Finance Department Notification FD 47 CSL 2017 dated 23 March 2018 (issued under s.164 of the KGST Act, bringing into force the rules notified on 15 March 2018), whereas Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, Delhi and others later chose ₹1 lakh. Three details matter for the pilot: when a registered yard buys from an unregistered kabadiwala, the yard (the registered party causing the movement) generates the bill and enters 'URP' as the supplier; loads on non-motorised conveyances (pushcarts, cycle carts) and loads under ₹50,000 are exempt; and Part B (vehicle number) is not needed for movement within Karnataka from consignor to transporter under 50 km. The SMS facility is an official NIC mode with no charge: register up to two mobile numbers per GSTIN on ewaybillgst.gov.in, then text 77382 99899 in a fixed format (EWBG to generate, EWBV to change vehicle, EWBC to cancel within 24 hours, EWBT for transporters), one e-way bill per SMS; NIC's manual of 31 March 2018 says it is meant for small taxpayers without IT systems and with few bills a day. That makes SMS adequate as a field backup for a small yard raising a handful of ≥₹50,000 bills a day, but not as the main tool: HSN, pincode, invoice number, value and vehicle are all typed into one message, there is no printout, and it cannot be shared across staff; the free web portal (2FA by SMS OTP, Sandes or the NIC-GST-Shield app has been mandatory for every taxpayer since 1 April 2025), NIC's IMEI-registered Android app and the Excel bulk tool are the other official modes, and since 1 January 2025 a bill cannot be raised on a document older than 180 days. A GSP is not required for anything: direct API access to NIC is limited to taxpayers with turnover of ₹10 crore or more, and everyone else who wants software integration goes through a GSP-backed product, but the portal, SMS and app work without one. E-invoicing is irrelevant to small yards: it applies only where aggregate turnover exceeded ₹5 crore in any year since 2017-18 (Notification 10/2023-Central Tax dated 10 May 2023, effective 1 August 2023), and even a yard above that threshold does not e-invoice the reverse-charge self-invoices it raises for purchases from unregistered suppliers (GSTN e-invoice FAQ v1.3, Q24). Costs of GSP-backed software, all excluding 18% GST: Vyapar Gold ₹799/year (mobile) or ₹4,799/year (mobile + desktop) with unlimited e-way bills and e-invoices (Silver ₹699/₹4,399 caps at 10 a month); myBillBook Pro Max ₹570/month billed yearly (about ₹6,840/year) with unlimited e-way bills; Zoho Books Standard ₹899/month (₹749/month on annual billing) with e-way bills and e-invoicing; TallyPrime Silver ₹22,500 one-time or ₹750/month rental with e-invoicing and e-way bills included; ClearTax's e-invoicing suite starts at ₹7,777/month and is aimed at enterprises. Pure GSP API pricing (Masters India, ClearTax, GSTZen) is quote-only, so it is an open item if Luma.Green ever wants to generate e-way bills from its own app on yards' behalf.
answers.decision: Do not build e-way bill generation into the pilot. Require yards to raise bills on the free NIC portal (SMS as the field backup), and have the pickup/receipt screen ask for the 12-digit e-way bill number whenever consignment value is ₹50,000 or more and the vehicle is motorised; if a yard wants it in-app, recommend Vyapar Gold (₹4,799/year) rather than an enterprise GSP.
answers.whoToAsk: The 10 pilot yards, on whether typical kabadiwala-to-yard loads actually cross ₹50,000 at current Bengaluru scrap prices (decides how often the rule bites); Masters India or ClearTax sales, for a GSP API quote if Luma.Green wants to generate bills on yards' behalf later.

answers.question: Is the MSME 45-day payment rule (MSMED Act s.15–16 and Income-tax s.43B(h)) still in force in 2026, and do Bengaluru yards buying metal from unregistered kabadiwalas issue reverse-charge self-invoices in practice?
answers.answer: Yes, both halves are in force. Section 15 of the MSMED Act 2006 requires a buyer to pay a micro or small enterprise by the agreed date, capped at 45 days from acceptance (15 days if nothing is agreed in writing), and s.16 charges compound interest with monthly rests at three times the RBI bank rate on late payment; the MSMED (Amendment) Bill 2026 (introduced 28 July, passed Rajya Sabha 3 August and Lok Sabha 7 August 2026) leaves ss.15–16 untouched and instead tightens enforcement (mediation within 90 days, arbitration referral within 30 days, award within 90 days, online dispute resolution, release of at least 50% of an award if a challenge is pending over six months, TReDS mandatory for CPSEs, recovery as arrears of land revenue), with Presidential assent and commencement not confirmed on any page opened as of 29 September 2026. On the tax side, s.43B(h) of the 1961 Act governs FY 2025-26 (tax audit due 30 September 2026), and from 1 April 2026 the identical rule sits in s.37(2)(g) of the Income-tax Act 2025, which disallows any 'amount payable by the assessee to a micro or small enterprise beyond the time limit specified in section 15 of the MSMED Act' until the year it is actually paid, with no year-end grace; the Finance Ministry confirmed in the Rajya Sabha (Unstarred Q.242, 21 July 2026, MoS Pankaj Chaudhary) that the rule stays and there is no proposal to relax it. It bites only on dues to Udyam-registered micro or small enterprises, and under MSME Ministry office memoranda of 2 July and 1 September 2021 wholesale and retail traders get Udyam registration only for priority-sector lending, so trader-suppliers (which is what most kabadiwalas are, and most are not Udyam-registered anyway) are generally outside it, while a yard or recycler that sorts or processes could be a manufacturing or service MSE; practitioners still call the trader point a grey area. For Luma.Green this only matters once the platform itself pays anyone (the pilot moves no money): capture the Udyam number at admin verification and pay within 15 days by default. On reverse charge: Notification 06/2024-Central Tax (Rate) dated 8 October 2024 (effective 10 October 2024) makes any registered person buying metal scrap of Customs Tariff Chapters 72–81 from any unregistered person liable to pay 18% GST under reverse charge with no value threshold, paid in cash through the electronic cash ledger and creditable as ITC; the yard must raise a self-invoice under s.31(3)(f) within 30 days of receipt (rule 47A, Notification 20/2024-Central Tax dated 8 October 2024, effective 1 November 2024) plus a payment voucher, and its ITC time limit runs from the year of that self-invoice (Circular 211/5/2024 of 26 June 2024). Alongside, a registered buyer must deduct 2% GST TDS on metal scrap bought from registered suppliers where the contract exceeds ₹2.5 lakh (Notification 25/2024-Central Tax) after registering in Form REG-07; metal scrap stayed at 18% after the 22 September 2025 rate rationalisation, while plastic, paper, rubber and e-waste scrap are at 5% and outside this RCM. Households selling their own scrap are not making a supply in the course of business, so no RCM arises on the household-to-kabadiwala leg, but no official page opened says this in terms, so confirm it with a CA. Whether Bengaluru yards actually issue the self-invoices cannot be settled from public pages: an industry post of 29 August 2026 says many small aggregators have not yet absorbed the October 2024 rules and warns those near the ₹40 lakh registration threshold to register, a practitioner note of July 2025 says large cash deals without a tax trail have become high-risk and dealers must segregate ledgers, and practitioner forums (October 2024 to April 2025) show basic confusion over what even counts as 'scrap', so the law is clear but compliance is uneven, and the rule was lobbied for by parts of the recycling industry to level the field against informal traders.
answers.decision: Treat every kabadiwala-to-yard metal purchase as a reverse-charge transaction unless the kabadiwala has a GSTIN, and design the pilot's yard purchase record as a self-invoice-ready RCM register (yard GSTIN, supplier name/address/phone, 'unregistered' flag, HSN chapter, weight, value, date) with a monthly export; when Luma.Green starts paying suppliers, collect Udyam numbers and pay within 15 days.
answers.whoToAsk: A Bengaluru GST practitioner or CA, for the self-invoice mechanics, the household leg and whether trader-kabadiwalas fall under s.37(2)(g); the 10 pilot yards, on whether they actually raise self-invoices and pay RCM monthly (this decides how much the app must do for them); the Gazette of India or the MSME Ministry, for the assent and commencement date of the 2026 Amendment.

answers.question: Which accounting software do small scrap yards and recyclers in India use (Tally, Busy, Marg, Excel), which Tally release is common, and does Tally accept Excel imports or only XML? Do yards weigh on their own stamped weighbridge, a public weighbridge or platform scales, and do slips carry serial numbers?
answers.answer: No public survey covers scrap yards specifically, but the general market points to Tally: Tally says 2.5 million+ businesses use it (tallysolutions.com, read 30 Sep 2026), IMARC (7 Jul 2026) sizes India's accounting-software market at USD 698.87 million in 2025 with SMEs at 65% and names Tally, Busy, Marg and Zoho as the key players, and Marg positions itself for pharma/FMCG distribution, not scrap. The scrap-specific evidence is about informality rather than software: the ILO-SNDT Pune study found retail scrap traders issue no receipts to collectors and that 'cheating in weights' and credit slips instead of cash are common; a 22 Sep 2026 tax guide notes dealers under Rs 2 crore turnover (Rs 3 crore if cash receipts are 5% or less) can file under presumptive section 44AD with no books at all, though it advises keeping purchase and sales registers and weighment slips; a 11 Nov 2025 GST guide lists the registers, e-way bills and the Oct 2024 metal-scrap TDS (2% above Rs 2.5 lakh) and RCM rules a registered dealer must handle. Working assumption for the pilot: GST-registered yards and recyclers keep books in Tally (often run by their CA), kabadiwalas keep a notebook, WhatsApp or Excel. On Tally releases: the current version is TallyPrime 7.1 (20 May 2026); Excel import (default template or a mapped custom sheet, covering masters and transactions such as sales, purchase, receipt and payment) only exists from TallyPrime 4.0 (27 Nov 2023), JSON from 7.0, while XML import works on every release including older TallyPrime and Tally.ERP 9, so pre-4.0 installs are XML-only; there is no public data on which release yards run, so that is an open item. On weighing: section 24 of the Legal Metrology Act 2009 requires every weight or measure used in a transaction to be verified and stamped, Rule 27(2) of the Legal Metrology (General) Rules 2011 sets re-verification at 12 months for weighbridges and platform scales (24 months for beam scales and counter machines), and a 6 Jul 2026 amendment cut the standard weights needed to verify instruments of 1 tonne and above from 50% to 20% of capacity; a 3 Jun 2026 guide for new scrap dealers recommends a 30–60 tonne platform scale at Rs 2.5–6 lakh certified by the district Weights and Measures inspector, and in practice kabadiwalas use small platform or hanging scales while truck loads go over the yard's own weighbridge or a nearby public weighbridge. On slips: the 2011 rules prescribe no ticket format or serial numbers; computerised weighbridge software prints serial-numbered gross/tare/net tickets, and the ReMA ISRI Specifications (July 2026) show how the trade treats them, with the buyer's certified-scale weight governing and no adjustment for weight variance of 1% or less. Open items: the Karnataka verification-fee schedule (the 2021 Karnataka Legal Metrology (Enforcement) Amendment Rules revised fees but the weighbridge figure is not on an open page) and whether Bengaluru yards' scales are actually in-date.
answers.decision: Ship a Tally XML export (works on every Tally release) plus a plain CSV/Excel; do not build a live Tally connector for the pilot. Have the platform assign its own serial number to every weighment, store the scale ID, its stamp-expiry date and a photo of the yard's slip, and treat the yard's certified scale as the governing weight.
answers.whoToAsk: Ask 10 Bengaluru yards and recyclers which software and Tally release they run and whether they weigh on their own weighbridge, a public weighbridge or a platform scale; ask their CA how books are kept; ask the Assistant Controller of Legal Metrology, Bengaluru for the current verification fee for weighbridges and platform scales and whether a public-weighbridge licence is needed.

answers.question: What grade names, quality parameters and deduction rules do Bengaluru or South Indian buyers and paper mills apply to waste paper, PET and metal (ISRI names, mill specs, moisture and contamination deductions)? Do recyclers hold CPCB processor (PWP) registration, and does the plastic portal accept bulk uploads or only single-entry forms? Would GRS, ISCC PLUS auditors or CPCB physical verification accept a platform's weight and photo record as supporting evidence?
answers.answer: Grades are local trade names layered on the ReMA (ex-ISRI) specifications (July 2026 edition): for paper, OCC (11) allows prohibitives up to 1% and outthrows-plus-prohibitives up to 5%, double-sorted OCC (12) 0.5%/2%, sorted office paper (37) 1%/2%, unsorted office paper (36) 2%/10%, maximum moisture is 12% with the buyer entitled to test, adjust or reject, and no weight adjustment applies under 1% variance; Bengaluru listings (IndiaMART, 29 Sep 2026) trade as OCC Rs 15/kg, duplex Rs 16, newspaper Rs 18, mixed Rs 13, white cutting Rs 35, old books Rs 40 and colour record Rs 10/kg, and the Pune ILO study records the dealer names kraft, white record, RS, mixed mein and pushta. For PET the APR/ReMA bale spec (Sep 2022, carried in the July 2026 circular) grades bales A (94%+ PET fraction), B (83–93%) and C (73–82%), caps and labels may stay on, any single contaminant is capped at 2%, PVC is zero-tolerance and the India Plastics Pact (Nov 2022) notes 83–88% of Indian bottles are clear and 10–15% green so traders colour-sort before selling; Bengaluru listings on 29 Sep 2026 run Rs 15–20/kg loose and Rs 35–57/kg baled or washed clear. For metals, BIS IS 2549:2023 (17 Feb 2023) classifies ferrous scrap into home, prompt and obsolete with HMS, LMS, bundles, turnings and foundry grades, IS 2066 (Part 1):2024 codes aluminium scrap, and the Aluminium Association of India was still pressing on 8 Jul 2026 for notification of the pending 'Aluminium & Aluminium Alloy Scrap – Requirements & Conditions of Delivery' standard; ReMA names in use are Taint/Tabor (clean mixed old alloy sheet, oil under 1%), Zorba, Barley/Berry/Candy copper, Honey brass and No.1 HMS (code 200, quarter-inch thick), and Bengaluru listings quote aluminium utensil/'bartan'/Tense Rs 215–220/kg, extrusion Rs 285, wire Rs 122, Millberry/Berry-Candy copper Rs 1,330/kg, cast iron Rs 27/kg and GI Rs 42/kg. South Indian mills' actual moisture and dirt ('kachra') deduction formulas are contract terms and are not on any open page, so that is an open item. On CPCB: every recycler and end-of-life processor must register as a PWP with its SPCB (KSPCB here) on eprplastic.cpcb.gov.in, paying Rs 5,000 (under 200 TPA), Rs 20,000 (200–2,000 TPA) or Rs 50,000 (over 2,000 TPA) plus 25% a year as processing fee, with a fresh registration valid one year and renewals three years, and can issue certificates only after the SPCB regional officer's physical verification (due within 30 days) that checks PAN/GST, GPS location, machinery, power load, electricity bill and geo-tagged photos and fixes a 'conversion factor' (CPCB SOP 15 Mar 2022; guidance manual Feb 2023); collectors, kabadiwalas and yards that only aggregate do not register (FAQ Q14). The PWP portal is single-entry: CPCB's module guidance (Nov 2022, Q18) says 'only single entries can be made in the procurement section', each procurement needs the supplier's GST or PAN/Aadhaar and invoice, each sale needs a signed GST e-invoice with IRN and QR code (the 7 Apr 2025 CEPP app scans one QR at a time), and the 'bulk upload' in the Feb 2023 manual is a PIBO-side aggregate of two years of purchases from one unregistered entity plus a PDF statement, not a row-wise Excel; note e-invoicing is mandatory only above Rs 5 crore turnover (from 1 Aug 2023) and optional below, so a small recycler must self-enable on the IRP to sell into the EPR system. Enforcement is tightening: CSE (Oct 2024) counted 2,499 registered PWPs as of 14 Aug 2024 and 6 lakh fraudulent certificates, CPCB's April 2024 EC guidelines levy Rs 5,000 per tonne for misreported quantities, and the PWM (Amendment) Rules 2026 (G.S.R. 237(E), 31 Mar 2026) let 'registered environment auditors' verify processors and require recycled packaging to conform to IS 14534:2023. On auditors: GRS 5.0 (published 1 Jul 2026, mandatory 31 Dec 2026) requires the first certified entity to hold a Reclaimed Material Supplier Agreement and a signed Reclaimed Material Declaration Form (which since 24 Jul 2025 covers non-textile waste such as PET) for every input, to inspect incoming shipments and keep records, exempts collection from individuals, and has certification bodies verify 10% of collectors (2% on site) for RMDF authenticity; ISCC PLUS 203-1 v1.1 (13 Nov 2025) requires records of incoming material 'e.g. weighbridge tickets, bill of lading and sustainability declarations' kept 'as hard copies and/or electronically' for five years, each delivery documented by weighbridge tickets 'or similar documents', collecting points to run plausibility checks on amounts, and signed self-declarations from points of origin (which may sit inside a contract or terms and conditions), while household post-consumer collection stays outside the certified chain; CPCB physical verification checks the facility, not transactions, and the portal accepts only invoices. So a platform weight-and-photo record is good supporting evidence (delivery documentation, inspection records, plausibility checks, the data to pre-fill an RMDF or self-declaration) but never a substitute for the signed RMDF, self-declaration or GST invoice, and whether a given auditor will lean on it is a pilot question.
answers.decision: Adopt ReMA/ISRI names as the canonical grade codes with a local-name alias per grade (OCC/duplex/record/white cutting; PET clear/green/mixed with an A/B/C PET-fraction field; HMS/cast/GI, aluminium utensil/extrusion/wire, copper Millberry/Berry) and capture moisture % and contamination % per lot with a free-text deduction field, since mill deduction formulas are contract-specific. Treat recyclers as CPCB-registered PWPs and build a one-invoice-per-row export (supplier GST or PAN/Aadhaar, quantity, category, date, invoice number, IRN) that an operator keys into the portal, not a bulk feed. Design the weight-and-photo record as an audit exhibit that sits beside, and pre-fills, the signed RMDF/ISCC self-declaration and the GST invoice.
answers.whoToAsk: Purchase desks at three South Indian mills (for example South India Paper Mills, Nanjangud; Seshasayee; TNPL) and two Bengaluru PET and metal recyclers for their written moisture/contamination deduction rules; KSPCB's regional office for how it runs physical verification and conversion factors; one accredited GRS certification body and one ISCC PLUS certification body active in India to confirm they will accept the platform record as delivery documentation; the CPCB helpline (011-43102469) and a CA on e-invoice enablement for a sub-Rs 5 crore recycler.

answers.question: Has the Karnataka Platform-Based Gig Workers (Social Security and Welfare) Act 2025 been brought into force with rules, what welfare-fee rates and categories were notified (Feb 2026), and what is the status of the reported 2026 Karnataka High Court challenge?
answers.answer: Yes, the Act is in force and operational. Karnataka Act No. 72 of 2025 received the Governor's assent on 11 Sep 2025, was gazetted on 12 Sep 2025 and is deemed in force from 30 May 2025 (s.1(2), replacing Ordinance 04 of 2025); the Karnataka Platform Based Gig Workers (Social Security and Welfare) Rules, 2025 were notified on 19 Nov 2025 (No. LD 413 LET 2023, Gazette Part IVA No. 739 of 20 Nov 2025) and took effect on publication; the 16-member Welfare Board was constituted by notification on 27 Jan 2026 with a 45-day window for aggregators to register. The welfare-fee order under s.20 was issued on 13 Feb 2026 and set every notified category at 1% of the payout per transaction (the Act allows 1-5%) with per-transaction rupee caps: ride-hailing Rs 0.50 (2W) / Rs 0.75 (3W) / Rs 1.00 (4W); food and grocery delivery Rs 0.50 (2W); logistics Rs 0.50 (2W) / Rs 0.75 (3W) / Rs 1.00 (LCV) / Rs 1.50 (HCV); e-marketplace Rs 0.50 (2W) / Rs 0.75 (3W) / Rs 1.00 (LCV); professional activity providers Rs 1.50 (any vehicle). The fee is charged on the aggregator/platform (workers keep 100% of payouts), is self-declared and remitted within 5 working days of each quarter-end, excludes tips/incentives/referral 'settled payments' (Rule 17), and platforms may self-report payouts quarterly until the PWFVS portal is live (s.21 proviso); no rate has been reported for the Schedule's healthcare, travel-and-hospitality or content-and-media categories, which is an open item. The High Court challenge is real and pending: IAMAI, Eternal (Zomato/Blinkit), Swiggy, Zepto, Urban Company and Valmo Transportation filed WP 19746/2026 in late June 2026 (27-29 Jun) arguing the Act is repugnant to the Code on Social Security 2020 under Article 254, and the Union of India's ASG supported them in court; on 3 Jul 2026 Justice M. Nagaprasanna refused to stay the Act, ordered the petitioners to deposit the April-June quarter's fee with the Court registry by 23 Jul 2026, barred coercive steps against them in the meantime, set objections by 31 Jul and rejoinder by 10 Aug, and listed the matter for 14 Aug 2026. Uber's separate WP 19776/2026 received the same interim protection on 28 Jul 2026 (Justice Suraj Govindaraj), with three weeks to deposit, notice returnable 24 Aug 2026 and tagging with the IAMAI batch. As of the last public reporting on 31 Aug 2026, six platforms had deposited about Rs 4 crore with the Court for the April-June quarter, 15 platforms covering roughly 7 lakh workers had registered with the Board, Yulu paid the Board directly, and Uber, Eternal and Porter had resigned from the Board; no judgment or stay has been reported, and I could not find what happened at the 14 Aug and 24 Aug listings (open item). Practical reading for 29 Sep 2026: the law binds every aggregator and platform in Karnataka now; only the named petitioners have court cover, and even they must put the money down.
answers.decision: Plan as if the Karnataka Act fully applies from pilot day one (13 Oct 2026): register with the Board, upload Saathi data, and budget 1% of Saathi payouts capped at Rs 0.50-1.50 per job (a few thousand rupees a month at pilot scale); do not bank on the High Court striking the Act down.
answers.whoToAsk: Check the current stage of WP 19746/2026 and WP 19776/2026 on the Karnataka High Court case-status portal or via counsel (nothing public after 31 Aug 2026); ask the Karnataka Platform Based Gig Workers Welfare Board (Labour Department, Bengaluru) whether rates have been notified for the Schedule categories absent from the 13 Feb 2026 order.

answers.question: Is a scrap-pickup marketplace or a Saathi job board an 'aggregator' or 'e-marketplace' under the Karnataka Act and under the Social Security Code's Seventh Schedule and the Social Security (Central) Rules 2026, if the kabadiwala pays the Saathi directly rather than the platform? If so, which fee category, who pays, and does the internal dispute committee duty apply?
answers.answer: Almost certainly yes, and the payment route does not take Luma.Green outside either law. Both definitions are payment-agnostic: the Karnataka Act s.2(b) makes an 'aggregator' any 'digital intermediary for a buyer of goods or user of a service to connect with the seller or the service provider' (plus any entity that coordinates with aggregators), and the Code s.2(2) wording is near-identical; a Saathi job board connects kabadiwalas (users of pickup/sorting services) with Saathis (service providers) and the scrap marketplace connects buyers and sellers of goods, so both limbs are met, and Karnataka independently catches Luma.Green as a 'platform' (s.2(g): a service arranged electronically that organises work by individuals at a location for payment using data-driven or automated decisions), with s.1(3)(ii) applying the Act to every platform. Saathis are 'gig workers' (s.2(e)) only if the work is in a Schedule service: pickups fit item 3 'Logistics services' and the marketplace fits item 4 'e-Market place... B2B/B2C'; sorting shifts fit item 5 'Professional activity provider' less cleanly, and Karnataka's Schedule has only eight entries with no residual category (the central Seventh Schedule has nine, including 'any other goods and services provider platform'), although the Rules' Form A quarterly return does carry 'Warehousing' and 'Any other not in the category' rows. Under the 13 Feb 2026 order the Karnataka fee for pickups is 1% of each payout capped at Rs 0.50 per 2W logistics job (Rs 0.75 3W, Rs 1.00 LCV, Rs 1.50 HCV) and Rs 1.50 per professional-services job, e.g. 10 Saathis x 20 pickups x 26 days = 5,200 jobs, about Rs 2,600 a month at most; it is charged on the aggregator/platform (s.20(1)), not on the Saathi and not on the kabadiwala, who is not a digital intermediary, and s.20(5) makes whatever Karnataka collects count toward the central s.114(4) contribution so there is no double payment. The direct-pay wrinkle is real: s.2(f) defines 'payout' as final payments 'made by the aggregator or platform to the gig worker', so on a literal reading a kabadiwala-pays-cash model has no payout and a zero fee base, but s.21 requires 'all payments made to workers generated on platform' to be mapped to PWFVS and s.15 assumes the platform itself pays at least weekly, so the Board is likely to treat the kabadiwala's payment as the payout and the rest of the Act's machinery presupposes it; this is the one point only counsel or the Board can settle. Under the central Code, Luma.Green is an aggregator in Seventh Schedule categories 3 (logistics), 4 (e-marketplace B2B/B2C) and/or 9 (any other), and Saathis are platform workers under s.2(60)-(61); the money obligation (s.114(4): 1-2% of annual turnover, capped at 5% of amounts 'paid or payable by an aggregator' to gig and platform workers, which would be near zero if Luma.Green pays them nothing) is dormant because the s.114(5) commencement date has not been notified as of September 2026, but the registration duties are live under the Social Security (Central) Rules 2026 (G.S.R. 344(E), 8 May 2026): Rule 48(2)(b) gave 45 days (to about 22 Jun 2026) to upload existing workers, Rule 48(2)(c) requires real-time or daily API registration of new workers and exits, Rule 49(5) requires the aggregator to register on the designated portal, and once contributions start Form XX self-assessment is due by 30 June and Form XXI return by 31 October, with 1% per month interest on late payment (Rule 49(2)). The IDRC duty does apply and has no size threshold: s.22(2) and Rule 21 require every registered aggregator or platform to constitute a committee of 1 senior-management chairperson, 2 management members and at least 3 senior gig workers, with at least 2 women; grievances about payouts, deductions or termination must be filed within 7 working days (Rule 11(1)), the committee must issue a written action-taken report within 14 days and a final order within 45 days (s.22(4),(6); Rule 22(2)), and the worker can appeal to the Board's authorised person within 30 days (Rule 11(3)). The app must also carry the grievance-portal link and disclosures in Kannada and English (s.17, s.22(2) proviso, Rule 13), a human point of contact (s.18), 14-day written notice before deactivation (s.14), at-least-weekly pay with deductions explained (s.15), Saathi database updates within 7 days (Rule 8), PWFVS uploads within 7 days of each transaction (Rule 20), the fee within 5 working days of quarter-end (Rule 17) and a Form A return within 30 working days of quarter-end (Rule 29). Penalties are 12% p.a. interest on late fee and fines up to Rs 5,000 for a first contravention and Rs 1 lakh thereafter (s.23), but the larger exposure is Rule 7(7), under which the Board can order an unregistered platform to produce work histories of every gig worker since the Act commenced and to deposit the fee for all of them.
answers.decision: Treat Luma.Green as an 'aggregator' and a 'platform' under both the Karnataka Act and the central Code from 13 Oct 2026 regardless of who pays the Saathi: register with the Karnataka Board under 'Logistics services - 2W' for pickups and 'Professional activity provider' for sorting (record vehicle type per job so the cap is computable), treat the kabadiwala's recorded cash/UPI amount as the payout, self-report quarterly and remit 1% capped per job, constitute a 6-person IDRC (3 senior Saathis, at least 2 women) and put the grievance link plus Kannada/English disclosures in the Saathi app before launch; register on the central designated portal and upload Saathi details, budgeting Rs 0 central contribution until s.114(5) is notified.
answers.whoToAsk: A Bengaluru labour/platform-law counsel for one written opinion on whether a direct-pay job board creates a 'payout' under s.2(f)/s.20 (and whether to route Saathi payments through Luma.Green's ledger or in-app UPI to make the base clean) and whether sorting falls under Schedule item 5; then the Karnataka Platform Based Gig Workers Welfare Board (Labour Department, Bengaluru) to confirm the registration category under Rule 7(2)(h) and the interim self-reporting format.

answers.question: Will UIDAI register an early-stage startup as an Offline Verification Seeking Entity (OVSE), at what fee and process, and does the Aadhaar app's credential-sharing flow work from a web app or PWA rather than a native app? Should a pilot accept masked Aadhaar at all given the QR-signature check, or only driving licence, voter ID, PAN or DigiLocker documents?
answers.answer: Yes in principle: UIDAI's OVSE page (published 13 May 2026, updated 18 Sep 2026) invites "any other entity requiring Aadhaar offline verification" (gig economy and NGOs are listed use cases) to apply at https://ovse.uidai.gov.in/, and Regulation 13A (inserted 9 Dec 2025) sets no size, age or turnover test, only a lawful purpose, UIDAI's terms, and the documents the January 2026 handbook lists: PAN, certificate of incorporation/CIN, company profile, a self-declaration, a registered domain, an HTTPS callback URL, a Class 2 or 3 public certificate valid 2 years and an SVG logo under 10 KB. About 100 entities (fintechs, event and hospitality firms, background-verification companies, government departments) were registered within roughly three months of the January 2026 rollout and IAMAI was onboarded in August 2026, so private companies of all sizes are being accepted. Fee: Regulation 13A(9) lets UIDAI charge registration and per-transaction fees, but no amount is published on any official page; secondary guides (Decentro, 27 Apr 2026; SecuredApp, 22 Aug 2026) call it nominal or unpublished and report a few weeks to a couple of months from application to go-live, so the fee is an open item and OVSE registration cannot sit on the 13 Oct critical path. Web/PWA: the Aadhaar app's credential flow does work for web verifiers. UIDAI's developer docs describe a portal-initiated journey in which your web page shows a QR code carrying a JWT signed with your certificate, the person scans it with the Aadhaar app (face auth, picks which fields to share), and the app POSTs a selectively-disclosed SD-JWT to your HTTPS callback URL, which your backend verifies against UIDAI's public key; the handbook names three pathways (cross-device QR, app-to-app intent, web-to-app intent) and an Android/iOS App ID is mandatory only for app-to-app. Practical consequences: request signing and the callback must live server-side (a Convex HTTP action), and the same-phone web-to-app handoff from an installed PWA, especially on iOS, is not documented in detail, so treat it as a pilot test, while the cross-device QR (admin's screen, worker's phone) is the safe path and fits your one-admin model. Masked Aadhaar: the secure QR on every e-Aadhaar, masked e-Aadhaar and PVC card is digitally signed by UIDAI (2048-bit) and by regulatory definition carries only the last 4 digits plus name, DOB, gender, address and photo, so masking does not break verification; Regulation 16C forbids accepting Aadhaar in any form without checking that signature, and the handbook says QR and e-Aadhaar signature checks do not require OVSE registration. UIDAI's FAQ (updated 18 Sep 2026) says QR reading is limited to the Aadhaar App and the Aadhaar QR Scanner app, so for the pilot do not build a parser or accept card uploads: the admin validates in person with UIDAI's scanner app and records only name, last 4 digits, a QR-verified flag, date and admin ID. Storing the Aadhaar number is barred (Regulations 14A(b) and 20A; Act s.29(4); s.40 penalty up to Rs 1 lakh for a company) and Regulation 5(3) requires that nobody is refused service for not offering Aadhaar, so driving licence, voter ID and PAN must be accepted in any case.
answers.decision: For the 13 Oct pilot verify people with driving licence, voter ID or PAN (DigiLocker once live) checked by the admin, and accept Aadhaar only as an in-person secure-QR check using UIDAI's own scanner app (masked e-Aadhaar is fine), storing last 4 digits and a verified flag and never an image or the full number. Apply for OVSE registration this week (cross-device QR pathway, domain plus callback URL, Class 3 DSC) and move Saathi and kabadiwala verification to the Aadhaar-app credential flow once approved.
answers.whoToAsk: ovse.registration@uidai.net.in / ovse.support@uidai.net.in for the current fee, terms and typical approval time; a two-phone pilot test for the same-device web-to-app handoff from the PWA on Android and iOS; counsel for the DPDP consent notice wording shown before any ID check.

answers.question: How does a private company onboard as a DigiLocker requester through API Setu (process, cost, timeline), and can an NGO's attestation stand in for ID for undocumented migrant waste pickers under KYC-style verification?
answers.answer: Route: DigiLocker requester access is granted by NeGD (MeitY) through the API Setu partners portal (https://partners.apisetu.gov.in) under the Partner Organisation Onboarding SOP dated 5 June 2024: a senior authorised person registers with an official-domain email, the entity is verified (CIN/GSTIN/PAN/Udyam) through Entity Locker with the nodal officer's Aadhaar OTP, you submit the use cases and integration flow, a business-development manager and an onboarding committee (which meets weekly) review it, the CEO gives final approval, you sign the Requester Terms of Use, integrate against the Requester API (v1.12, Oct 2023) or Meri Pehchaan API (v2.4, Sep 2026), demo the flow and go live; afterwards NeGD expects quarterly usage reports and an STQC audit report of your application. Eligibility: the SOP says "all private organisations" registered under the Companies Act, MSME, Startup India etc. can be partners, but you need a functional website describing your service, your own digital signature certificate, and it refuses "temporary access for testing" and deletes unverified accounts after 3 months; the "3 completed fiscal years" rule often quoted comes from NeGD's separate API-as-a-service provider empanelment (June 2025), not the requester path. Cost: the Requester Terms of Use (updated 2 June 2025) state "Currently, there are no platform charges applicable", so your costs are the DSC, engineering and the STQC audit. Timeline: no official SLA is published; practitioners (NamoID, 6 Jun 2026) call organisational approval "the long pole" with the technical work about a day, so plan on several weeks to a couple of months, use a TSP such as Setu (sandbox and production, credentials issued by Setu, no public pricing) or manual checks for a 13 Oct start, and apply directly in parallel; MeitY's Request for Empanelment of 21 Sep 2026 signals a push to bring private-sector requesters on through empanelled agencies. NGO attestation: under the RBI KYC Master Direction (updated 14 Aug 2025) an officially valid document is a passport, driving licence, Aadhaar, voter ID, NREGA job card or NPR letter; the 2014 relaxation accepting a gazetted officer's letter no longer appears in the Direction and NGO letters have never been OVDs, so the only formal banking fallback is the Small Account (self-attested photo plus signature or thumb impression before a bank officer; credits up to Rs 1 lakh a year, withdrawals up to Rs 10,000 a month, balance up to Rs 50,000; 12 months, extendable by 12 if an OVD has been applied for). Because Luma moves no money in the pilot and is not an RBI-regulated entity, RBI KYC does not bind your own verification, and there is official precedent for community attestation of occupation: the NAMASTE waste-picker guidelines (SFC approval 20 Jun 2024) let ULB-engaged CSOs profile waste pickers and accept "endorsement by scrap shop owners / other registered waste pickers / local sanitation staff or membership of recognised waste picker organisations", after which the ULB validates and the system issues an ID card (1.52 lakh enumerated nationally as of 3 Feb 2026). Bengaluru specifics: BBMP's occupational ID cards (about 10,437 issued through Hasiru Dala since 2011) required proof of city residence and excluded migrants, and BBMP has stopped issuing or renewing them (Citizen Matters, 15 Sep 2025); e-Shram needs an Aadhaar number plus an Aadhaar-linked mobile or CSC biometrics. So an attestation letter from a recognised waste-picker organisation (Hasiru Dala) or a verified kabadiwala plus an admin-taken photo can support a capped provisional Saathi tier (no cash custody, pickups paired with a verified partner) with a 90-day path to a NAMASTE ID, e-Shram or Aadhaar via the NGO's social-security desk and a DPDP-compliant notice and consent, but it can never substitute at the payment layer: when escrow goes live, payouts need a bank or UPI account, which needs the bank's own KYC.
answers.decision: Apply for direct DigiLocker requester access now (no platform charge; expect weeks) and, if you need DigiLocker on day one, integrate through a TSP for the pilot. Treat NGO or kabadiwala attestation as a capped provisional tier with an expiry, not as identity proof, and have counsel sign off the tier and the DPDP notice before 13 Oct.
answers.whoToAsk: The DigiLocker onboarding team via the partners portal for current approval time, whether the SOP's 'authorisation from regulatory bodies' clause applies to requesters, and the STQC audit scope; counsel for the provisional tier and DPDP notice; Hasiru Dala and the city corporation's NAMASTE nodal officer for enumeration status in Bengaluru and whether the NAMASTE app needs Aadhaar; a bank branch for Small Account practice.

answers.question: For investors, should Luma.Green quote e-waste at 1.4 Mt (CPCB, FY2024-25) or 6.19 Mt (NITI Aayog, 2024)? Explain how each is measured and which to lead with. What figure is defensible for India's recycling market size and for the number of waste pickers?
answers.answer: The two numbers measure different things, so quote both but never in the same series. CPCB's figure is administrative: 13,97,955.59 tonnes (about 1.4 Mt) for FY2024-25, up from 12,54,286.55 t in FY2023-24, computed from sales data filed by registered producers times the average life of the 106 EEE items notified under the E-Waste (Management) Rules 2022 (Lok Sabha written reply, PIB, 11 Aug 2025); the March 2026 reply moved it to 14.14 lakh t generated and 9.79 lakh t recycled (about 69%) for FY2025-26 (PTI/NewsDrum, 9 Mar 2026). NITI Aayog's 6.19 Mt for 2024 (report launched 22 Jan 2026 with TERI) is not a count but a model: the report attributes it to the ITU/UNITAR Global E-waste Monitor series, which estimates e-waste from everything placed on the market across 54 product categories (toys, lamps, tools, all appliances) and their lifespans, independent of producer filings; GEM 2024's own published India figure is 4.1 Mt for 2022, and NITI's Fig. 3 is labelled a projection. Lead with the CPCB number as the official, regulator-backed figure that ties to the EPR system, then show NITI's 6.19 Mt as the modelled upper bound, framed as 'the formal system records roughly a quarter of the modelled stream' -- that gap is Luma.Green's pitch, and NITI supplies the supporting stats: formal recycling about 10% versus a 22% global average, informal sector handling about 62%, only 2,808 collection centres, formal capacity about 1.75 Mt across 400+ recyclers, and an e-waste stream worth about Rs 51,000 crore a year of which only 18% of the technically recoverable value is captured. There is no official 'India recycling market size'; the most quotable analyst figures are EY-Parthenon's India waste-management market of about USD 32 billion (2023), MRAI's projection that scrap demand reaches 65 Mt a year by 2030 with domestic generation covering only half, and MRAI's non-ferrous metals industry at USD 18 billion heading to USD 30 billion in five years (MRAI/ANI, 22 Feb 2025) -- cite the source and year each time and prefer a bottom-up Bengaluru tonnage-times-price model for the deck's own TAM. For waste pickers there is no census: the defensible line is '1.5 to 4 million' (ILO and Chintan estimates, as reported by Down To Earth, 15 May 2026), with the ILO's 2019 paper tracing the 1.5 million to the Alliance of Indian Waste Pickers; a useful proof point is that the Centre's own NAMASTE scheme only set out to enumerate 2.5 lakh waste pickers when it added them in June 2024 (PIB, 5 Jun 2025). One open item: parliamentary replies give different FY2024-25 processing figures (70.7% in one dataset, 11.59 lakh t recycled in another), so quote the FY2025-26 pair (9.79 of 14.14 lakh t) for the recycled share.
answers.decision: Lead with CPCB 1.4 Mt (FY2024-25; 14.1 lakh t FY2025-26) as the official figure, and cite NITI Aayog's 6.19 Mt only as the modelled upper bound that shows the formal-system gap. For market size use sourced analyst figures (USD 32 bn waste management, MRAI 65 Mt scrap demand by 2030) plus a bottom-up model; for waste pickers say '1.5-4 million, no official count'.
answers.whoToAsk: A licensed analyst report (EY-Parthenon or Avendus) or MRAI directly if the deck needs one headline 'recycling market' number; everything else is settled from public pages.

answers.question: Recommend defaults with reasoning for the founders' open product decisions: pickup charges or minimum load; recycle points value and CSR funding; zero-value items earning points; excluding batteries and e-waste from the household pilot; auto-accept limited to shop hours; a no-show rule; Saathi accident insurance options and cost; business fees after the pilot.
answers.answer: Pickups: do not charge households (the kabadiwala habit is 'I get paid', and a fee flips it) but set a minimum by estimated value, not weight; Delhi comparables show the norm is free pickup with a value floor (ScrapBuddy Rs 200; KabadiwalaOnline Rs 999 plus a Rs 499 cancellation charge), and at Bengaluru rates (newspaper Rs 10/kg, iron Rs 22/kg, PET Rs 10/kg on The Kabadiwala's Bangalore card) a Rs 150-200 floor is roughly 15-20 kg of paper; below the floor, route the request into a weekly area round or a drop-at-shop option rather than on-demand, and set the final floor after two weeks of measured kg-per-stop and Saathi stop time. Points: keep them a closed loop (1 point = Re 1 for easy mental math, earned at about 5% of scrap value, capped per pickup and per month, redeemable only for partner vouchers or a pickup bonus, never cash) and fund them from Luma.Green's own marketing budget; CSR is not a realistic funder of points because the MCA's CSR FAQ (General Circular 14/2021, 25 Aug 2021) excludes activities in a company's normal course of business, sponsorship for marketing benefit, activities benefiting a company's own employees, and spending that fulfils a statutory obligation (which is what EPR is), and CSR money can only flow through an implementing agency that is a Section 8 company, registered trust or society with 12A/80G registration, a three-year track record and CSR-1 registration -- a private company like Luma.Green cannot receive it directly, so the workable CSR route is Saathi welfare (PPE, insurance, training) via a registered NGO partner, while EPR-obligated producers are the natural per-kg funders of collection (NITI's Annexure IV notes CPCB sets EPR certificate prices at 30-100% of environmental compensation, paid only after verification, i.e. slow money that reaches registered recyclers, not collectors). Zero-value items: yes, they can earn points without distorting cash prices as long as points sit on a separate ledger from the cash price and are never cash-convertible, so the shop's price for glass or film stays whatever the market pays (The Kabadiwala's Bangalore card lists no price for glass or clothes, Delhi's KabadiwalaOnline states it does not handle glass or fabrics, ScrapBuddy lists glass at Rs 3/kg, and multilayer plastic fetches about Rs 5/kg in Delhi NCR); the real risk is dumping unsaleable material on the shop, so enable each zero-value category only when a downstream taker (a BBMP dry-waste centre, a textile-reuse partner) is mapped and the shop opts in, with old clothes off by default. Batteries and e-waste: exclude from the household pilot; the E-Waste (Management) Rules 2022 (in force 1 Apr 2023) cover 106 items, require recyclers to register on the CPCB portal (Rule 9) and bulk consumers to hand e-waste only to registered producers, refurbishers or recyclers (Rule 8), and CPCB's directions of 6 Sep 2022 and 30 Jan 2024 make informal e-waste collection the thing SPCBs are told to police, while the Battery Waste Management Rules 2022 (24 Aug 2022) require consumers to keep batteries separate and hand them only to an entity engaged in collection, refurbishment or recycling; add both streams in phase 2 once a KSPCB-registered recycler or a producer take-back partner is contracted and its registration number is recorded on every trade (the pull is real: e-waste pays Rs 10/kg and inverter batteries Rs 70/kg in Bengaluru). Auto-accept: yes, limit it to declared shop hours and to shops with a Saathi marked available, with a daily cap; outside hours, queue the request with the next-opening ETA, because an accepted request is a time promise and a silent no-show costs more trust than a visible delay (product judgement, no public source). No-show rule: since the pilot moves no money, use no cash penalties yet; define a household no-show as Saathi waiting 10 minutes, two calls and a timestamped door photo; first offence forfeits that pickup's points, second within 30 days forces a confirm-one-hour-before step and scheduled rounds only, third suspends on-demand for 30 days; a shop or Saathi no-show switches that shop's auto-accept off for 24 hours and triggers review after two in a week; log reason codes so a Rs 50-100 fee paid to the Saathi can be introduced when payments go live -- Urban Company's model, where the entire customer cancellation fee is passed to the partner for travel cost (UC blog, 25 Oct 2023). Insurance: enrol every Saathi in PMSBY at onboarding (Rs 20 a year for Rs 2 lakh accidental death or total disability and Rs 1 lakh partial, ages 18-70, auto-debit from a bank or post-office account; official rules w.e.f. 1 Jun 2022) and add a group personal-accident policy from day one, which gig workers can join without an employer-employee relationship (Pazcare, 19 Jul 2026); indicative group PA pricing is Rs 100-150 per head per year for Rs 10 lakh in low-risk classes and Rs 200-400 for drivers and riders (Plum), or ICICI Lombard's group rate of about Rs 0.45 per Rs 1,000 sum insured, roughly Rs 450 a year for Rs 10 lakh before GST (Ditto, 15 Jul 2026), so budget Rs 300-600 plus 18% GST per Saathi for Rs 5-10 lakh cover, or a bundled gig product such as Bharatsure's health-plus-accident plan at Rs 69 a month (Business Standard, 6 Sep 2024); legally, the Code on Social Security 2020 took effect 21 Nov 2025 with aggregator contributions of 1-2% of turnover (capped at 5% of payouts) whose start date was still un-notified as of 7 Sep 2026 while worker registration on the central portal is already live (Taxmann, 3 Sep 2026), and Karnataka's Platform Based Gig Workers Act 2025 (commenced 30 May 2025) requires aggregators to register within 45 days and, since 16 Feb 2026, to pay a welfare fee of 1% of each payout capped at Rs 0.50 per two-wheeler, Rs 0.75 per three-wheeler and Rs 1.00 per light-commercial transaction, self-declared quarterly (SCC Online, 18 Feb 2026) -- Luma.Green, a digital platform paying piece-rate Saathis, should assume it is an aggregator. Business fees: comparables are IndiaMART (no commission; subscriptions of Rs 28,000 a year for a Mini Dynamic Catalog, Rs 45,000 for TrustSEAL, Rs 60,000 for Maximiser), Udaan at 0.5-2% per sale, JioMart 1-15% plus Rs 15-30 per order, Amazon Business referral fees from 2%, and Recykal, which discloses only that it charges a marketplace fee plus enterprise SaaS; scrap trades are thin-margin and easy to take off-platform, so the default is kabadiwalas free forever (they are supply), yards and recyclers free during the pilot and then a 0.5-1% per-trade fee capped per trade and charged to the buyer side (the side with GST invoices and bank rails), plus an optional IndiaMART-style paid tier of Rs 2,000-5,000 a month for verification badges, traceability and EPR documentation for recyclers and manufacturers; Karnataka's 1% welfare fee is a cost line, not revenue. Open items: no public source gives Saathi stop cost, Bengaluru glass or textile prices, or Recykal's actual take rate.
answers.decision: Free pickups with a Rs 150-200 estimated-value floor (below it, weekly rounds or drop-at-shop); closed-loop points at 1 point = Re 1, about 5% of scrap value, capped, never cash, funded by Luma.Green not CSR; zero-value items earn points only where a downstream taker is mapped; no batteries or e-waste in the household pilot; auto-accept only in shop hours with a Saathi available; a three-strike no-show ladder with no cash penalty until payments go live; PMSBY plus a Rs 5-10 lakh group PA policy for every Saathi (about Rs 300-600 plus GST per head per year) and register under the Karnataka Gig Workers Act; post-pilot fees of 0.5-1% per trade on the buyer side plus optional paid tiers, kabadiwalas free.
answers.whoToAsk: The pilot itself for the minimum-load floor, no-show thresholds and auto-accept caps (measure kg per stop and Saathi stop time in weeks 1-2); a CA/CS with CSR practice on whether any points programme can sit inside a registered NGO's Schedule VII project; counsel on the Karnataka Gig Workers Act applicability, aggregator registration and whether closed-loop points stay outside RBI's PPI rules; an insurance broker (Plum, Pazcare or Onsurity) for a group PA quote and minimum group size; KSPCB's registered e-waste recycler list and the CPCB EPR portal before enabling e-waste; ten Bengaluru shops on glass, film and old-clothes disposal routes.

answers.question: How many kabadiwalas operate in Bengaluru, and what share of household dry waste reaches them rather than the city's collection or DWCCs? What gross margin does a kabadiwala keep per material after rent, transport, credit and losses (any published studies or interviews)?
answers.answer: There is no census of Bengaluru scrap shops: when BBMP started registering informal waste workers in 2011-12 it printed 3,000 enumeration forms for scrap dealers (Hasiru Dala/SWMRT paper, 2014), but WIEGO's 2013 case study records that the scrap-shop enumeration never went ahead, so roughly 3,000 shops is the only official-order figure; Chennai's mapped 2,500 aggregators (Circulate Initiative, Jan 2023) makes 3,000-4,000 for Bengaluru plausible but unverified, and the city has over 35,000 waste pickers and itinerant buyers (Mongabay, Feb 2022). Bengaluru generates 5,000-6,000 t/day (Citizen Matters, 4 Nov 2025) of which 25-35% is dry (IntechOpen 2020; B.PAC, Nov 2023), i.e. about 1,300-2,000 t/day of dry waste. The DWCC network is small: Hasiru Dala's 34 operator-run centres took in 19,811 t in Apr 2024-Mar 2025 (about 54 t/day, 1.6 t/day per centre) and sent only 6,231 t (31%) to recyclers, the rest being multilayer plastic and rejects (Hasiru Dala Annual Report 2024-25); with 119 functioning centres (Citizen Matters, Sep 2025) to 164 (Nov 2025) that scales to roughly 200-270 t/day, or 10-20% of dry waste, of which only about a third is saleable. By contrast Hasiru Dala/SWMRT estimated in 2014 that 15,000 waste pickers alone retrieve about 1,050 t/day (23% of all MSW, most of the dry fraction), and South First (Mar 2025) still cites 800 t/day handled by waste pickers, so the kabadiwala and waste-picker chain, not DWCCs, moves most saleable dry waste; 60-80% is a defensible planning share, but nobody has measured it. No Bengaluru study publishes a per-material margin net of rent, transport, credit and losses. Circulate Initiative interviews (Jan 2023, Delhi/Mumbai/Chennai) find recyclers capture 70-80% of the trade benefit with collectors and aggregators sharing the remaining 20-30%, and put a scrap dealer's throughput at 800 kg-1 t/day; an unsourced industry glossary (Adhara Viveka, Jun 2026) says each layer adds Rs 2-8/kg. Bengaluru rate cards on 29 Sep 2026 show the spread between buyers: newspaper Rs 10-16/kg, cardboard Rs 3-10, PET/plastic Rs 10-25, iron Rs 22-38, aluminium Rs 150-180, copper Rs 500-720 (The Kabadiwala, ScrapKabadi, scraprates.in). The Sep 2017 DWCC feasibility analysis shows why margins are thin: plastic fell from Rs 30/kg in 2014 to Rs 15 in 2017, white record fetched Rs 11 and cardboard Rs 8, sorting needed 5-8 workers per tonne, and most DWCCs ran at a net loss.
answers.decision: Plan for about 3,000 shops and assume 60-80% of saleable dry waste already flows through them rather than DWCCs; do not hard-code margins in the product, record the buy price and sell price of every lot and compute the spread, using Rs 2-8/kg gross on paper and plastics as the working range until the pilot shops give real numbers.
answers.whoToAsk: Hasiru Dala (Nalini Shekar, Pinky Chandran) and SWMRT for the unpublished 2011-12 scrap-dealer enumeration and DWCC inflow data; BSWML for citywide DWCC throughput; a one-month buy/sell ledger from 10 pilot shops for margins by material; also open Hasiru Dala's 'Valuing Urban Waste' (2019) PDF at https://hasirudala.in/assets/Valuing-Urban-Waste-2019-Bp9XVHLf.pdf, which was too large to fetch here.

answers.question: What minimum load (kg or Rs) makes a home pickup worthwhile for a kabadiwala, how often does a household have enough scrap to sell, and is there evidence on whether households pick the nearest shop or the best price?
answers.answer: Published minimums come from the market, not studies: the Bengaluru buyer directory scraprates.in (29 Sep 2026) says verified dealers give free doorstep pickup above a minimum of usually 10-20 kg, and Delhi's Kabadiwala Online says most online kabadiwalas keep a minimum pickup value of around Rs 800-1,000 to cover fuel and labour for van-based collection. Kabadi Man, a Belagavi/Bengaluru pickup platform (Newstrail India, 15 Apr 2026), interviewed 150+ scrap dealers and reports collectors previously walked 15-20 km a day for only 3-5 customers earning Rs 400-500, rising to about Rs 1,500 with routed pickups, so density and routing, not price, is the binding constraint. On accumulation, Bengaluru generates about 0.5 kg/person/day of which paper is 9%, plastic 7%, glass 1% and metal 1% (IntechOpen 2020, using a 2013 sample), so a four-person home yields roughly 0.35 kg/day or 10-11 kg a month of saleable material, worth about Rs 100-150 at today's Bengaluru rates, i.e. one 10 kg sale per month is the natural cadence (this is a derived estimate, not a measured one). Income matters: a Dhanbad household study measured 51 g of plastic waste per person per day in high-income homes versus 8 g in low-income homes (Kumar et al., Waste Management 2018), so richer households reach a sellable load several times faster. On buyer choice, no Indian study directly tests nearest-shop versus best-price; the qualitative evidence is that pre-sorted recyclables come mainly from middle- and high-income homes and are sold to itinerant buyers who come to the door (Circulate Initiative, Jan 2023), that households store items and sell to the scrap dealer to extract full value (CSE, 2021), and that Bengaluru's own DWCC door-to-door data reversed to 80% non-saleable in 2017 because households had already sold the good material to kabadiwalas. In short, households behave convenience-first (whoever comes, or the nearest shop), and price comparison only appears once an app shows rates side by side.
answers.decision: Default a free Saathi home pickup to a 10 kg or roughly Rs 150 minimum, nudge households monthly (that is when a typical home has ~10 kg), and batch pickups by lane so a Saathi does five or more stops per trip; design for convenience-first households and price-sensitive shops.
answers.whoToAsk: Weigh the first three lots from 30 pilot households and log the trip time of every Saathi pickup to set the real minimum; ask 10 pilot shops what load they will collect for free today; ask Hasiru Dala for DWCC buy-back weights per household.

answers.question: What are the usual payment terms from yard to kabadiwala (cash at pickup vs 7-30 days' credit), typical lot sizes per material, who transports and who pays freight, and the smallest load worth a yard collection?
answers.answer: The chain structure is documented but the exact credit days are not. Circulate Initiative interviews (Jan 2023) put a scrap dealer at 800 kg-1 t/day of mixed dry waste and a single-material aggregator (PET bottles, paper, LDPE pouches) at 1-10 t/day, and explain that the extra aggregation layers exist to bridge payment/credit chains between collectors who must be paid on delivery and recyclers who buy minimum volumes weekly or monthly; traders and agents sit in between taking a margin without adding value, larger aggregators bale and shred, and space for bulking is scarce in cities. Cash is the norm at the bottom: Hasiru Dala's demonetisation study (31 Bengaluru waste pickers, scrap dealers and DWCC operators, fieldwork 2017) records that the recycling chain transacts in cash daily, and that when cash vanished traders issued paper slips, cheques that cost Rs 200 per Rs 10,000 to encash, old notes, or simply promised to pay later, while DWCC operators needed cash every morning to pay pickers and sorters, so credit flows upward, from the shop to its buyer, not the reverse. Recykal's marketplace pitch to sellers (2026), no chasing buyers or waiting weeks for your money, confirms that multi-week waits from larger buyers are common. Reference prices for what yards pay: Bengaluru DWCC sale prices in 2017 were white record Rs 11/kg, cardboard Rs 8 and plastic Rs 15 (down from Rs 30 in 2014); informal purchase prices for plastics were PET Rs 22-32/kg, HDPE/PP Rs 12-14 and LDPE Rs 6-15 (CSE, 2021, Mumbai survey), and polyolefin recyclers themselves run on margins under 10% (India Plastics Pact landscape assessment). On freight, TERI (Dec 2021) and the India Plastics Pact note that aggregators haul high-value plastics to Gujarat and Delhi clusters at significant transport cost, but no source states who pays freight at the kabadiwala-to-yard step or the smallest lot a yard will collect; the daily volumes above imply a yard vehicle comes when a shop has roughly half a tonne to a tonne, i.e. a small-truck load, and below that the shop delivers. Hasiru Dala's 2024-25 annual report also flags irregular payments to DWCC operators (from BBMP) and unsold multilayer plastic as the recurring cash-flow problems.
answers.decision: Give every yard-to-kabadiwala lot a payment-terms field (cash at pickup, or credit with a due date defaulting to 7-15 days) and a freight-payer flag; assume a yard collection starts at about 500 kg-1 t per material and that below that the shop delivers or pays freight; treat these as pilot defaults to be corrected in week one.
answers.whoToAsk: Three to five Bengaluru yards (one each for paper, plastics and metals) on their real credit days, lot minimums and who pays freight; the 10 pilot shops on how long they currently wait to be paid; Hasiru Dala's DWCC operators on their present buyer terms.

answers.question: What are Bengaluru's standing entry hours and no-entry rules for goods vehicles (city-wide, not temporary notices)? What do local transporters and Porter/Vahak charge per km and for loading for mini-trucks and tempos?
answers.answer: Standing city-wide rule (reconfirmed by Joint Commissioner (Traffic) M N Anucheth on 3 Aug 2024): heavy goods vehicles (HGVs) may not move inside Bengaluru city 07:00–11:00 and 16:00–22:00 on Monday–Friday and Sunday, and on Saturdays roughly 10:00/10:30–14:30 and 16:30–21:00 (Deccan Herald prints 10 am, Public TV 10.30 am), so the legal HGV windows are 11:00–16:00 and 22:00–07:00 on weekdays and 14:30–16:30 plus 21:00–10:00 on Saturdays. Under Section 2 of the Motor Vehicles Act 1988 an HGV is a goods carriage over 12,000 kg gross vehicle weight and anything up to 7,500 kg GVW is a light motor vehicle, so 3-wheeler goods autos, Tata Ace, Bolero/8-ft pickups and even a Tata 407 or Eicher rated at or under 7.5 t are not caught by the city-wide ban on ordinary roads; medium goods vehicles (7.5–12 t) are not named in the 2024 orders and lorry associations were still asking in Aug 2024 for small and medium vehicles to be let through, so MGV status is an open item to confirm with BTP. Separate corridor bans are standing orders 'until further orders' from 4 Sep 2026 (Electronics City from 11 Sep 2026): Electronics City elevated corridor bars all goods vehicles including light ones 06:00–22:00 and 3-wheeler goods autos 24 h; Airport Road elevated corridor (Sanjeevnagar Cross to Vidyashilp Junction) bars all goods vehicles 06:00–22:00; BGS/Sirsi Circle flyover on Mysuru Road bars HGVs 24 h and every other goods vehicle including 3-wheeler goods autos 07:00–11:00 and 16:00–22:00; Peenya elevated corridor bars 3-wheeler goods autos 24 h and heavy/medium goods vehicles 07:00–11:00 and 16:00–22:00; the Silk Board–Ragigudda double-decker flyover bars HGVs 24 h. Stretch-level orders also appear, e.g. heavy vehicles barred on Varthur–Gunjur Road (SH-35) 07:00–11:00, 13:00–15:00 and 16:00–21:00 from 24 Sep 2026 until road-widening ends. Watch October 2026: BTP circulated a draft on 15 Jul 2026 (trucks of 8–16 t barred 07:00–22:00, a permanent ban above 16 t with transshipment hubs outside the city, light vehicles carrying milk and vegetables exempt) and JCP (Traffic) Karthik Reddy told Public TV on 25 Sep 2026 that HGVs would be barred 07:00–22:00 'from next month' after talks with transport associations; that is a single news source and no notification had been published by 29 Sep 2026. Prices: Porter's Bengaluru pages publish only starting fares — 3-wheeler (500 kg) ₹205, Tata Ace (750 kg) ₹230, e-loader (350 kg) ₹150, Pickup 8 ft ₹330 — and the per-km/per-minute rate appears only in the in-app quote; Porter's FAQ and terms say tolls are inside the fare, loading/unloading beyond 60 minutes raises it, helpers ('Load Assist') and parking are extra and paid to the driver, cancellation after a driver is assigned costs ₹50, and GST-registered customers pay 5% GST under reverse charge. Vahak has no rate card at all: you post the load and verified lorry owners bid (it claims 10 lakh+ transporters in 850+ cities), which suits yard-to-recycler and outstation LCV loads rather than on-demand pickups. Local-transporter benchmarks from marketing pages (AssureShift updated 29 Sep 2025; Moving Solutions, BookMyTempo and TruckGuru undated): Tata Ace base ₹250–255 including 1 km and 60 minutes, then ₹25–45/km plus ₹5–8/minute waiting; Super Ace or Mahindra pickup ₹300–350 base and ₹30/km; Tata 407 ₹500 base and ₹50/km; intercity Tata Ace ₹26–29/km and Eicher 14 ft ₹31–35/km; loading labour ₹390 when the driver loads, or ₹400–800 per helper per trip. Open items: Porter's actual per-km and helper price in Bengaluru (read from an app quote), MGV treatment under the city ban, and whether the October regime gets notified.
answers.decision: Run pilot pickups on light vehicles (3-wheeler goods autos, Tata Ace, pickups up to 7.5 t GVW) at any hour on surface roads, but route them off the Electronics City and Airport Road elevated corridors, the BGS flyover and the Peenya corridor; schedule any HGV (over 12 t) yard-to-recycler-to-manufacturer leg for 11:00–16:00 or 22:00–07:00 (Saturday 14:30–16:30 or after 21:00) and be ready to shift those to 22:00–07:00 if the October order lands. Book on-demand runs on Porter (₹205/₹230 start, upfront in-app quote), tender recurring or outstation loads on Vahak, and budget ₹25–30/km plus ₹5/min waiting plus ₹400–800 per helper for local transporters until a phone check settles the real rate.
answers.whoToAsk: Bengaluru Traffic Police (JCP Traffic office; press notes on btp.karnataka.gov.in and BTP's X account) for the October 2026 notification and whether medium goods vehicles are covered; 10 local tempo operators plus a live Porter app quote for the real per-km and helper rates.

answers.question: Can a startup use ULIP (the government's logistics data platform) to check transporters' vehicles and drivers, and what does access require?
answers.answer: Yes. ULIP (goulip.in, run by NICDC Logistics Data Services Ltd, a Government of India–NEC joint venture under DPIIT) is open to private companies including startups: PIB's 1 Oct 2022 release describes the path — register on the portal, submit a use case, pass review, sign a Non-Disclosure Agreement, integrate, clear a system security check and testing, then fetch live data — and by 19 Mar 2025 PIB counted 1,300+ registered companies, 350+ agreements, 43 systems from 11 ministries through 129 APIs and 100 crore+ API transactions, citing transporter verification by UltraTech and Tata Steel as a standard use case. A third-party how-to (NirmanKit, 25 Jun 2026) lists the practical requirements: an incorporated Pvt Ltd, LLP or registered proprietorship with an active GSTIN matching the company name, PAN and address, a developer point of contact, and a written use case with data-retention and security policy; review takes 3–5 working days; the NDA is printed on ₹100 stamp paper, signed, uploaded and posted to NLDSL; you then get sandbox client ID/secret and move to production after uploading integration logs or a demo; expect 7–14 working days to sandbox and ₹0 in government fees (goulip.in itself publishes no fee, so confirm at NDA stage). The relevant APIs are VAHAN/01 (vehicle number → owner name, registration date, RC status, vehicle class, maker, fuel, fitness, insurance and PUCC validity; VAHAN/02 by chassis, /03 by engine), SARATHI/01 (DL number plus date of birth → name, DL status, validity, class of vehicle, badge), plus e-Challan, FASTag and a 'State/UT-specific No entry' API; all endpoints are lookup-only (you need the number from the transporter or Saathi), authentication is username/password to a bearer token with a 30-minute idle expiry at ulip.dpiit.gov.in/ulip/v1.0.0 with a separate staging host, and the helpdesk is 1800 309 8908 / Helpdesk@goulip.in. Two cautions. First, MoRTH's Policy for Data Sharing from the National Transport Repository (released 18 Aug 2025) now governs Vahan/Sarathi data: private recipients need MoRTH approval, PII in API mode is masked unless specifically granted, personal data requires the data principal's consent via an Aadhaar-authenticated OTP to the mobile number on record, and recipients sign a memorandum of data compliances and submit a CERT-In empanelled security-audit certificate; the policy never mentions ULIP, and whether ULIP's VAHAN/SARATHI responses are now masked or consent-gated is not published anywhere, so ask NLDSL before designing the verification flow. Second, Internet Freedom Foundation (23 Sep 2026) documented apps selling full Vahan/Sarathi records for about ₹2 a lookup with no OTP — those are not a lawful source. A priced, licensed fallback for pilot day one is a KYC API vendor such as EKO (RC ₹3.00 and DL ₹1.80 per successful call, excluding 18% GST, no monthly minimum, setup from ₹6,000 per API family) or the admin checking RC and DL photos against mParivahan/Parivahan. Open items: ULIP's fee, if any, and whether a recycling platform's transporter/Saathi verification use case is accepted on first review.
answers.decision: Register on goulip.in this week with a 'transporter vehicle and Saathi driver verification' use case and sign the NDA, aiming for sandbox before 13 Oct 2026; ship the pilot with a licensed KYC API (EKO-class, about ₹3 per RC and ₹1.80 per DL) plus in-app driver consent, and cut over to ULIP VAHAN/01 and SARATHI/01 when production credentials arrive.
answers.whoToAsk: NLDSL ULIP helpdesk (1800 309 8908, Helpdesk@goulip.in) on fees, use-case fit, and whether responses are masked or consent-gated after the Aug 2025 MoRTH policy; counsel for the DPDP consent wording and the NDA.

answers.question: What are the exact 8-digit ITC-HS lines for glass cullet (7001), lead scrap (7802), the 8549 sub-headings (lithium-ion cells, dry cells, CRT glass, circuit boards) and textiles (6309/6310)? Which E-Waste Rules 2022 schedule item codes (ITEW, CEEW, LSEEW numbers) match phones, laptops, TVs, fridges, washing machines and ACs?
answers.answer: Glass cullet: use 70010010 (Cullet and other waste and scrap of glass); the only other lines under 7001 are 70010020 (enamel glass in the mass) and 70010090 (other), which a scrap chain never needs. Lead scrap: 78020010 is lead scrap by ISRI code word (Racks soft lead, Radio mixed hard/soft, Ropes wheel weights, Roses babbit, Rink whole intact wet lead-acid batteries, plus intact industrial lead cells) and is import-policy Free; 78020090 'Other' is Restricted, so battery lead and soft lead both go to 78020010. Heading 8549 (new in HS 2022; every Indian line ends in 00): 85491100 waste/spent lead-acid accumulators; 85491200 other cells/batteries containing lead, cadmium or mercury; 85491300 sorted by chemical type and free of Pb/Cd/Hg; 85491400 the same but unsorted; 85491900 other battery waste; 85492100 and 85492900 waste of a kind used principally for precious-metal recovery (with/without the hazardous items); 85493100 electrical/electronic assemblies and printed circuit boards that contain cells, batteries, mercury switches, 'glass from cathode-ray tubes or other activated glass' or Cd/Hg/Pb/PCB-bearing components; 85493900 other assemblies and boards; 85499100 other e-waste containing those same items; 85499900 other e-waste. So map sorted lithium-ion cells to 85491300 (a mixed household battery bin is 85491400), zinc-carbon/alkaline dry cells to 85491300 (85491200 only if mercury cells), populated circuit boards to 85493100 with bare or depopulated boards at 85493900, and CRT glass to 85499100 while it is tube, panel or funnel glass from dismantling (only clean processed cullet would drop to 70010010). Textiles: 63090000 is the single line for worn clothing and other worn articles (the old-clothes stream), and 6310 has nine lines for rags — 63101010/63101020/63101030/63101090 sorted woollen rags, cotton rags, gunny cuttings, other; 63109010/63109020/63109030/63109040/63109090 other (unsorted) woollen, cotton, gunny, synthetic rags, other. E-Waste (Management) Rules 2022 were notified as G.S.R. 801(E) in Gazette No. 713 on 2 November 2022, came into force on 1 April 2023 and list 106 EEE items in seven categories in Schedule I: mobile phones are ITEW15 'Cellular telephones' (tablets ITEW19, phablets ITEW20, cordless phones ITEW14, landline telephones ITEW12); laptops are ITEW3 'Personal Computing: Laptop Computers' (desktops ITEW2, notebooks ITEW4, notepads ITEW5); televisions including LCD/LED are CEEW1 (monitors, screens and display panels CEEW6); refrigerators CEEW2; washing machines CEEW3; air-conditioners excluding centralised plants CEEW4. Useful extras for a kabadiwala catalogue: electric fans LSEEW14, microwaves LSEEW9, irons LSEEW20, grinders/mixers LSEEW21, kettles LSEEW33, UPS ITEW24, inverters ITEW25, printers ITEW6; LSEEW1–LSEEW3 (large cooling appliances, freezers, other large refrigeration) are the commercial cooling lines, not household fridges. One caveat: CBIC's own tariff pages could not be opened (old.cbic.gov.in no longer resolves and the taxinformation portal is script-driven), so the 8-digit lines above come from the DGCI&S ITC-HS chapter PDF (a government copy) and three trade mirrors of the Customs Tariff that agree with each other; a five-minute check on CBIC's tariff browser before anyone exports is enough.
answers.decision: Give every material two optional attributes — an 8-digit ITC-HS line and, for electricals, a Schedule I code — seeded with the mappings above; keep Luma.Green's own material code as the primary key because kabadiwala grades (HM vs LD film, single vs double-door fridge) are finer than HS.
answers.whoToAsk: Nothing for the pilot; a customs broker or CA only if a yard ever exports, to confirm the 8549 line for populated boards and CRT glass on that consignment.
