answers.question: What words do Bengaluru kabadiwalas use for plastics and other scrap (Delhi's Teri, Phugga, Jhaap, Panni; English PET, PP, HD, LD; Kannada terms)? Is 'gujari' used for scrap shops in Bengaluru? Are milk pouches a separate paid stream? Are small appliances and fans priced per kg or per piece?
answers.answer: Yes, 'gujari' (ಗುಜರಿ, also spelt gujri) is the Bengaluru word: Kannada dictionaries give 'junk shop' as its main sense and 'gujari vyapari' as 'scrap merchant', and the Shivaji Nagar furniture-scrap lanes are simply called 'the Gujri', so 'gujari angadi' is the shop while 'kabadiwala' is the understood Hindi/Urdu import. Dictionary Kannada for the materials is kabbiṇa (ಕಬ್ಬಿಣ, iron), gāju (ಗಾಜು, glass), tāmra (ತಾಮ್ರ, copper), hittāḷe (ಹಿತ್ತಾಳೆ, brass) and raddi for waste paper (hence raddiwala), while plastic is just 'plastic'; but the grade names on Bengaluru price lists are English trade names — PET bottle, Polythene bags (LD), Polythene bags (HM), Plastic (PP) bags, Hard plastic, Soft plastic, Mix plastic, Milk covers, Packaging film, PVC pipe, Sintex/water tank, plastic jar/can/drum. Of the Delhi words only 'panni' (film or carry-bag; 'PP panni' appears in Delhi trade listings) could be confirmed on a page I could open; Teri, Phugga and Jhaap appeared nowhere public (a 2025 Delhi collector article lists only PET, LDPE carry bags and multilayer), so treat them as unverified and collect Bengaluru equivalents in the pilot. Milk pouches are a separate stream but not a paid one: The Kabadiwala's Bengaluru and HSR Layout lists show 'Milk Covers ₹0/kg' and 'Packaging Film ₹0/kg', and the informal trade generally refuses multilayer, thermocol and sub-50-micron bags; the policy backdrop is the 22 August 2019 dairy-ministry '3R' push (rebate for returned pouches at Nandini, Amul, Mother Dairy) and KMF's corn-starch compostable Nandini pouch rolled out across Bengaluru from July 2025 (KMF uses 20–25 lakh pouches a day), so during the pilot LDPE and compostable pouches will arrive side by side and must not be mixed. Appliances: Bengaluru lists price large items per piece — TV LCD/LED ₹50, CRT TV ₹100, laptop ₹250, single-door fridge ₹350, double-door ₹550, washing machine ₹300, microwave ₹130, geyser ₹100, UPS ₹250, CPU ₹150, AC 1.5 T ₹2,500, 2 T ₹3,000 per piece on The Kabadiwala (read 29 September 2026), with other Bengaluru sites quoting fridges ₹1,500–3,000, washing machines ₹800–2,000 and split ACs ₹2,000–4,000 per unit — and small or mixed e-waste per kg (e-waste ₹10/kg, printer ₹10/kg, cooler ₹8–12/kg on the same list; ₹45/kg on scraprates.in). No Bengaluru list I could open prices fans at all, and Delhi dealers disagree (₹36/kg for a ceiling fan at one, ₹200/₹300 per piece small/big at another), so fans, mixers and irons are priced both ways depending on the shop and the copper inside.
answers.decision: Give every material a unit (kg or piece) that the shop can override: default per piece for TV, fridge, washing machine, AC, laptop, CPU, monitor, microwave, geyser and UPS; default per kg for fans, mixers, irons, kettles, printers, coolers and mixed e-waste. Keep 'Milk covers (LDPE, rinsed)' as its own code with ₹0 allowed, plus a separate 'compostable Nandini pouch' code that is never sold as plastic. Use the English trade grades (PET, HM, LD, PP, hard, soft, mix) as canonical labels with a Kannada display name and a free-text local-name field per shop.
answers.whoToAsk: 10 gujari shops across three BBMP zones plus two Hasiru Dala DWCC operators, visited with a Kannada-speaking Saathi: the local words for PET/HM/LD/PP, whether anyone pays for milk covers, and per-kg versus per-piece for fans, mixers and irons.

answers.question: Which published source should supply the CO2e emission factor for recycling each material (paper, PET, HDPE, PP, LDPE, ferrous, aluminium, copper, brass, glass, e-waste): CDM AMS-III.AJ, Gold Standard 448, India-specific studies? Who should own an open material-code standard long term (an industry body such as MRAI or IARPMA, a BIS committee, a foundation), and under which licence?
answers.answer: Use CDM AMS-III.AJ 'Recovery and recycling of materials from solid wastes' (version 9.0, adopted 8 September 2022) as the backbone: it is public, free, written for non-Annex I hosts like India, and gives formulas plus conservative defaults for HDPE, LDPE, PET, PP, container-glass cullet, steel and aluminium, with paper and cardboard credited only for avoided landfill methane. Its defaults are baseline energy for virgin plastic of 1.11 MWh/t plus 15 GJ/t (PET), 0.83 + 15 (HDPE), 1.67 + 15 (LDPE), 0.56 + 11.6 (PP), 0.026 MWh/t for glass cullet (cullet displaces batch preparation, not melting), and 'Bi' correction factors of 0.72 aluminium, 0.68 steel, 0.56 plastics and 0.67 glass, with metal-specific CO2 factors in the same document; feed its electricity term with CEA's CO2 Baseline Database v21.0 (November 2025), whose FY 2024-25 weighted-average grid factor is 0.710 tCO2/MWh (OM 0.961, BM 0.512, CM 0.736). For copper and mixed e-waste use the sister method AMS-III.BA (e-waste; the Bi factors above come from its Appendix 1); brass has no CDM default and is an open item. Gold Standard methodology 448 (v1.0, published 2 May 2025, written by South Pole) expands AMS-III.AJ and III.BA but its scope is 'metals, alloys and minerals' and it points to LCA databases such as ecoinvent for factors, so it is the route only if you later want Gold Standard credits for metal or e-waste, not a plastics or paper source; Verra's VMR0007 (v1.0, 4 September 2023) is just a VCS wrapper that sends you back to AMS-III.AJ's values. No India-specific per-material recycling factor set exists in public: the India GHG Program (WRI India, CII, TERI) publishes tools rather than material factors, and the Indian LCA papers are single-material academic studies, so do not advertise 'India-specific' factors yet. Where AMS-III.AJ is silent and you need an on-screen indicative number, US EPA WARM v15 (November 2020) is the most complete public table of net recycling factors — corrugated −3.14, newspaper −2.71, mixed paper −3.55, HDPE −0.76, PET −1.04, PP −0.79, aluminium cans −9.13, steel cans −1.83, copper wire −4.49, glass −0.28, mixed electronics −0.79 MTCO2e per short ton (multiply by 1.1023 for per tonne) — but label it 'indicative, US grid'. On ownership, BIS is the wrong first home: its aluminium-scrap standard 'Aluminium & Aluminium Alloy Scrap – Requirements & Conditions of Delivery' had been pending more than two years as of 8 July 2026 after primary producers and recyclers fell out over the draft, BIS told MRAI's February 2024 conference only that 'standardisation will be the norm', and BIS standards are sold, not open. MRAI is metals-only and IARPMA (paper) has no published grade list I could reach, so neither can own a cross-material code on its own. On licence, the Open Definition lists CC0, CC BY 4.0, CC BY-SA, ODC-BY and ODbL as conformant, Mozilla's preferred spec licence is CC0 plus an OWFa patent non-assert, and Beckn's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 is the cautionary Indian precedent because 'non-commercial' would stop a gujari app or a yard's ERP from using the codes.
answers.decision: Emission factors: AMS-III.AJ v9.0 (plus AMS-III.BA for e-waste metals) with the CEA v21.0 grid factor as the single method for the pilot, WARM v15 only as a labelled indicative fallback, and a pinned factor-version on every carbon number shown. Standard: Luma.Green publishes the material-code list now under CC BY 4.0 (spec and code list) with Apache-2.0 for JSON schemas and SDKs, then within 12–18 months moves governance to a neutral Section 8 foundation whose steering group seats MRAI, IARPMA, a plastics body, Hasiru Dala/waste-picker representatives and CPCB as observer, offering the stable list to BIS as a reference input rather than making BIS the owner; avoid NC and SA clauses.
answers.whoToAsk: A lawyer for the Section 8 foundation set-up and the patent non-assert wording; MRAI and Hasiru Dala for steering-group seats; a CDM/Gold Standard validator only if credits are ever sold. Open items: a brass factor (ask TERI or CEEW whether any Indian secondary-brass LCA exists) and downloading AMS-III.AJ v9.0 itself from cdm.unfccc.int in a browser (the site blocks scripted access; the v8.0 draft was used for the default tables).

answers.question: What penalty applies to an unverified or unstamped weighing scale after the Jan Vishwas amendments to the Legal Metrology Act in force from 1 May 2026, and does Karnataka require yearly re-verification of electronic scales? What does e-Mapan (Karnataka) offer traders online?
answers.answer: The Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Act, 2026 (passed by Lok Sabha 1 April and Rajya Sabha 2 April 2026, issued 8 April 2026) was brought into force for the Legal Metrology Act by notification S.O. 2103(E) of 27 April 2026, effective 1 May 2026. The catch for scrap shops is that it does NOT touch Section 33 (use of an unverified weight or measure): the Act's schedule entry 66 amends sections 25, 26, 27, 28, 29, 30, 31, 32, 34 to 39, 41 and 45 to 48 and skips 33, and the PIB list of 29 June 2026 of improvement-notice offences also leaves out section 33. So using or supplying an unstamped or expired-stamp scale still carries the old penalty: a fine of not less than Rs 2,000 and up to Rs 10,000 for the first offence, and for a second or subsequent offence imprisonment up to one year plus fine; it remains compoundable under the new section 48 (which covers sections 25 to 39). The softer regime applies only if the scale is 'non-standard' (section 25): first offence a written improvement notice, second offence a penalty up to Rs 1 lakh, later offences a fine of Rs 2 lakh to Rs 5 lakh; the Act's 10 percent-every-three-years escalation (section 3) applies only to the amounts in the schedule, so the Rs 2,000 to Rs 10,000 under section 33 stays fixed. The Act also gives any legal metrology officer a general power (new section 15(6) and (7)) to serve an improvement notice for any non-compliance and to suspend or revoke a registration if it is ignored. Yes, Karnataka requires yearly re-verification of electronic scales: the Karnataka Legal Metrology (Enforcement) Rules, 2011 (rule 4(6) and 4(9)) work off Rule 27 of the central Legal Metrology (General) Rules, 2011, which fixes re-verification at 12 months for all weights or measures other than weights, capacity/length measures, beam scales and counter machines (24 months) and storage tanks (60 months); fees follow Karnataka's Schedule IX (last revised 3 December 2022), capped at Rs 5,000 per instrument. e-Mapan (www.emapan.karnataka.gov.in, Department of Legal Metrology, No.1 Ali Asker Road, Bengaluru, 080 2225 3500) offers online new/renewal/amendment of manufacturer, dealer and repairer registrations, packaged-commodity registration, verification-certificate (VC) and model-register (MR) search and download, application status tracking and a dashboard, and runs the consumer complaint toll-free line 1800 599 1100; new licence and packaging registrations are now routed through the Karnataka single-window (KUM) at investkarnataka.co.in. The exact re-verification fee for a 100 to 300 kg platform scale is an open item (Schedule IX figures were not on any open page).
answers.decision: Treat a valid verification stamp as a hard requirement: every Saathi and kabadiwala scale in the pilot must show a current stamp and VC number, the app should store the VC number and 12-month expiry and refuse weigh-ins on an expired scale, and only model-approved scales bought from an e-Mapan-registered dealer should be onboarded. Budget one re-verification per scale per year and get the Schedule IX fee from the local Inspector before launch.
answers.whoToAsk: Inspector of Legal Metrology for the Bengaluru zone (via e-Mapan or 080 2225 3500) for the Schedule IX fee and how to book a re-verification visit; counsel only if a Saathi will carry a company-owned scale (who is 'the user' liable under s.33).

answers.question: Do plain kabadiwala shops that only collect and store scrap need any KSPCB consent or authorisation under the waste rules? Does Bengaluru police require scrap dealers to hold a licence or keep purchase registers (any Karnataka Police Act provision or city order)? Which materials are high theft risk in Bengaluru (BESCOM copper, BWSSB manhole covers, metro fittings), and is there a police or utility alert channel?
answers.answer: On KSPCB: consent to establish/operate under the Water and Air Acts follows the CPCB category list (January 2025 report, issued as a direction on 12 February 2025), and KSPCB's own page says White category units are 'not included in the consent mechanism'. Collect-and-store activities sit in White or are not listed at all: 'bailing (hydraulic press) of waste papers' and 'collection centres (without depollution, dismantling and shredding)' are both White, while anything that processes scrap is consent-bearing (plastic flakes/granules Orange, aluminium or copper extraction from scrap Orange, lead-acid battery recycling Red, e-waste dismantling listed separately). The Solid Waste Management Rules 2016 define 'informal waste collector' to include 'waste traders' and put the duty on the local body (BBMP/BSWML), not the trader, to register and integrate them (rule 15(c)); SPCB authorisation under those rules is for processing and disposal facilities, and KSPCB's plastics page requires registration only of producers, importers, brand owners and plastic waste processors. So the default is: a kabadiwala who only buys, sorts and stores paper, plastic, metal and glass needs no KSPCB consent, but the pilot should keep used oil, lead-acid batteries and e-waste dismantling out of scope (Hazardous Waste Rules authorisation) and read CPCB's 11 June 2026 'Classification of Waste Battery Collection Centre' before adding batteries. On police: the Karnataka Police Act, 1963 has no scrap-dealer licence, but section 99 makes a 'pawnbroker, dealer in second hand property, or worker in metals' who has received written or printed information from the police about suspected stolen property liable (fine up to Rs 50 per article) unless he reports forthwith and 'takes all reasonable means to ascertain' the name and address of the person offering it; section 100 penalises melting or altering such property without police permission, section 98 covers unexplained possession of suspected stolen goods (up to 3 months or Rs 100), and section 31 lets the Commissioner make regulatory orders. I found no Bengaluru city order mandating purchase registers or CCTV for scrap shops on any open page; that is an open item for the zonal DCP, and a separate BBMP trade-licence check belongs to the licensing cluster. On theft risk, dated Bengaluru cases were: BESCOM Ring Main Unit batteries stolen from poles and sold through a Kogilu Cross scrap shop (about 100 batteries worth Rs 5 lakh, 11 cases, Deccan Herald 23 August 2022); hundreds of metres of Namma Metro power cable stolen from the Peenya, Rajajinagar and Basavanagudi lines between October 2023 and January 2024 (Hans India 21 January 2025); and an interstate gang posing as BSNL staff stripping copper cable and modules in Sadashivanagar, Malleswaram, Mathikere and Yeshwanthpur, with police 'examining links to scrap dealers' (Organiser 25 April 2026). No dated Bengaluru report of BWSSB manhole-cover theft was found in this session, so that stays an open item. There is no public 'stolen-metal alert' feed: the legal channel is the section 99 written information from police, reporting goes to Police 112 (Namma 112, which the Commissioner asked delivery platforms to use in November 2025) and to BESCOM on 1912, WhatsApp 9449844640 or the safety WhatsApp lines 9483191212 and 9483191222.
answers.decision: Do not ask kabadiwalas for KSPCB consent in the pilot; instead have the app keep a purchase register per lot (seller name, address, ID, photo, weight, price) which satisfies the section 99 duty, and flag insulated copper cable, transformer or motor windings, batteries, cast-iron covers and rail or metro fittings as 'infrastructure metal' that cannot be accepted without a provenance note and a manager override. Write to the KSPCB regional office once to confirm the no-consent reading and register pilot kabadiwalas with BBMP/BSWML as dry-waste collectors.
answers.whoToAsk: KSPCB Regional Officer (Bengaluru) in writing for the consent position; the zonal DCP or Bengaluru City Police (Law and Order) for any standing order on scrap dealers; BWSSB PRO and BESCOM vigilance (via 1912) for theft-alert practice; environmental counsel before adding batteries or e-waste.

answers.question: Can a Saathi apply for the Seva Sindhu Police Verification Certificate themselves, at what fee and turnaround, and should a kabadiwala's helpers who enter homes be verified too?
answers.answer: Yes, with one wrinkle: Seva Sindhu has no generic 'private-sector individual' PVC, so the route for a Saathi is the Karnataka State Police service 'Police Verification Certificate (PVC) for Domestic servants/House Keeping', whose page says 'Individual/Employer/Government Department can approach the police department' and lists Rs 375 for antecedents-only or Rs 750 for antecedents plus address verification, a Rs 35 service charge if filed at a Grama One/Bangalore One/Karnataka One counter, a stated service time of 21 days, eligibility 'any citizen currently staying in Karnataka', and documents of a passport photo, identity proof and address proof. The Karnataka State Police FAQ confirms PVCs are issued only through Seva Sindhu as e-signed certificates, and a Bengaluru RWA guide (Citizen Matters, 25 January 2025) reports the same Rs 375/Rs 750 and about 21 days in practice. If Luma applies as the employer instead, the 'PVC for Institutions/Companies' service costs Rs 1,500 per person (antecedents and address, 21 days); the other listed services are Rs 375 for government employees applying directly and Rs 150 for airport Class IV staff, so Rs 750 via the domestic-help route is the cheapest full check. On whether helpers should be verified: nothing in Karnataka law makes police verification of scrap collectors or their helpers mandatory today, but Bengaluru's Police Commissioner told Deccan Herald on 2 November 2025 that verification of work history and police records 'will soon be made mandatory' for quick-commerce delivery workers, and on 8 November 2025 asked platforms to run thorough background checks and verify vehicle and licence documents before onboarding. Every person Luma sends into a home (Saathi or a kabadiwala's helper on a Luma pickup) should therefore carry an antecedents-plus-address PVC before the first home visit, refreshed every two years as the RWA guidance suggests. Timing matters: with a 21-day service time and launch on 13 October 2026, certificates applied for today will land around 20 October, so the first week should run with only already-verified people entering homes.
answers.decision: Make a Rs 750 antecedents-plus-address PVC (Seva Sindhu domestic-help service, applied for by the worker with Luma reimbursing) a precondition for any Saathi or helper doing in-home pickups, show a 'police verified' badge with the PO-number and date in the app, renew every 24 months, and file all applications this week so the first batch clears by 20 October; until then route unverified people to kerbside or shop-side work only.
answers.whoToAsk: The local police station (jurisdiction of the worker's address) if a self-applied domestic-help PVC is questioned for a non-domestic role; employment counsel on whether Luma or the kabadiwala is the 'employer' who should apply and pay; the Karnataka Gig Workers Welfare Board on Saathi registration once its portal is live.

answers.question: Which reference-price sources can Luma.Green use legally and cheaply: MCX delayed data (terms and yearly cost through an authorised vendor), a BigMint data licence (price), mill price notices (paper mills publishing waste-paper buying prices)? May anonymised yard buy-price posts be combined into a public board line?
answers.answer: MCX: the exchange's own datafeed policy (page checked 29 Sep 2026, policy document dated 10 Jul 2026) lets a non-member show exchange data on its website or app only under a signed data-feed agreement, allows only delayed data for public website display, bars resale, and requires MCX's explicit permission for any public-internet display; the domestic price list effective 1 Jul 2024 charges Rs 2,00,000 a year for a 15-minute-delayed feed across terminal, website and mobile (80% of list, Rs 1,60,000, for a single segment such as website-only; 10-min Rs 3,00,000; 5-min Rs 4,50,000), Rs 2,00,000 a year for end-of-day Bhav copy or for polled spot prices, plus Rs 1,00,000 a year internet connectivity, all before 18% GST, so the cheapest lawful public MCX line costs about Rs 3.1-3.5 lakh a year. Authorised real-time vendors (list dated 5 Jun 2024: Bloomberg, Refinitiv, ICE, FactSet, Cogencis, Global Financial Datafeeds, TrueData, Ticker Data) sell screen access to individuals (TrueData advertises a free 15-minute-delayed tier), but the vendor tariff's delayed entitlement is Rs 300 per terminal per month for the subscriber's own screen, any onward display still needs MCX approval and fees, and MCX's website terms forbid copying, republishing or scraping the free quotes on mcxindia.com. BigMint: its terms make every subscription single-user and non-redistributable, its data-licensing FAQ says you may not post BigMint prices on your website or any public domain without a redistribution licence that is 'priced at a slight premium' on request, no price is published for any plan (Silver/Gold/Platinum/Platinum+ web, Price Only/Standard/Professional app), and its scrap coverage is ferrous and non-ferrous metal with no paper series and no Bengaluru series visible. Mill notices: no Indian kraft mill was found publishing a public waste-paper buying price; the public, dated figures come from trade press quoting the Indian Recovered Paper Traders Association (Pulp & Paper Times, 26 Jul 2023: kraft waste Rs 15.80/kg Meerut, Rs 15/kg Gujarat, Rs 13-13.5/kg at southern mills; 25 Sep 2024: kraft waste to finished kraft gap Rs 12.50-13/kg; 28 Jan 2025: North India corrugated waste Rs 20,500/MT), so a mill line for Bengaluru has to be a weekly phone poll of two or three mills recorded with date and source. Anonymised yard posts: section 3(3) of the Competition Act presumes harm from any arrangement among competitors that directly or indirectly determines purchase prices, the CCI Compliance Manual (2 May 2017) lists 'past, current or future prices' and 'individual company prices' as don'ts for any competitor contact while allowing a firm to confirm market prices through 'open market sources', and since the bearings (2020), beer and paper cartel orders (2021) the CCI treats price-information exchange as a standalone violation even without implementation (AZB analysis, 31 Dec 2021); India has no formal safe harbour, but the EU's 2023 Horizontal Guidelines (21 Jul 2023) spell out the accepted design: rely on aggregate and historical data, reduce frequency, restrict access, and never circulate individualised figures. A board line that is Luma.Green's own aggregation of the previous day's posts from at least five independent yards, shown as a median and range with no yard names, where yards cannot see one another's posts and Luma.Green publishes no 'suggested' or floor price for yards, fits that design and is legally the safer way to give the chain a reference; it still needs a competition lawyer's sign-off before launch.
answers.decision: For the pilot, publish only Luma.Green's own aggregated yard line (previous-day median and range, at least five yards, no identities, yards blind to each other's posts) plus a dated weekly phone poll of two or three kraft mills; do not license MCX or BigMint yet, use their free public pages internally for direction only, and budget about Rs 3.5 lakh a year (15-minute-delayed website licence plus connectivity plus GST) if the board later needs an exchange number.
answers.whoToAsk: Competition counsel, for the aggregated board line and for how the household floor is framed; MCX datafeed desk (datafeed@mcxindia.com, +91 22 6731 8888 ext 9206) for a written quote and the exact permission scope for a website line; BigMint sales (info@steelmint.com) for a single-user plan price and a redistribution-licence quote; IRPTA and two or three Karnataka/Tamil Nadu kraft mills for a standing weekly mill-gate quote.

answers.question: Aluminium cans: should the household price be per kg or per can, and what does a beverage can weigh (cans per kg)? Above the household level, should prices be shown GST-inclusive or exclusive? Should drop-off pay a published premium over doorstep pickup, and is one city-wide floor enough for a pilot? What evidence is there that WhatsApp groups and calls from the next buyer set daily rates for kabadiwalas and yards?
answers.answer: Price cans per kg, not per can: Bengaluru's trade already does so, with The Kabadiwala's Bangalore list (29 Sep 2026) showing 'Beverage Cans (Aluminium) Rs 60/kg' against Rs 150/kg for ordinary aluminium and scraprates.in showing aluminium at Rs 156/kg, because cans are thin, lacquered and usually crushed, so counting invites disputes while weight is what the yard pays on. An empty can weighs roughly 10-15 g: about 14 g (some 70 per kg) for a US 355 ml can per Wikipedia's EPA-sourced figure (2011), 14.9 g average for Australian 330 ml cans (2001), 11.3 g in the Australian Aluminium Council/Roland Berger assessment (May 2023, about 88 per kg) and as low as 9.5 g for Ball's lightweight 330 ml (2012); Ball India makes 185, 250, 330, 355 and 500 ml cans (Jan 2022), so India's slim-and-sleek-heavy mix implies about 75-100 cans per kg, and at Rs 60/kg a can is worth under one rupee, which is why a per-can price would look absurd. GST: under Notification 9/2025-Central Tax (Rate) of 17 Sep 2025, effective 22 Sep 2025, metal scrap including aluminium (7602) and plastic scrap (3915) sit in Schedule II at 18%, while paper waste (4707), glass cullet (7001) and rubber waste (4004) sit in Schedule I at 5%; since 10 Oct 2024 a registered buyer pays 18% under reverse charge on metal scrap bought from unregistered sellers (Notification 06/2024-CT(R), 8 Oct 2024) and must deduct 2% GST-TDS on registered-to-registered metal scrap where the taxable value exceeds Rs 2,50,000 per transaction (Notification 25/2024-CT, 9 Oct 2024). The trade quotes ex-GST (Steel Baba: every price 'excludes 18% GST', 29 Sep 2026; Tata nexarc: prices exclude tax and freight, 7 Sep 2026), so above the household level show the base price ex-GST with the rate badge and the computed total beside it, store base, rate and tax as separate integers, and flag whether reverse charge applies; households, who are unregistered, see one all-in number. Drop-off versus pickup: Bengaluru dealers quote doorstep pickups Rs 5-7/kg below the wholesale baseline and give free pickup only from about 25-50 kg (walk-ins from 10-20 kg), with 100 kg-plus lots earning better rates (scraprates.in, 29 Sep 2026); Delhi-NCR apps enforce minimum pickups of Rs 999 (Kabadiwala Online) or Rs 5,000 and 30 kg (Recycle Baba) and a Rs 499 cancellation charge to cover vehicle and manpower, and Prime Scrap (Noida) sets 15 kg minimum with rates 'updated daily based on MCX and regional markets', so yes, publish a drop-off premium (equivalently a pickup deduction) and a minimum pickup lot, with the amount set from the pilot's measured Saathi cost per stop rather than guessed now. Floor: public sources treat Bengaluru as one market (5-8% above the Karnataka average, quotes differentiated by PIN code only), so one city-wide floor is enough for the pilot, with zone offsets added only if pilot data show a consistent spread above 5%, and the floor should be framed as Luma.Green's own guaranteed offer rather than a rate agreed among kabadiwalas, which would raise the competition-law issue in question 1. WhatsApp and calls: the daily-rate economy is visibly WhatsApp- and phone-first (Steel Baba and Tata nexarc push daily scrap rates by WhatsApp and missed call; the 'Scrap Price Daily (Kabad Rate)' Android app has 50,000-plus downloads, last updated 23 Aug 2026; kabadiwala apps state rates 'change daily' and that 'there is no single scrap price', asking sellers to 'call or WhatsApp' to confirm), and Bengaluru studies record the resulting power imbalance (WIEGO 2013: pickers 'exploited by scrap dealers on the price and weight'; Systemiq 2024 Bengaluru case: 68% of surveyed pickers know the price before selling, with 'lack of transparency ... with buyers (prices)' a leading complaint), but no public study documents the specific group-and-callback mechanism for kabadiwalas and yards, so that claim rests on trade practice and should be confirmed shop by shop.
answers.decision: Household aluminium cans priced per kg with an on-screen helper of '~Rs x per can' at 80 cans/kg until the pilot weighs 100 cans; above households show ex-GST base + rate + total (18% metal and plastic, 5% paper and glass) and record reverse-charge status; one Bengaluru floor framed as Luma.Green's own offer; publish a drop-off premium and a minimum pickup lot, with the size fixed from Saathi cost per stop in the first pilot weeks.
answers.whoToAsk: Ten kabadiwala shops and two yards, for the real rate-setting channel and the current pickup-versus-drop-off spread in Bengaluru; a CA, for booking reverse-charge GST and 2% GST-TDS when kabadiwalas are unregistered or cross Rs 2.5 lakh per invoice; the pilot itself, to weigh 100 mixed cans in week one and to cost a Saathi stop.

answers.question: (1) Legal review lands after real users arrive — is 'book the review for 6–12 Oct, open with household pickups and kabadiwala tools, switch on business trades and Saathi jobs once it clears' enough?
answers.answer: The dates that bite are statutory, not the lawyer's. The DPDP Rules 2025 were notified on 13 Nov 2025 (G.S.R. 846(E)); rule 1 puts the substantive rules (3, 5–16, 22, 23: notice, consent, security, breach, erasure, rights) in force 18 months later, i.e. 13 May 2027, and consent-manager rule 4 at 12 months (13 Nov 2026), so DPDP does not bite on 13 Oct 2026 — but penalties run to ₹250 crore for security failures and ₹50 crore for other breaches, so the design must be right now. What does apply from day one is the Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules 2020 (G.S.R. 462(E), 23 Jul 2020): any person operating a digital platform for e-commerce must display a grievance officer's name and contact, acknowledge complaints within 48 hours and resolve them within one month, and the rules expect the entity to be a company; the IT Rules 2021 add a 24-hour acknowledgement and 15-day resolution for intermediaries. Karnataka's gig Act (in force 30 May 2025) requires aggregator registration within 45 days and a 1% welfare fee from 13 Feb 2026 — so Saathi jobs do need to wait for registration, which the guard already does. The guard is enough for business trades and Saathi jobs but not for the household phase: terms, a privacy notice, receipt wording and a named grievance officer must exist on 13 Oct, and those cannot wait for a review that may slip. Split the review into a day-one pack (terms, privacy notice, grievance officer, receipt text, Kannada versions) that must clear by 12 Oct, and a phase-two pack (business rulebook, Saathi terms, escrow) that gates those features.
answers.decision: Split the legal review: a day-one pack (terms, privacy notice, named grievance officer, receipt wording) cleared by 12 Oct or the household launch becomes invite-only; a phase-two pack gates business trades and Saathi jobs.
answers.whoToAsk: Counsel (day-one pack and whether the entity is a company as the E-Commerce Rules expect) and a CA for receipts and GST wording.

answers.question: (2) Overclaiming traceability — is 'trace by mass balance and say so; records are supporting evidence, never certification' enough?
answers.answer: Mass balance is the recognised chain-of-custody method for exactly this situation: ISCC's guidance (13 Feb 2026) defines it as certified and non-certified material physically mixed through the value chain but kept separate by verifiable bookkeeping, with credits never exceeding inputs. India's own EPR machinery is quantity-based, not item-based: CPCB's e-waste FAQ (23 Jan 2024) says a recycler proves purchases with the seller's sales invoice, or, for informal-sector purchases, 'any sales receipt having name and address of the seller', and certificates are generated against quantities processed; the SWM Rules 2026 returns (rule 8(g)) are likewise tonnage by source and destination. So no regulator expects bottle-level identity, and a weighed, dated, receipted hand-off ledger is the standard of evidence. The guard is enough provided every export and receipt carries the one-line statement that this is a mass-balance record, not a chain-of-custody certificate, and the app never says 'your bottle became X'. Build the ledger so a later ISCC or Verra auditor can reconcile inputs against outputs per site per period (weight, material code, from, to, timestamp, photo hash); that is what converts a record into certifiable evidence if a brand ever asks.
answers.decision: Keep mass balance; add the disclaimer line to every receipt and export; structure the ledger as per-site, per-period input/output so it can be audited later.

answers.question: (3) Exchange prices (MCX/LME) on public pages — is 'no exchange number on any public screen; reference prices stay with the admin' enough?
answers.answer: I could not re-open the MCX data-feed page or the LME data-distribution page today: mcxindia.com returned an Akamai 'Access Denied' to both a browser fetch and curl, and lme.com sat behind a Cloudflare challenge; the plan's sources list records both as opened on 29 Sep 2026, and the search summaries of the MCX page say only delayed data may be shown on public websites, that non-members must subscribe via MCX or an authorised distributor, and that resale and public-internet display need the exchange's permission. What I could verify today is how licensed and unlicensed display looks in practice: a SEBI-registered broker (Upstox) publishes MCX copper with a timestamp (₹1,392.50 at 22:36 IST on 29 Sep 2026), and a trade magazine republishes MCX aluminium ₹351/kg and LME aluminium US$3,251.50/t (29 Sep 2026) with the note that the MCX figure is 'manually updated with verified rates' — i.e. hand-typed, not a feed. The guard is enough for launch. For the admin console, have the admin type a reference number by hand with source and date into the audit log rather than storing or redistributing any feed; that is ordinary use of a published figure, not redistribution. Licence a delayed feed only if the public price board later needs exchange-linked charts, and keep the plan's second point in mind: showing factory or exchange numbers to households exposes kabadiwala margins and is a relationship risk before it is a legal one.
answers.decision: Keep exchange numbers off public and shop-facing screens; the admin enters reference prices manually with source and date; no data feed until a licence is bought.
answers.whoToAsk: MCX market-data team via the data-feed page and LME market-data licensing, if a delayed feed is ever wanted; counsel is not needed for the launch position.

answers.question: (4) Shared price floors read as price-fixing under Competition Act s.3 — any CCI precedent on platform-set floors or MSP-like minimums, and is 'floors framed as household protection; shops price freely above them; counsel to confirm' enough?
answers.answer: Section 3(3)(a) presumes harm from agreements among enterprises in the same trade that directly or indirectly determine purchase or sale prices, so buying-price coordination among shops is squarely covered, and the Competition (Amendment) Act 2023 added a proviso (notified 19 May 2023) presuming a party 'not engaged in identical or similar trade' — a platform — to be part of such an agreement 'if it participates or intends to participate in the furtherance of such agreement' (hub-and-spoke). There is no CCI or court ruling on a platform-set purchase-price floor for independent sellers; the closest precedents cut in your favour and against you at once. In favour: the Supreme Court in Samir Agrawal v CCI (15 Dec 2020) held that Ola's and Uber's app-set fares were not a hub-and-spoke cartel because thousands of drivers had no meeting of minds and merely accepted a price the platform set unilaterally. Against: the CCI found the Trustees' Association of India and three trustee companies guilty under s.3(3) for fixing minimum fees (order reported 3 Sep 2026, no penalty because members often charged below the floor), fined the Agro Input Dealers Association and office-bearers for coordinating members (21 Aug 2026, s.3(3)(b), penalties from ₹8,622 to ₹4.98 lakh), and has treated buyer–seller price arrangements (Godrej/Panasonic) under s.3(3). The line the precedents draw is agreement among competitors: a floor the admin sets alone from a documented formula, protecting the weaker side, with shops free to pay more, looks like Uber/Ola; a floor that shops vote on, that an association endorses, that is fed by shop-to-shop price sharing, or that becomes the price everyone pays looks like the trustees' case with Luma.Green as the hub. The guard is enough only with those conditions written into the product: never consult shop groups on the floor, never show one shop another shop's buying prices, and watch the share of trades struck exactly at the floor.
answers.decision: Keep admin-set floors from the documented formula (75% of the 28-day median), no shop consultation or association role, no shop-to-shop price visibility, and an audit metric for trades at exactly the floor; hand counsel a one-page memo on this design.
answers.whoToAsk: Competition counsel to confirm the design and the wording on the price board.

answers.question: (5) Price crashes and stale floors — is 'floors as a share of the reference price, a suspend switch, dated rows' enough?
answers.answer: The crash the plan cites is real and sourced: the Indian Recovered Paper Traders Association said on 9 Jun 2023 that domestic recovered-paper collection had fallen 50–55% and about 30% of kabadiwalas and feriwalas had left the trade when kraft waste paper dropped to ₹11,000–13,500 per tonne (₹11,000 in Chennai); on 16 Feb 2024 the same association reported a further 20% fall within about ten days (₹19.50 to ₹15.50–16 per kg) as mills cut rates. Today's retail kabadiwala rates in Bangalore on a public rate card are newspaper ₹10/kg, carton ₹3/kg, PET ₹10/kg, iron ₹22/kg, aluminium ₹150/kg and copper ₹500/kg, so a 20% move in ten days on paper is a ₹2/kg move against a ₹10 price. A floor set at 75% of a 28-day median is above market within about two weeks of a 2023-style fall, because the median lags; the suspend switch then depends on someone noticing. The guard's mechanics are right but need a trigger: flag a material when its 7-day median falls below floor ÷ 0.9, auto-suspend the floor for that material when a set share of trades is refused or struck at the floor for three days, and show the floor's date on the price board so shops see it is not stale. No further figures are needed; the missing item is your own trade data, which the pilot will produce.
answers.decision: Keep 75% of the 28-day median as the default, add a 7-day trigger and a per-material auto-suspend, and print the floor date on the board.

answers.question: (6) Hazardous material to the wrong buyer — is 'sell only to businesses whose registration the admin verified; decide whether to hide them from the household pilot' enough?
answers.answer: The rules are explicit about who may receive each stream. E-Waste (Management) Rules 2022 (in force 1 Apr 2023): CPCB's FAQ of 23 Jan 2024 says only producers, recyclers and refurbishers registered on the EPR portal may collect e-waste, bulk consumers must hand e-waste only to them, and registered entities may not deal with unregistered ones; a recycler buying from the informal sector must upload a receipt with the seller's name and address. Battery Waste Management Rules 2022 (22 Aug 2022) make consumers discard batteries separately to a collection or recycling entity and keep the list of registered recyclers with the State Pollution Control Boards. Used oil has had EPR since 1 Apr 2024 (Hazardous and Other Wastes Second Amendment Rules 2023): collection agents and recyclers must register on CPCB's portal. Waste tyres have EPR under the Hazardous and Other Wastes Amendment Rules 2022, with producers, recyclers and retreaders registered on CPCB's tyre portal. A kabadiwala is not a registered e-waste collector, so a household-to-kabadiwala e-waste sale inside the app is the informal channel these rules try to close; the exposure sits with the shop and the recycler, but the platform that arranged it will be named. The guard is right for business trades if the admin records the CPCB or KSPCB registration number and its expiry and checks it on the portal; for households the answer to the plan's open decision is to keep e-waste, batteries, tyres and used oil out of the pilot and show a 'where to take this' note instead.
answers.decision: Exclude e-waste, batteries, tyres and used oil from the household pilot; allow them only business-to-registered-recycler with the registration number verified on the CPCB or KSPCB portal.
answers.whoToAsk: KSPCB for the Karnataka authorised-recycler lists; the CPCB e-waste, battery, used-oil and tyre portals for registration checks.

answers.question: (7) Gig-worker law — is 'Saathi work register, written terms, fee calculator; counsel on classification' enough?
answers.answer: Two regimes apply and neither turns on whether Saathis are employees. The Code on Social Security 2020 came into force on 21 Nov 2025; an 'aggregator' is 'a digital intermediary or a market place for a buyer or user of a service to connect with the seller or the service provider', Schedule VII lists nine categories including logistics, e-marketplace and 'any other goods and services provider platform', and s.114(4) sets a contribution of 1–2% of annual turnover capped at 5% of payments to gig workers — but as of 1 Jul 2026 neither the rate nor the start date had been notified. Karnataka's Platform Based Gig Workers (Social Security and Welfare) Act 2025 is live: effective 30 May 2025 (ordinance), Act notified 12 Sep 2025, Rules 19 Nov 2025; aggregators register with the Welfare Board within 45 days and file a machine-readable worker database; the welfare fee was notified on 16 Feb 2026 at 1% per transaction with caps of ₹0.50–₹1.50 (logistics two-wheeler ₹0.50, e-marketplace two-wheeler ₹0.50, professional services ₹1.50), effective 13 Feb 2026, deposited quarterly and self-reported until the verification system runs; the Rules give Saathi-type grievances 7 working days to be raised and 15 working days to be resolved; penalties run ₹5,000–₹1 lakh with 12% interest on unpaid fees. Swiggy, Zomato, Zepto and IAMAI have challenged the Act in the Karnataka High Court, which refused a stay (8 Jul 2026). A pickup-and-sorting app paying Saathis per job through the platform is an aggregator on either definition; the open point is only which schedule row (logistics or e-marketplace) sets the cap. The guard is right and the cost is small (1% of Saathi payouts, at most ₹1.50 a job); what is missing is the registration itself, which must precede the first paid job.
answers.decision: Register as an aggregator with the Karnataka Welfare Board before the first Saathi job, budget the 1% welfare fee as a line in the fee calculator, and keep the Code on Social Security contribution as a watch item.
answers.whoToAsk: Karnataka Labour Department / Platform Based Gig Workers Welfare Board for the schedule row; counsel for the Saathi terms.

answers.question: (8) SWM Rules 2026 making informal shops visible — is 'city exports carry totals only; business data shared with consent; a help-me-register task' enough?
answers.answer: The Solid Waste Management Rules 2026 (S.O. 388(E), 27 Jan 2026, in force 1 Apr 2026) define an 'informal waste collector' to include 'individuals, associations or waste traders' engaged in 'collecting, segregating, sorting, sale and purchase of waste materials' — that is the kabadiwala. The duties I could find run through the local body rather than the shop: rule 39(53) makes urban local bodies build a ward-wise database on the central portal of everyone, 'including in informal sector such as waste pickers or collectors', involved in collection, sorting, transport or recycling, and rule 39(54) tells them to integrate those people and organisations; rule 8 makes local bodies, concessionaires and any third party they authorise register on the portal; CPCB's summary adds 'no engagement with unregistered or unauthorised entities' and a portal target of 1 Oct 2026. Rule 17 lets State Pollution Control Boards levy environmental compensation on 'entities carrying out activities without registration as mandated' and on entities engaged in collection, sorting or transport, under guidelines CPCB has yet to publish, with action under s.15 of the Environment (Protection) Act on top. So the text does not fine a kabadiwala today for being unregistered, but it makes unregistered shops non-compliant counterparties as soon as the local database and CPCB's guidelines exist, and Down To Earth (29 Jan 2026) notes the rules say little about how integration should happen. The guard is enough for the pilot; the 'help me register' task is the right response because the ward database is where shops will need to appear. Add one thing: treat any request from GBA, BSWML or KSPCB for shop-level data as a legal request that goes to counsel, not an export button.
answers.decision: Keep totals-only exports and per-business consent; add a 'share my registration with GBA' consent flag; route any authority data request through counsel; watch for CPCB's environmental-compensation guidelines.
answers.whoToAsk: GBA/BSWML solid-waste cell on the ward database and KSPCB on compensation guidelines once CPCB publishes them.

answers.question: (9) DPDP retention (logs kept a year) vs the promise to delete household photos at 90 days — is 'delete images, keep a hash and metadata; counsel to reconcile' enough?
answers.answer: The two obligations are about different things and do not collide. Rule 6(1)(e) of the DPDP Rules 2025 requires a data fiduciary to 'retain such logs and personal data for a period of one year' for detecting and investigating unauthorised access — the access logs and what is needed to investigate a breach, unless another law says otherwise. Rule 8(3) requires retaining 'personal data, associated traffic data and other logs of the processing' for at least one year for the Seventh Schedule (state-request) purposes, and its illustration is an e-book platform keeping order, payment and delivery events for a year even after the user deletes the account. The Third Schedule's three-years-from-last-activity rule applies only to e-commerce entities with at least two crore registered users, gaming intermediaries with fifty lakh and social-media intermediaries with two crore, so it does not reach Luma.Green. All of this (rules 3, 5–16) starts on 13 May 2027, and the Act itself wants personal data erased once its purpose is served. A household photo is content whose purpose ends with the pickup; the event record (who uploaded what, when, its hash, the pickup and payment events) is the log. Deleting the image at 90 days while keeping that record for twelve months and then erasing it satisfies both rules, so the guard is enough; write it into the privacy notice in those words.
answers.decision: Keep: photo deleted at 90 days; event log with hash retained 12 months then erased; state both in the privacy notice before 13 May 2027.
answers.whoToAsk: Counsel only to sign off the notice wording.

answers.question: (10) App weights read as certified — is 'receipts say recorded weight; the stamped scale stays the legal record' enough?
answers.answer: The law attaches to the scale, not the app. Section 24 of the Legal Metrology Act 2009 requires any weight or measure that is or is likely to be 'used in any transaction' to be verified and stamped before use; s.33 punishes use of an unverified weight with a fine of ₹2,000 to ₹10,000 and up to one year's imprisonment for a repeat; s.25 punishes non-standard weights with fines up to ₹25,000; ss.10–11 require prices to be quoted in standard units. Electronic scales are re-stamped annually, and Karnataka's e-Mapan portal issues and lets you search verification certificates. The Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Act 2026 (passed 1–2 Apr 2026) brings improvement notices for a first offence; the Department of Consumer Affairs brought the Legal Metrology amendments into force from 1 May 2026 (S.O. 2103(E), 27 Apr 2026). So the app's 'recorded weight' label is fine, and the real exposure is a shop pricing a household on an unstamped or expired scale. The guard is enough but incomplete: capture each business's e-Mapan verification certificate number and expiry at onboarding, print 'weighed on the shop's scale, certificate no. …' on receipts, and never use the word 'certified' for an app value.
answers.decision: Keep 'recorded weight'; add a per-business scale-certificate field with expiry (e-Mapan) and show it on receipts.

answers.question: (11) Waste-picker politics in Bengaluru — is 'co-design with Hasiru Dala and the union; pickers must earn more, not less' enough?
answers.answer: Bengaluru's dry-waste chain runs through ward Dry Waste Collection Centres operated by waste-picker entrepreneurs with Hasiru Dala's support: each ward has a DWCC that sorts dry waste and sells it to recyclers, Hasiru Dala manages 40 of them across eight divisions, and 30–40% of dry waste is recycled through them. The 2026 picture is unsettled: BSWML is replacing the ad hoc door-to-door contracts with 33 constituency packages using GPS-tracked three-tonne vehicles (21 approved, work orders being issued, 5 Sep 2026), seven packages had to be re-tendered on 22 Sep 2026 after the lowest bidders declined, and in March 2026 a blocked landfill and contractors paying workers irregularly produced a city-wide crisis. The SWM Rules 2026 now oblige local bodies to database and integrate waste pickers and informal collectors (rule 39(53)–(54)). A household-to-kabadiwala app therefore competes at ward level for the same sellable dry waste the DWCC depends on, and pickers and DWCC operators will read it as diversion unless they are inside it. The guard names the right partners but no mechanism; the mechanism is to onboard DWCC operators as shops (they are the ward's authorised dry-waste receivers), let pickers register as Saathis, and start only in wards whose DWCC operator has agreed. This cannot be settled from public pages; it is a negotiation.
answers.decision: Sign an MoU with Hasiru Dala before 13 Oct; pilot only in wards whose DWCC operator is onboarded as a shop; offer pickers Saathi registration first.

answers.question: (12) Support promises one person can't keep (15-minute replies, 10-minute safety callbacks) — is 'a rota of at least two before 13 Oct; auto-accept limited to shop hours' enough?
answers.answer: No law requires 15-minute replies or 10-minute callbacks; the legal minimums are slower and are the ones that must be met. The Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules 2020 require a displayed grievance officer who acknowledges within 48 hours and resolves within one month; the IT Rules 2021 require intermediaries to acknowledge within 24 hours and resolve within 15 days; Karnataka's gig Rules give Saathi grievances 15 working days to be resolved. A published 15-minute promise becomes a term of service the moment it appears on the site, and a missed safety callback is a reputational and possibly tortious problem regardless of law. The guard (two people on a rota, auto-accept only in shop hours) is the right operational floor, but the promise should be rewritten: publish 24-hour acknowledgement and 15-day resolution as commitments, keep 15 minutes as an internal target shown nowhere, and for safety callbacks promise only what a two-person duty phone can deliver (for example 30 minutes, 8am–8pm) with a plain 'call 112' line for emergencies.
answers.decision: Publish 24 h / 15 days as the commitments and a named grievance officer; keep 15 minutes and 10 minutes as internal targets; staff a two-person duty phone for safety callbacks in stated hours.

answers.question: (13) Plastic-credit revenue and additionality — is 'kept out of the base case' enough?
answers.answer: Yes, and the reason is now written into the standard. Verra's corrections and clarifications to the Plastic Waste Collection Methodology PWRM0001 (12 Aug 2024, effective immediately) require project proponents to list every binding law on plastic collection in the region and to treat 'mandated extended producer responsibility (EPR) schemes in a project region' as part of the regulatory-surplus test; a project may still claim surplus only by showing those requirements are not systematically enforced, for example that the regional compliance rate is below 50%. India's Plastic Waste Management Rules run a CPCB EPR-certificate market in which registered recyclers generate credits by tonnage and producers buy them, so plastic that Luma.Green's chain sells into that certificate stream is already counted against a producer's obligation and cannot also be sold as a voluntary credit without double counting. Proving a sub-50% compliance rate for Bengaluru is a research project with a validation body, not a pilot task. Keeping plastic credits out of the base case is the right call; if it is revisited, the first question is whether the recyclers in the chain generate EPR certificates on that material.
answers.decision: Keep plastic credits out of the base case; revisit only with a Verra validation body and evidence on regional EPR compliance.
answers.whoToAsk: A Verra-approved validation body, if ever pursued.

answers.question: (14) Escrow eligibility — split settlement needs ₹40 lakh of our own turnover; is 'bank escrow with a trustee, or each yard as its own merchant' enough?
answers.answer: The ₹40 lakh figure is confirmed and comes from the regulator, not just the vendor. The RBI (Regulation of Payment Aggregators) Directions 2025 (15 Sep 2025, effective immediately) require a non-bank PA to hold ₹15 crore net worth at application and ₹25 crore within three years, bar a PA from running a marketplace, let a marketplace onboarded by a PA accept payments only for sellers onboarded on its platform, and allow a PA to pay a third party on a merchant's instruction only where the merchant has annual turnover above ₹40 lakh (or export turnover above ₹5 lakh) and the third party is the payee who interfaces with the payer. Razorpay Route applies exactly that: domestic turnover above ₹40 lakh on GSTR-3B in FY25 or FY26, a written use-case confirmation, and proofs that were due by 31 Dec 2025. A new company with no filed turnover therefore cannot use Route-style split settlement, so the pilot's simulated escrow is the only honest option now. The two fallbacks in the plan are the right ones: each yard or recycler as its own merchant on a PA, with the buyer paying the yard directly and Luma.Green invoicing its fee separately; or a bank escrow with a trustee (RazorpayX Escrow+ routes through ICICI, RBL and Yes Bank with trusteeship bundled; pricing is not published). The guard is enough; the missing numbers are escrow fees and setup time, which only a quote will give.
answers.decision: Pilot with simulated escrow; at go-live use direct-to-yard payment through a PA with Luma.Green's fee invoiced separately; move to a bank escrow with trustee when volumes justify the fees; revisit Route once GSTR-3B shows ₹40 lakh.

answers.question: (15) Demo data mistaken for real firms — is 'demo GSTINs fail the GSTIN checksum, names are invented, every screen with sample figures says so' enough?
answers.answer: A GSTIN is 15 characters: a two-digit state code, the ten-character PAN, an entity code, the letter Z and a check character computed from the first 14 with a 36-symbol alphabet and alternating weights of 1 and 2 (the ISO 7064 MOD 37-36 family). A string whose check character does not match cannot be a real registration, and the GST portal's search rejects it, so a checksum-invalid demo GSTIN can never collide with a real firm; the converse also holds — a checksum-valid string is only 'internally consistent' and only GSTN's search or API proves it exists (dev.to, 8 Aug 2026). The guard is therefore enough for GSTINs, and the invented names and sample-figures banner cover the rest of the screen. Extend the same idea to the other identifiers demo screens show: consent numbers are not checksummed, so prefix them 'DEMO-'; use phone numbers that cannot be Indian mobiles (Indian mobiles start with 6–9); and keep demo tenants in a separate environment so a demo row can never be exported with real ones. At onboarding, verify every real GSTIN against the GST portal's public search before the admin approves a business.
answers.decision: Keep; add DEMO- prefixes to consent numbers, impossible phone numbers, a separate demo tenant, and GST-portal verification of real GSTINs at onboarding.

answers.question: Did the Finance Act 2026 enact the 2% income-tax TCS on the sale of scrap (up from 1%)? Which sellers are covered (turnover thresholds), and does the exemption for buyers who use scrap in manufacturing survive under the Income-tax Act 2025? Which section carries it now?
answers.answer: Yes. The Finance Act, 2026 (No. 4 of 2026) received the President's assent on 30 March 2026, and its section 85 amends the Table in section 394(1) of the Income-tax Act, 2025 so that against Sl. No. 4 ('Sale of scrap', collected by the seller) '1%' is replaced by '2%'; under section 1(2)(a) of the Act this is in force from 1 April 2026 (the same clause was Clause 73 of the Finance Bill introduced on 1 February 2026 and was carried through unchanged). TCS on scrap is therefore now section 394(1), Table Sl. No. 4, at 2% of the amount debited or received, whichever is earlier; the old section 206C(1) of the 1961 Act is repealed. 'Seller' is defined in section 402(33): the Central or State Government, a local authority, a corporation or authority set up by statute, a company, a firm, a co-operative society, and an individual or HUF only if total sales/gross receipts/turnover from business exceeded Rs 1 crore (Rs 50 lakh for a profession) in the immediately preceding tax year — so a sole-proprietor kabadiwala below Rs 1 crore is not a 'seller' and collects nothing, while a yard or recycler that is a firm or company always is. 'Buyer' (section 402(6)) excludes public sector companies, the Central and State Governments, foreign embassies/missions, clubs, and a person buying in retail for personal consumption. The manufacturing exemption survives: section 394(2) says no tax shall be collected from a resident buyer who furnishes a written declaration in duplicate that the goods are for manufacturing, processing or producing articles or things or for generating power and not for trading; section 394(3) makes the seller deliver one copy to the Principal Chief Commissioner/Commissioner by the 7th of the following month. The declaration is now Form No. 127 under Rule 212 of the Income-tax Rules, 2026 (it replaces Form 27C), and the buyer's PAN is mandatory or the form is invalid. Whether TCS applies at all to post-consumer material depends on the definition of 'scrap' — see question 2.
answers.decision: Model TCS as a seller-side flag: off for individual/HUF sellers under Rs 1 crore prior-year turnover, on for firms/companies; when on and the material is 'scrap', collect 2% from 1 April 2026 unless the buyer has a valid Form 127 on file (store the form and PAN per buyer). Ask the CA to confirm whether the 2% is charged on the GST-inclusive invoice value and how it interacts with buyer-side TDS on purchase of goods under section 393(1).
answers.whoToAsk: The CA (GST-inclusive base for TCS, interplay with section 393(1) TDS, higher rate where a buyer has no PAN).

answers.question: Does the Act's definition of 'scrap' cover post-consumer recyclables that yards sell, such as newspaper, PET bottles and cartons?
answers.answer: Probably not, but it is not settled by statute or circular. Section 402(31) of the Income-tax Act, 2025 defines scrap word-for-word as the 1961 Act did: 'waste and scrap from the manufacture or mechanical working of materials which is definitely not usable as such because of breakage, cutting up, wear and other reasons' — two conditions, an origin in manufacture or mechanical working and unusability as such. Old newspapers, PET bottles, cartons, glass bottles and rags come from consumption, not from a manufacturing process, and are bought precisely because they are usable as raw material, so on the plain words they fall outside the definition. The courts have mostly read it that way: the Gujarat High Court in CIT (TDS) v. Priya Blue Industries (Tax Appeal 604 of 2015, 3 November 2015) held that items usable as such are not scrap even if the trade calls them scrap and that the material must arise from manufacture or mechanical working; ITAT Ahmedabad in Dhasawala Traders (1 September 2016), ITAT Lucknow in Lala Bharat Lal & Sons (ITA 14-16/LKW/2019, 19 February 2020) and another ITAT bench in March 2020 held that a mere trader whose scrap did not arise from manufacture need not collect TCS; and the Madras High Court in Adisankara Spinning Mills (2010) treated cotton waste bought as raw material as not scrap. The contrary view is the Rajkot Special Bench in Bharti Auto Products v. CIT (2013) 145 ITD 1, which held traders liable regardless of source; later tribunals have followed the High Court over the Special Bench, but there is no CBDT circular on post-consumer recyclables and no ruling on kabadiwala material specifically. Two caveats matter for the pilot: metal scrap sold by a yard often does originate in mechanical working (industrial offcuts, turnings, broken machinery), so metal is the family most exposed to TCS; and since the definition is unchanged, all the 206C case law carries over to section 394.
answers.decision: Default: treat post-consumer paper, PET, cartons, glass and rags as outside 'scrap' (no TCS) and treat metal scrap sold by a firm/company yard as potentially in scope; neutralise the question wherever possible by collecting Form 127 from recycler and manufacturer buyers, and get a written opinion from tax counsel before the first yard-to-recycler metal sale above trivial value.
answers.whoToAsk: Tax counsel (written opinion on section 402(31) for post-consumer material and for yard metal sales), then the CA to set the per-material TCS flag.

answers.question: After the GST rate changes of 22 September 2025 (Notification 9/2025-CT(Rate)), which GST rate and HSN code apply to each material family: waste paper (4707), plastic scrap (3915), ferrous scrap (7204), copper/aluminium/brass scrap (7404/7602), glass cullet (7001), rags (6309/6310), e-waste (8549), batteries? Which value threshold applies to the 2% GST TDS on metal scrap under Notification 25/2024?
answers.answer: Notification 9/2025-Central Tax (Rate) dated 17 September 2025 (in force 22 September 2025) is now the single master rate schedule, and its text places the scrap families as follows: waste paper 4707 in Schedule I (2.5% CGST, so 5% GST, Sl. 317); glass cullet 7001 in Schedule I (5%, Sl. 406); worn clothing and rags 6309/6310 in Schedule I (5%, Sl. 391); plastic waste, parings and scrap 3915 in Schedule II (9% CGST, so 18% GST, Sl. 116); ferrous scrap 7204 (Sl. 263), copper scrap 7404 (Sl. 309, which also covers brass as a copper alloy), aluminium scrap 7602 (Sl. 331), plus nickel 7503, lead 7802, zinc 7902 and tin 8002 scrap, all in Schedule II at 18%; and electrical and electronic waste and scrap 8549 in Schedule II at 18% (Sl. 521). Batteries: all electric accumulators under 8507 (lead-acid, lithium-ion, others) are 18% from 22 September 2025 (Sl. 480) — the GST Council FAQ of 3 September 2025 confirms lithium-ion was already 18% and other batteries came down from 28% — and primary cells 8506 are 18% (Sl. 479); spent batteries sold as waste are classified under 8549 at 18%. None of the scrap headings changed on 22 September 2025 (the Council's HSN-wise change annexure lists no scrap entry), so note the history for plastic: 3915 was cut to 5% on 13 October 2017 (Notification 34/2017) but moved back to 18% on 1 October 2021 (Notification 8/2021, which omitted Schedule I entry 187A and inserted 101A in the 18% schedule), and e-waste went from 5% to 18% on 18 July 2022 (Notification 6/2022). Metal scrap has two extra rules since 10 October 2024: under Notification 6/2024-CT(Rate) a registered buyer who purchases metal scrap of Chapters 72-81 from an unregistered supplier pays the 18% GST under reverse charge with no threshold (so a registered yard buying from an unregistered kabadiwala self-pays the tax), and under Notification 25/2024-Central Tax (9 October 2024, G.S.R. 629(E)) a registered person receiving metal scrap of Chapters 72-81 from another registered person must deduct TDS under section 51 CGST Act at 2% (1% CGST + 1% SGST, or 2% IGST). The threshold is the one in section 51(1) itself: deduction applies 'where the total value of such supply, under a contract, exceeds two lakh and fifty thousand rupees', value taken excluding CGST/SGST/IGST/cess shown on the invoice, so Rs 2,50,000 per contract ex-GST, not per invoice (multiple invoices under one contract are aggregated); no deduction if the supplier's location and the place of supply are in a different State from the recipient's registration. The deductor must register separately in Form GST REG-07 (select 'Others' and type 'Metal Scrap Dealers', per the GSTN advisory of 22 October 2024), deposit by the 10th of the following month and file GSTR-7, with GSTR-7A as the certificate; the supplier gets the credit in its electronic cash ledger. This GST TDS is separate from, and additional to, the 2% income-tax TCS in question 1.
answers.decision: Hard-code a per-material table: 4707, 7001, 6309/6310 at 5%; 3915, 7204, 7404 (incl. brass), 7602, 7503/7802/7902/8002, 8549 and 8507/8506 at 18%; require every registered yard buying metal scrap from an unregistered seller to book reverse-charge GST, and flag any registered-to-registered metal contract whose ex-GST value passes Rs 2,50,000 for 2% GST TDS by the buyer. Ask the CA how a 'contract' is delimited for recurring spot purchases from the same supplier; until then treat a standing supply arrangement as one contract (aggregate its invoices).
answers.whoToAsk: The CA (definition of 'contract' for the Rs 2.5 lakh GST-TDS threshold in recurring purchases; REG-07 set-up for each yard).

answers.question: For a pilot support line: SIM vs virtual number, and can the same number move from the WhatsApp Business app to the WhatsApp Cloud API or a provider such as MSG91 later without losing the number? Do outbound IVR or automated voice reminders need TRAI DLT registration (140/160 number series) before scale?
answers.answer: Number type: Meta's Cloud API accepts any number you own that can receive an SMS or a voice call for the one-time code (mobile recommended; fixed-line and VoIP allowed with limits), and cloud-telephony 'longcode' virtual numbers such as MSG91's cannot receive SMS, so they verify by phone call and must not already be on personal WhatsApp; a virtual number also stays in the provider's pool and costs money (MyOperator's cheapest plan with unlimited calling and WhatsApp is ₹5,000/month; Exotel and MSG91 only quote on request), whereas a SIM is yours and moves between phones and providers. Recommendation: a dedicated SIM in the company's or a founder's name, run in the WhatsApp Business app, for the pilot; add a virtual number only when you need inbound IVR, call recording or multi-agent routing. Moving to the API without losing the number: Meta documents two routes — (a) 'coexistence' (Business app and Cloud API on the same number via a partner; MSG91's onboarding has a 'Connect WhatsApp Business App Number' option), which needs app version 2.24.17 or higher, syncs up to 180 days of 1:1 chats if done within 24 hours, caps throughput at 20 messages/second, disables broadcast lists, disappearing and view-once messages, does not sync groups, has no calling API, and can be disconnected from the app under Settings > Account > Business Platform; India is covered (Wati, 17 Aug 2026; AiSensy) — or (b) full migration: back up, delete the account in the app, wait about 3 minutes, register on the Cloud API; chat history is lost and the number cannot return to the app unless deregistered. Moving between providers later (MSG91 to another BSP or direct Cloud API): Meta's WABA-to-WABA migration keeps the number, display name, messaging limits and Official Business Account status, copies only templates that are APPROVED with GREEN quality, resets template quality ratings, and requires two-step verification switched off and Business Verification done; MSG91's own guide says just disable 2FA and cancel the plan, no need to delete the number; one caveat from 360dialog: WABA migration is not supported for a coexistence number, so disconnect coexistence first. TRAI: yes — TRAI's 18 June 2024 guidelines under TCCCPR-2018 require every sender, explicitly including 'SMEs, big and small businesses, and any entity', to register on a telecom operator's DLT platform before sending any commercial communication by voice or SMS, to make commercial voice calls only from the 140 (promotional) or 160 (service/transactional) series with registered voice headers, and not to use ordinary 10-digit fixed or mobile numbers for promotional, service or transactional calls; the 12 Feb 2025 amendment (in force 30 days after gazette publication, some clauses 60 days) adds that 'Every Sender shall notify the Originating Access Provider, in advance, about the use of Auto Dialer or Robo-Calls' and their objective in writing, defines a transactional call as one within 30 minutes of a customer-initiated transaction, and treats service calls to existing customers as needing no explicit consent. The practical catch: DoT allotted the 160 series on 30 May 2024 with operators verifying each entity, the first stage covers RBI/SEBI/IRDAI/PFRDA-regulated entities and government, and provider pages as of 24 Sep 2026 (Acefone; Plivo) still say non-BFSI businesses cannot get a 160 number (Acefone mentions a 1601 sub-series for utilities, logistics and couriers), with inventory of only 1,000 numbers per operator per circle (Exotel, 26 Jun 2024). So for the 13 Oct 2026 pilot: send pickup reminders as WhatsApp utility templates and human calls, start DLT registration on an operator portal (Airtel, Jio, Vi, BSNL or Tata) now because entity, header and template approvals take days, and before scaling automated voice get a 140-series number through a registered telemarketer or cloud-telephony provider for anything promotional and ask the provider whether a 160 number can be allotted to a non-BFSI Karnataka entity. Open items: monthly price of an Exotel or MSG91 virtual number (quote-only), and whether a landline-type virtual number placed in the WhatsApp Business app qualifies for coexistence (Meta only says the number must already be registered in the app).
answers.decision: Buy a dedicated SIM for the pilot support line and run it in the WhatsApp Business app; when you need the API, onboard through a partner's coexistence flow (MSG91 offers it) so the number and up to 180 days of chats carry over, and keep two-step verification off before any provider move. Register Luma.Green on a DLT portal now, keep automated outbound voice off until that is done, and use WhatsApp utility templates plus human calls for reminders during the pilot.
answers.whoToAsk: Your cloud-telephony provider (Exotel or MSG91) for virtual-number pricing and whether a 160-series number can be allotted to a non-BFSI entity in Karnataka today; the operator DLT portal (Airtel/Jio/Vi) for registration timelines; a telecom-compliance counsel to confirm that low-volume human callbacks from the support SIM are acceptable during the pilot.

answers.question: Which text-to-speech service fits a pilot in Kannada, Tamil, Telugu, Hindi and Urdu: Google Chirp 3 HD, AI4Bharat Indic Parler-TTS, Bhashini, Sarvam? Compare pricing, language coverage and startup access. Who could record human voice clips quickly and cheaply in Bengaluru?
answers.answer: Coverage: Google's Chirp 3: HD (docs updated 24 Sep 2026) lists hi-IN, kn-IN, ta-IN, te-IN and ur-IN, the only paid option here that covers all five; Sarvam's Bulbul v3 covers 11 languages (bn, en, gu, hi, kn, ml, mr, od, pa, ta, te) — Hindi, Kannada, Tamil and Telugu but no Urdu — with 30+ voices, 2,500 characters per request, REST and streaming; AI4Bharat's Indic Parler-TTS (Apache 2.0, self-hosted) covers 21 languages including all five with 69 voices (its Urdu native-speaker score is 77.75 vs 95–99 for the best languages), while the newer IndicF5 (MIT, voice cloning from a reference clip, consent required) covers 11 languages without Urdu; the government Bhashini platform lists TTS models for Kannada, Tamil, Telugu and Hindi from AI4Bharat, IISc, Bodhan and IIT Madras, and Urdu only from IIT Madras. Pricing: Google Chirp 3: HD is US$30 per 1 million characters after 1 million free characters per month (legacy Standard and WaveNet US$4 per million after 4 million free, Neural2 US$16, Studio US$160, instant custom voice US$60; pricing page accessed 30 Sep 2026); Sarvam is ₹30 per 10,000 characters (₹3 per 1,000) for TTS and the same for voice cloning, with ₹100 free credits at signup, so the two are within the same order of magnitude once Google's free tier is used up; Parler-TTS and IndicF5 cost only your GPU time; Bhashini is free for proof-of-concept after registering at dashboard.bhashini.co.in (approval by the DIBD team), but its docs say production use or charging end users needs the paid version by contacting the Bhashini team, and no public price exists (its CEO said on 18 Apr 2024 that many services would be charged). Startup access: Google gives a US$300 free trial, US$2,000 for pre-funded startups and up to US$200,000 (US$350,000 for AI-first) for Seed–Series A through the Google for Startups Cloud Program; Sarvam runs a startup programme offering '6–12 months of credits matched to your scale' through an application form, amount unspecified; Bhashini's Startup Velocity page is a JavaScript app I could not read, so its terms are an open item — and note that bhashini.ai is a private company, not the government platform. Recommendation: use Google Chirp 3: HD for the pilot (one API, Urdu included, and 1 million free characters a month means a 150-character reminder played about 6,600 times costs nothing), keep Sarvam Bulbul v3 as the India-hosted alternative for the four non-Urdu languages, run Indic Parler-TTS only if you want zero per-character cost and can host a GPU, and treat Bhashini as PoC-only until it quotes a price. Human clips in Bengaluru: Karya (sales@karya.in, CMH Road, Bengaluru) is a nonprofit speech-data house working across the 22 official languages that takes custom recording projects with paid workers; Talentrack's Bangalore directory lists 30+ voice artists in Kannada, Tamil, Telugu and Hindi (Urdu not listed) whom you contact directly; studio hire in the city starts around ₹600/hour (Polite Productions, Indiranagar, IndiaMART listing) and Taperfox is a dedicated Bangalore voice-over studio that quotes per project. The market reference for IVR work is ₹400 per prompt with a 20-prompt minimum (a Mumbai artist's 2026 rate card), so 30 prompts in 5 languages is roughly ₹60,000 at that rate, or a fraction of that if a native-speaking team member or Saathi records the fixed prompts in a ₹600/hour studio and TTS handles the variable parts. Open items: an Urdu voice artist in Bengaluru (none of the pages opened lists one), Bhashini's production price, and the size of Sarvam's startup credits.
answers.decision: Default to Google Chirp 3: HD for all five languages during the pilot, with Sarvam Bulbul v3 as the India-hosted fallback for Hindi, Kannada, Tamil and Telugu. Record the fixed greetings and menu prompts with humans — brief Karya or a Talentrack artist, or a native-speaking team member in a ₹600/hour studio — and budget on the ₹400-per-prompt reference.
answers.whoToAsk: Karya (sales@karya.in) and two Talentrack Kannada/Urdu artists for quotes on a 30-prompt, 5-language set; the Bhashini team via the dashboard.bhashini.co.in registration for production pricing and Startup Velocity terms; Sarvam's startup programme form for the credit amount.
